title: OLIVE: Online Low-Rank Incremental Learning for Efficient Adaptive Exoskeletons
summary: Wearable exoskeleton systems hold promise for restoring mobility in individuals with physical impairments, yet most existing controllers rely on static gait policies that lack the ability to adapt to dynamic real-world environments or individual user characteristics. We present \olive (\underline{O}nline \underline{L}ow-rank \underline{I}ncremental Learning for Efficient Adapti\underline{ve} Exoskeletons), a parameter-efficient online adaptation framework that continuously personalizes exoskeleton control during deployment. \olive decomposes the adaptive component of the control policy into a low-rank residual form~$\dW = \At\Bt^\top$ with rank~$r!\ll!\min(d,k)$, reducing online update cost from $\mathcal{O}(dk)$ to $\mathcal{O}(r(d{+}k))$ while preserving the stability of a pretrained base controller~$\Wz$. Parameters are updated via a reward-shaped policy gradient driven purely by on-body sensor feedback (EMG, IMU, vibration), eliminating dependence on offline reference trajectories. A gating mechanism modulates the strength of personalization based on contextual state, and a dynamic rank scheduler adapts the update dimensionality to terrain complexity -- allocating minimal capacity on simple flat terrain and expanding to higher-rank updates on demanding uneven surfaces -- enabling robust performance across diverse activities: flat walking, stair navigation, slopes, and uneven terrain. Experiments on the wearable platform demonstrate that \olive achieves +13, +22, and +15 percentage-point improvements in gait smoothness, effort reduction, and motion stability over the strongest baseline, converging within $\sim$1{,}800 walking steps at 7.4,ms end-to-end latency. Our code implementation is available at https://github.com/FastLM/OLIVE.

AI.tldr: OLIVE is a parameter-efficient online adaptation framework for wearable exoskeletons that uses low-rank residual learning (dW = AtBt^T) to continuously personalize control policies during deployment. It achieves +13-22% improvements in gait smoothness, effort reduction, and motion stability over baselines, converging within ~1,800 steps at 7.4ms latency, by dynamically adjusting update rank based on terrain complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing exoskeleton controllers rely on static gait policies that cannot adapt to dynamic real-world environments or individual user characteristics, limiting their practical deployment.
AI.method: OLIVE decomposes the adaptive control component into a low-rank residual form (dW = AtBt^T with rank r ≪ min(d,k)), reducing online update cost from O(dk) to O(r(d+k)). It uses reward-shaped policy gradient from on-body sensors (EMG, IMU, vibration), a gating mechanism for context-dependent personalization, and a dynamic rank scheduler that allocates minimal capacity on simple terrain and higher-rank updates on uneven surfaces.
AI.result: +13, +22, and +15 percentage-point improvements in gait smoothness, effort reduction, and motion stability over the strongest baseline; converges within ~1,800 walking steps at 7.4ms end-to-end latency.
AI.conclusion: OLIVE enables efficient, real-time personalization of exoskeleton control across diverse activities (flat walking, stairs, slopes, uneven terrain) while maintaining stability of a pretrained base controller, demonstrating practical viability for real-world deployment.

title: A New Quaternion-Joint Cable-Driven Redundant Manipulator Configuration and its Control Through FABRIK and Residual Reinforcement Learning
summary: Robotic arms capable of traversing arbitrary spatial paths, especially in highly obstructed workspaces, are highly desired across several industries. Quaternion-joints have recently empowered a specific class of robotic arms -- cable-driven redundant manipulators -- beyond its prior capabilities. Specifically, quaternion-joints reduce the number of required motors per degree of freedom, paving the way for more compact solutions.An ongoing challenge is that the complexity of the kinematic model of quaternion joints challenges a priori decisions on manipulator configurations and imposes higher computational demands on the control system and its non-linearities amplify all discrepancies between design and physical artifact arising from fabrication imprecision. Here we show a that a 4-segment, 8-joint manipulator can achieve a broader workspace than extant configurations, at lower hardware cost, and that Residual Reinforcement Learning outperforms extant state-of-the-art methods -- specifically, the FABRIK algorithm -- on the control of such manipulator. Our results show that this configuration is more workspace-effective than prior designs, and that Residual Reinforcement Learning outperforms FABRIK by three orders of magnitude on positional and orientational accuracy, effecting precise control of the novel 4-segment, 8-joint manipulator. Additionally, the control implementation is simpler: we describe the complete FABRIK process for control and corresponding learning implementation. Our methodology is applicable to the design of new systems, providing designers with further tools for the development of this class of manipulators and corresponding control systems for novel configurations.

AI.tldr: A 4-segment, 8-joint cable-driven manipulator with quaternion-joints achieves broader workspace at lower hardware cost, and Residual Reinforcement Learning outperforms FABRIK by three orders of magnitude in control accuracy.
AI.motivation: Robotic arms capable of traversing arbitrary spatial paths in highly obstructed workspaces are desired across industries, but quaternion-joint kinematic complexity challenges configuration decisions, increases control computational demands, and amplifies fabrication imprecision.
AI.method: The authors propose a 4-segment, 8-joint quaternion-joint manipulator configuration and apply Residual Reinforcement Learning for control, comparing against the FABRIK algorithm.
AI.result: The 4-segment, 8-joint configuration achieves broader workspace than extant configurations at lower hardware cost. Residual Reinforcement Learning outperforms FABRIK by three orders of magnitude in positional and orientational accuracy.
AI.conclusion: This methodology is applicable to designing new systems, providing tools for developing quaternion-joint manipulators and their control systems for novel configurations.

title: Inverse Manipulation through Symbolic Planning and Residual Operator Learning
summary: Inverting a robotic task requires more than reversing symbolic state transitions or rewinding motor trajectories. In robot manipulation tasks, symbolic inverse plans often fail to fully restore the effects of forward executions under continuous interaction dynamics. We present a hybrid framework for inverse manipulation that derives inverse-skill objectives from STRIPS-like operators automatically extracted from demonstrations through soft geometric predicates. For each extracted operator, we construct an inverse restoration objective that preserves preconditions, restores delete effects, and negates add effects. A task planner first attempts to satisfy this objective using available action primitives. Unresolved symbolic predicates then induce a residual operator learning problem solved through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We evaluate the framework on the ManiSkill3 PushCube task. For a forward pushing skill, the symbolic inverse performs a coarse pick-and-place restoration, while a residual Soft Actor-Critic policy refines the cube pose to satisfy the remaining inverse predicates. Our results show that predicate-derived residual control can turn an approximate symbolic inverse into a physically grounded inverse skill.

AI.tldr: A hybrid framework for inverse manipulation that combines STRIPS-like symbolic planning with residual Reinforcement Learning to ground symbolic inverse plans into physically executable skills, demonstrated on a PushCube task.
AI.motivation: Inverse robotic manipulation tasks cannot be solved by simply reversing symbolic state transitions or motor trajectories, because continuous interaction dynamics cause forward execution effects that symbolic inverse plans fail to fully restore.
AI.method: A two-stage hybrid framework: (1) Extract STRIPS-like operators from demonstrations via soft geometric predicates; construct inverse restoration objectives (preserve preconditions, restore delete effects, negate add effects). (2) A task planner attempts to satisfy the objective using action primitives; unresolved symbolic predicates induce a residual operator learning problem solved via Reinforcement Learning (Soft Actor-Critic).
AI.result: On the ManiSkill3 PushCube task, the symbolic inverse produces a coarse pick-and-place restoration, while the residual SAC policy refines the cube pose to satisfy remaining inverse predicates, turning an approximate symbolic inverse into a physically grounded inverse skill.
AI.conclusion: Predicate-derived residual control bridges the gap between symbolic inverse planning and physically grounded inverse manipulation skills.

title: Efficient Computation of Distance Functions for Navigation Vector Fields in Lie Groups
summary: Vector-field-based methods are widely used for robot control and are often applied to the path-tracking problem. Some vector field approaches require repeatedly computing the distance between the robot configuration and the curve, as well as the corresponding closest point. Recently, vector fields have been extended to Lie Groups. In this case, this computation can be expensive, especially when performed at high control frequencies on embedded platforms. This paper proposes a method for efficiently computing the distance between a point and a curve represented as what is called a G-polynomial curve, which is a curve representation that generalizes polynomial curves to matrix Lie groups. The proposed approach exploits the structure of these curves to reduce the problem to a small number of polynomial root-finding computations. Simulation results show that the method significantly reduces computation time while maintaining accuracy compared to existing optimization-based approaches. Practical formulas are also provided for the case of the group SE(3), and the method is validated experimentally on a robotic manipulator. The methodology is implemented in a computational package, available online.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an efficient method for computing the distance between a point and a G-polynomial curve on matrix Lie groups, reducing the problem to polynomial root-finding, and demonstrates significant computational speedup on SE(3) with experimental validation on a robotic manipulator.
AI.motivation: Vector-field-based robot control methods require repeatedly computing the distance between robot configuration and a curve, which is computationally expensive on Lie groups, especially at high control frequencies on embedded platforms.
AI.method: Exploits the structure of G-polynomial curves (polynomial curves generalized to matrix Lie groups) to reduce the distance computation problem to a small number of polynomial root-finding computations, avoiding expensive optimization-based approaches.
AI.result: Simulations show significant reduction in computation time while maintaining accuracy compared to existing optimization-based methods. Practical formulas for SE(3) are provided, with experimental validation on a robotic manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables efficient real-time distance computation for vector-field-based control on Lie groups, and is released as an open-source computational package.

title: How Far Did They Go? The Persuasive Tactics of Covert LLM Agents in a Discontinued Field Experiment
summary: This study analyzes a publicly released dataset from a discontinued field experiment on Reddit's r/ChangeMyView. The intervention, conducted by unknown, external researchers and halted following ethical backlash, involved undisclosed AI-generated accounts engaging users in live debate. After public disclosure, Reddit authorized moderators to release an archive of the AI-generated comments, creating a rare opportunity to examine how large language models operated in an identity-rich deliberative forum without disclosure. We conduct a structured content analysis of this corpus, evaluating identity performance, authority signaling, alignment strategies, and activation of cognitive heuristics. Identity targeting or adoption appears in over two-thirds of comments, alignment moves and authority claims in nearly all of them, and cognitive-bias triggers -- particularly confirmation bias, representativeness, and availability -- in the large majority. These patterns co-occur systematically, composing a rhetorical architecture calibrated for persuasive efficiency rather than authentic deliberative participation. Compared against human-authored CMV counter-arguments, the agents inverted the typical distribution on every dimension: denser authority use, more adversarial alignment, and heavier reliance on external citation over experiential grounding. In such environments, distinctions between authentic and synthetic epistemic standing grow increasingly opaque -- an asymmetry that disclosure mandates alone cannot address. The results point toward auditing frameworks capable of assessing how AI systems structure credibility, not merely whether they are present.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a dataset from a Reddit field experiment where undisclosed AI-generated accounts engaged in debate on r/ChangeMyView. The authors find that AI comments systematically used identity targeting, authority signaling, and cognitive bias triggers at significantly higher rates than human comments, creating a rhetorical architecture optimized for persuasion rather than authentic deliberation.
AI.motivation: The study was motivated by a rare opportunity to examine how large language models operated in an identity-rich deliberative forum without disclosure, following a controversial field experiment on Reddit's r/ChangeMyView that was halted due to ethical backlash. The researchers aimed to understand the rhetorical strategies employed by undisclosed AI agents in public discourse.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a structured content analysis of the publicly released corpus of AI-generated comments from the r/ChangeMyView experiment, evaluating identity performance, authority signaling, alignment strategies, and activation of cognitive heuristics. They compared these patterns against human-authored counter-arguments from the same forum.
AI.result: Identity targeting appeared in over two-thirds of AI comments; alignment moves and authority claims appeared in nearly all; cognitive-bias triggers were present in the large majority. Compared to human comments, AI agents showed denser authority use, more adversarial alignment, and heavier reliance on external citation over experiential grounding.
AI.conclusion: The rhetorical architecture of AI comments was calibrated for persuasive efficiency rather than authentic deliberative participation. Disclosure mandates alone are insufficient to address the asymmetry between authentic and synthetic epistemic standing. The authors call for auditing frameworks that assess how AI systems structure credibility, not merely whether they are present.

title: VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents
summary: Reusable robot skills are becoming the basic units through which embodied agents turn open-ended instructions into long-horizon physical behavior. We argue that, while foundation models have collapsed the cost of creating these skills, the cost of trusting them has not. Existing skill-evolution loops refine skills through execution feedback, unit tests, environment reward, or LLM self-critique, but these signals provide only trace-level evidence: they show that a skill worked on sampled executions, not that skill-induced plans satisfy temporal safety contracts under untested conditions. We introduce VASO, a framework for verification-guided self-evolution of LLM-generated robot skill contracts. In VASO, each skill is represented as a semantic contract with two coupled interfaces: a formal interface that aligns robot states, observations, and control commands with logical propositions for model checking, and a planner-facing interface that guides executable behavior generation. A model checker first filters logically inconsistent skill contracts, then verifies plans induced by the skill against global and local temporal specifications. When verification fails, VASO translates the counterexample trace into a textual gradient that updates the reusable skill contract while keeping foundation-model weights frozen. On Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks, VASO reaches 97.2% formal-specification compliance using fewer than 100 optimization samples, outperforming execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines. To our knowledge, VASO is the first framework that closes the loop between formal verification and self-evolving LLM-generated skills for physical AI agents: formal counterexamples become optimization feedback for reusable robot skill contracts, rather than merely verifying one-off plans, tuning planner prompts, or fine-tuning model weights.

AI.tldr: VASO is a framework that uses formal verification (model checking) to provide feedback for self-evolving LLM-generated robot skill contracts, achieving 97.2% specification compliance on Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks by translating counterexample traces into textual gradients that update skill contracts without modifying foundation model weights.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-evolution loops rely on execution feedback, unit tests, environment rewards, or LLM self-critique, which provide only trace-level evidence (skill worked on sampled executions) rather than guaranteeing temporal safety contracts under untested conditions. The cost of trusting skills has not collapsed even though the cost of creating them has.
AI.method: VASO represents each skill as a semantic contract with a formal interface (aligning robot states/observations/commands with logical propositions for model checking) and a planner-facing interface (guiding executable behavior). A model checker filters inconsistent contracts and verifies induced plans against temporal specifications. Failed verification produces counterexample traces translated into textual gradients that update the skill contract while keeping foundation-model weights frozen.
AI.result: VASO reaches 97.2% formal-specification compliance on Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks using fewer than 100 optimization samples, outperforming execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines.
AI.conclusion: VASO is the first framework closing the loop between formal verification and self-evolving LLM-generated skills, where formal counterexamples serve as optimization feedback for reusable robot skill contracts rather than merely verifying one-off plans, tuning prompts, or fine-tuning model weights.

title: What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models are typically organized around roles, pipelines, and turn schedules, while the content that agents pass to one another is often left as unconstrained natural language. However, this free-form communication can rapidly inflate token usage, consume the shared context window, and ultimately affect both system performance and inference cost. We analyze five common inter-agent communication strategies across two MAS topologies, finding that no fixed strategy is universally optimal. Instead, effective inter-agent messages consistently preserve action-centered information needed by downstream agents. Building on this, we propose the PACT (Protocolized Action-state Communication and Transmission), which treats inter-agent communication as a public state-update problem and projects each raw agent output into a compact action-state record before it enters shared history. Across different MAS topologies, PACT consistently improves the performance-cost trade-off, achieving comparable or stronger task performance with substantially fewer tokens. The gains extend to production coding harnesses: PACT lifts OpenHands' resolve rate at -10% tokens-per-resolved, and is resolve-neutral on SWE-agent while halving input tokens. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/PACT.

AI.tldr: PACT is a protocol that compresses inter-agent communication in LLM-based multi-agent systems into compact action-state records, improving performance-cost trade-offs across different topologies.
AI.motivation: Free-form natural language communication between LLM-based agents inflates token usage, consumes shared context windows, and degrades both system performance and inference cost.
AI.method: PACT (Protocolized Action-state Communication and Transmission) treats inter-agent communication as a public state-update problem, projecting each raw agent output into a compact action-state record before entering shared history.
AI.result: PACT consistently improves the performance-cost trade-off across MAS topologies; on OpenHands it resolves at -10% tokens-per-resolved, and on SWE-agent it halves input tokens while being resolve-neutral.
AI.conclusion: No fixed inter-agent communication strategy is universally optimal; effective messages preserve action-centered information. PACT provides a principled protocolization approach that achieves comparable or stronger performance with substantially fewer tokens.

title: MoDex: A Diffusion Policy for Sequential Multi-Object Dexterous Grasping
summary: This work addresses sequentially grasping multiple objects with a single dexterous hand without releasing those already held. Most dexterous grasping methods commit all of the hand's degrees of freedom to a single object, underutilizing its dexterity and leaving no redundancy for subsequent grasps. The proposed solution, MoDex, is a diffusion policy that predicts the next gripper pose directly from observations, conditioned on an opposition space and point cloud. The opposition space condition specifies which fingers participate in the current grasp, enabling the gripper to use only a subset of its available degrees of freedom while reserving the remaining degrees of freedom for subsequent grasps. To facilitate sim-to-real transfer, MoDex is trained in two stages: first through imitation learning on expert demonstrations, and subsequently through reinforcement learning fine-tuning, which consistently improves success rates over the pre-trained policy. We evaluate MoDex in simulation on a MuJoCo-based Franka Emika Panda robot equipped with an Allegro Hand and on the corresponding real-world hardware platform. Across both simulation and real-world experiments, MoDex achieves higher success rates than the evaluated learning-based baselines, improving performance by 2.92-17.92% and 6.67-17.78%, respectively. Project page: https://modex2026.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MoDex is a diffusion-based policy for sequential multi-object grasping with a single dexterous hand, using opposition space conditioning to reserve degrees of freedom for subsequent grasps, trained via imitation learning then RL fine-tuning, achieving 2.92-17.92% (sim) and 6.67-17.78% (real) improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing dexterous grasping methods commit all hand DOFs to a single object, underutilizing dexterity and leaving no redundancy for sequential grasping of multiple objects without releasing held ones.
AI.method: MoDex is a diffusion policy that predicts next gripper pose from observations, conditioned on opposition space (specifying which fingers participate) and point cloud. Training: first imitation learning on expert demonstrations, then reinforcement learning fine-tuning for sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: In simulation (MuJoCo Franka Emika Panda + Allegro Hand) and real-world experiments, MoDex outperforms learning-based baselines by 2.92-17.92% and 6.67-17.78% respectively.
AI.conclusion: MoDex effectively enables sequential multi-object grasping by reserving DOFs via opposition space conditioning, with RL fine-tuning consistently improving success rates and enabling sim-to-real transfer.

title: I Know What You Meme, Even If it Emerged Today: Understanding Evolving Memes through Open-World Knowledge Acquisition
summary: Multimodal memes are dynamic and often require up to date background knowledge for interpretation. Existing methods often overlook such knowledge or rely on fixed parametric knowledge of pretrained models that may be incomplete, outdated, or unavailable for emerging memes. We introduce Query Retrieve Conclude, a zero shot framework that identifies missing knowledge, retrieves open web evidence, and synthesizes evidence grounded background knowledge for meme understanding and detection. We also introduce a curated meme understanding benchmark of recent memes from 2024 to 2026 with external background knowledge annotations. Experiments on three meme understanding datasets and five meme detection tasks show that our framework improves knowledge recovery, meme understanding and downstream detection over zero shot baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Query Retrieve Conclude (QRC), a zero-shot framework that identifies missing knowledge for multimodal memes, retrieves open web evidence, and synthesizes background knowledge to improve meme understanding and detection. It also introduces a new benchmark of 2024-2026 memes with external knowledge annotations, showing improvements over zero-shot baselines across three understanding datasets and five detection tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing meme understanding methods overlook dynamic, up-to-date background knowledge or rely on fixed parametric knowledge of pretrained models, which can be incomplete, outdated, or unavailable for emerging memes.
AI.method: Query Retrieve Conclude (QRC) — a zero-shot framework with three stages: (1) Query: identifies missing knowledge needed to interpret a meme; (2) Retrieve: fetches open web evidence; (3) Conclude: synthesizes evidence-grounded background knowledge for meme understanding and detection.
AI.result: QRC improves knowledge recovery, meme understanding, and downstream detection over zero-shot baselines, validated on three meme understanding datasets and five meme detection tasks. A new benchmark of memes from 2024-2026 with external background knowledge annotations was also created.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic retrieval of open-web background knowledge is effective for understanding and detecting emerging multimodal memes, outperforming reliance on fixed parametric knowledge alone.

title: Learning from Demonstrations over Riemannian Manifolds using Neural ODEs: An Extended Abstract
summary: Learning from demonstratins (LfD) is usually performed over Euclidean spaces, while the robot state, e.g. orientation, naturally evolves over curved spaces. Therefore, to ensure natural, complex motion generation, we investigate learning from demonstrations over Riemannian manifolds that are capable of encoding both position and orientation data. Here, geodesic paths provide for natural motion between two arbitrary points within the manifold. We propose to numerically estimate geodesics via neural ordinary differential equations, mitigating large computational overhead of existing approaches. Finally, these geodesics can be decoded back into the original task space before deploying on the robot. In this extended abstract, we discuss the architecture of our framework, provide some initial insights from our simulation experiments, including comparison to other geodesic computation mechanisms, and discuss the challenges and prospects for future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes learning robot demonstrations over Riemannian manifolds to encode position and orientation, using neural ODEs to efficiently estimate geodesics for natural motion generation.
AI.motivation: Standard LfD operates over Euclidean spaces, but robot state (e.g., orientation) naturally evolves over curved (non-Euclidean) spaces, requiring a manifold-aware approach for natural motion.
AI.method: The framework numerically estimates geodesics (natural motion paths on manifolds) via neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs), reducing computational overhead compared to existing geodesic computation methods, then decodes them into the original task space for robot deployment.
AI.result: Initial simulation experiments provide insights and comparisons to other geodesic computation mechanisms, though this is an extended abstract with preliminary results.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables encoding both position and orientation in a geometrically sound manner with improved computational efficiency; future work is needed to address remaining challenges.

title: GITCO: Gated Inference-Time Context Optimization in TSFMs
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: Patch-based Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) suffer from context poisoning: structurally anomalous patches capture disproportionate attention and silently degrade zero-shot forecast quality. We propose improving TSFM accuracy at inference time by optimizing the input context rather than modifying model weights. We present GITCO (Gated Inference-Time Context Optimization), a lightweight three-component framework: Gate, Router, and Critic that selectively identifies and suppresses harmful patches without any parameter updates. Evaluated on TimesFM 2.5 across 53 GIFT-Eval datasets under K-fold cross-validation, GITCO achieves an average +1.95% MASE reduction on TimesFM 2.5 while capturing 89.9% of the improvement upper bound. We introduce context sensitivity profiles as a new characterizable property of TSFMs: the mapping from time series meta-features to expected accuracy improvement under inference-time context intervention, shaped jointly by model architecture and the statistical structure of the data.

AI.tldr: GITCO improves zero-shot forecasting in patch-based Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) by identifying and suppressing harmful patches at inference time via a lightweight Gate-Router-Critic framework, achieving +1.95% MASE reduction on TimesFM 2.5 without model updates, and introduces context sensitivity profiles to characterize TSFMs.
AI.motivation: Patch-based TSFMs suffer from context poisoning, where structurally anomalous patches disproportionately degrade zero-shot forecast quality, motivating a need for inference-time mitigation without modifying model weights.
AI.method: GITCO (Gated Inference-Time Context Optimization): a three-component framework (Gate, Router, Critic) that selectively identifies and suppresses harmful patches at inference time, requiring no parameter updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on TimesFM 2.5 across 53 GIFT-Eval datasets under K-fold cross-validation, GITCO achieves an average +1.95% MASE reduction while capturing 89.9% of the improvement upper bound.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time context optimization effectively improves TSFM accuracy; context sensitivity profiles are introduced as a new property characterizing the mapping from time series meta-features to expected improvement under context intervention.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Navigation
summary: This work introduces a hybrid deep learning approach integrated with an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) to enhance pose estimation accuracy in Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) for autonomous navigation. The proposed model employs a Vision Transformer (ViT) network to effectively capture temporal dependencies from inertial measurement unit (IMU) data and utilizes a Multiscale Convolutional Neural Network (MCNN) to learn optical flow-based motion cues from visual data. An adaptive sensor fusion module dynamically weights IMU and visual features by leveraging estimated uncertainty, thus improving robustness in diverse and challenging environmental conditions. Additionally, a novel uncertainty-aware loss function is proposed to explicitly incorporate prediction uncertainty into the learning process, enabling robust and accurate navigation under noisy, incomplete, or unreliable sensor inputs. Comprehensive evaluations of the KITTI dataset demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline approaches, achieving superior performance in terms of Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE). The lightweight and computationally efficient model processes data at 155 FPS on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, making it highly suitable for deployment in resource-constrained autonomous systems.

AI.tldr: A hybrid deep learning + UKF framework using Vision Transformer for IMU data, Multiscale CNN for optical flow, adaptive uncertainty-aware sensor fusion, and a novel uncertainty-aware loss function achieves state-of-the-art pose estimation on KITTI (155 FPS on A100 GPU).
AI.motivation: To enhance pose estimation accuracy and robustness in Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) under challenging environmental conditions with noisy, incomplete, or unreliable sensor inputs, while maintaining computational efficiency for resource-constrained autonomous systems.
AI.method: (1) ViT network for temporal dependencies from IMU data; (2) MCNN for optical flow-based motion cues from visual data; (3) Adaptive sensor fusion module with uncertainty estimation for dynamic weighting of IMU and visual features; (4) Uncertainty-aware loss function incorporating prediction uncertainty into learning; (5) Integrated with UKF for state estimation.
AI.result: Outperforms baseline approaches on KITTI dataset in ATE and RPE metrics; achieves 155 FPS on NVIDIA A100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight, uncertainty-aware hybrid model significantly improves VIO pose estimation accuracy and robustness, suitable for deployment in resource-constrained autonomous navigation systems.

title: Uncertainty Aware Functional Behavior Prediction and Material Fatigue Assessment for Circular Factory
comment: 27 pages, submitted to the Journal of Manufacturing Systems' special issue about circular factories, the manuscript is under review
summary: Returned products in circular factories re-enter production with heterogeneous degradation states, usage histories, and remaining capability. Reuse cannot be decided from the current inspection alone, because future function fulfillment and component integrity may evolve differently under the next service scenario. Existing PHM approaches support degradation prediction, but often target fixed operating conditions or isolated component benchmarks, while material-fatigue assessment is rarely linked to system-level functional prognosis. This paper addresses this gap for an angle grinder by combining uncertainty-aware functional prediction with component-level fatigue assessment in an instance-specific reliability workflow. The proposed framework combines the current tool state with recent force--torque usage windows. A convolutional encoder extracts loading patterns from spindle forces and shaft torque, and an LSTM backbone predicts nine functional variables as Gaussian mean and variance estimates. In parallel, the same loading history is translated into output-shaft fatigue information through finite-element-supported stress reconstruction, S--N/Miner damage evaluation with Haibach extension, and Paris-law crack-growth analysis. A streaming replay algorithm consolidates both branches into functional, material, and system reliability trajectories. Held-out tests show mean \(2\%\)-tolerance accuracy of 0.9652 across nine outputs. Thermal variables are predicted near-perfectly, while drive motor current and load speed remain the most demanding dynamic outputs, with \(R^2\) values of 0.9750 and 0.9924. Torque history is especially important for these variables, and the conventional LSTM outperforms GRU and xLSTM in the short-history setting. AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework that combines uncertainty-aware functional prediction with component-level fatigue assessment for circular factories, using a convolutional encoder and LSTM to predict functional variables and finite-element fatigue analysis, achieving high accuracy on an angle grinder case study.
AI.motivation: Returned products in circular factories have heterogeneous degradation, and reuse decisions cannot rely on current inspection alone since future function fulfillment and component integrity depend on next-service scenarios. Existing PHM approaches lack integration of material-fatigue assessment with system-level functional prognosis.
AI.method: A framework combining convolutional encoder (extracting loading patterns from spindle force and shaft torque) with LSTM backbone predicting nine functional variables as Gaussian mean/variance estimates. Parallel finite-element-supported stress reconstruction, S-N/Miner damage evaluation with Haibach extension, and Paris-law crack-growth analysis provide fatigue information. A streaming replay algorithm consolidates both branches.
AI.result: Mean 2%-tolerance accuracy of 0.9652 across nine outputs. Thermal variables predicted near-perfectly; drive motor current (R²=0.9750) and load speed (R²=0.9924) are the most demanding dynamic outputs. Conventional LSTM outperforms GRU and xLSTM in short-history settings.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively integrates functional prediction with fatigue assessment for instance-specific reliability, with torque history being especially important for dynamic variables. Reliability calibration is most informative for drive motor current.

title: FlowPRO: Reward-Free Reinforced Fine-Tuning of Flow-Matching VLAs via Proximalized Preference Optimization
summary: Post-training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models into policies that can be reliably deployed on real robots remains a major bottleneck. SFT and DAgger exploit failure signals only indirectly, and reward-based RL is bottlenecked by the difficulty of real-world reward design and of training reliable critics. We present FlowPRO, a reward-free offline reinforced fine-tuning framework for flow-matching VLAs. Algorithmically, we propose RPRO (Robotic Flow-matching Proximalized Preference Optimization), a preference-optimization objective tailored to the flow-matching action head of VLA models. RPRO pairs a contrastive optimizer with an explicit proximal regularizer that anchors the absolute magnitude of the implicit reward, thereby eliminating the reward-hacking failure mode of plain Flow-DPO. On the data side, a teleoperated intervention-and-rollback paradigm produces naturally paired positive and negative trajectories $(τ^w, τ^l)$ on a real robot from a single operator action; a Smooth Interpolation procedure, combined with batch mixing, then converts these sparse corrections into dense per-state supervision while preserving the base policy's capabilities. On four long-horizon bimanual tasks, FlowPRO attains the highest success rate, outperforming four representative baselines, and ablations confirm the contribution of each loss component.

AI.tldr: FlowPRO is a reward-free offline reinforced fine-tuning framework for flow-matching VLAs that uses a preference-optimization objective (RPRO) with proximal regularization and a teleoperated intervention-and-rollback data collection paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art success rates on long-horizon bimanual tasks.
AI.motivation: Post-training VLA models for reliable real-robot deployment remains a major bottleneck: SFT and DAgger only indirectly exploit failure signals, while reward-based RL suffers from difficult real-world reward design and unreliable critic training.
AI.method: FlowPRO: (1) RPRO objective - preference optimization with a contrastive optimizer plus an explicit proximal regularizer to anchor implicit reward magnitude and prevent reward hacking; (2) Intervention-and-rollback data paradigm for naturally paired positive/negative trajectories; (3) Smooth Interpolation with batch mixing to convert sparse corrections into dense per-state supervision.
AI.result: On four long-horizon bimanual tasks, FlowPRO achieves the highest success rate, outperforming four representative baselines. Ablations confirm the contribution of each loss component.
AI.conclusion: FlowPRO demonstrates effective reward-free offline RL fine-tuning for flow-matching VLAs, eliminating reward-hacking via proximal regularization and enabling practical real-robot policy improvement without reward engineering.

title: SentinelBench: A Benchmark for Long-Running Monitoring Agents
summary:
AI agents are increasingly asked to carry out work that spans minutes, hours, or longer. Yet the default model of agent behavior is continuous action: issuing tool calls, refreshing pages, searching for alternatives, or otherwise trying to force progress. This is the wrong approach for many long-running tasks, which are better served by a strategy of sustained attention. Instead, agents should monitor an environment, notice when an external event makes progress possible, then respond promptly without wasting resources while waiting. To measure progress on this class of tasks, we introduce SentinelBench, an open-source benchmark for time-evolving monitoring tasks.
  SentinelBench contains 100 tasks across 10 synthetic web environments, including email, calendars, finance, professional networking, and entertainment. Each environment exposes a live web interface and replays a scripted sequence of events, requiring agents to navigate and reason about web pages whose state shifts underfoot. SentinelBench measures task completion, reaction time, and resource use, exposing the tradeoff between responsiveness and cost. We report results across three models and two browser-agent harnesses, establishing performance baselines for future comparison and demonstrating how agent design choices can dramatically impact key metrics. Together, these results show that SentinelBench distinguishes meaningful differences in agent behavior.

AI.tldr: SentinelBench is an open-source benchmark for evaluating AI agents on time-evolving monitoring tasks, where agents must observe environments and react to external events rather than continuously acting. It contains 100 tasks across 10 synthetic web environments, measuring task completion, reaction time, and resource usage tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents default to continuous action (e.g., issuing tool calls, refreshing pages) which is inefficient for long-running tasks. A strategy of sustained attention—monitoring environments and responding to external events—is better suited for such tasks, but no benchmark exists to measure progress on this class of problems.
AI.method: SentinelBench provides 100 tasks across 10 synthetic web environments (email, calendars, finance, professional networking, entertainment) with live web interfaces that replay scripted event sequences. It measures task completion, reaction time, and resource usage to capture the responsiveness-cost tradeoff. Experiments were conducted across three models and two browser-agent harnesses.
AI.result: The benchmark establishes performance baselines for future comparison and demonstrates that agent design choices significantly impact key metrics, showing SentinelBench effectively distinguishes meaningful differences in agent behavior across different models and harnesses.
AI.conclusion: SentinelBench successfully captures the responsiveness-cost tradeoff in time-evolving monitoring tasks, enabling systematic evaluation of agent behavior for long-running tasks where sustained attention is preferable to continuous action.

title: Learning Contact Representation for Leg Odometry
summary: The estimation of odometry in legged robots depends on the assumption that the velocity of the foot with respect to the world remains zero during the stance phase. Feedback for the main body velocity is derived from the kinematic serial chain of the feet making accurate leg phase detection is a critical subproblem. A considerable number of studies employ ground reaction force sensors mounted at the tip of the foot to classify, yet these sensors may not be universally available for all legged robots. Additionally, these sensors are often unresponsive to unaccounted disturbances, such as slippage, while the foot remains in contact with the ground. In this study, we propose a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection that utilizes the standard sensor set of joint encoders without reliance on force sensor augmentations. We employ learned representations to model the stance and swing phases probabilistically. The experimental results obtained confirm the efficacy of the proposed self-supervised contact detector. Our framework exhibited superior performance in comparison to supervised methods which necessitate sensor set augmentation and labeling, as well as baseline probabilistic approaches. Additionally, we make our code available to the public.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection in legged robots using only joint encoder data, without requiring force sensors. It models stance and swing phases probabilistically and outperforms supervised methods and baseline probabilistic approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing contact detection methods rely on force sensors at the foot, which are not universally available on all legged robots and fail under disturbances like slippage. The authors aim to develop a method using only standard joint encoders.
AI.method: The authors propose a self-supervised representation learning framework that learns from joint encoder data without requiring force sensor augmentations. Learned representations are used to probabilistically model stance and swing phases.
AI.result: The self-supervised contact detector demonstrates superior performance compared to supervised methods requiring sensor augmentation and labeling, as well as baseline probabilistic approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed self-supervised framework is effective for contact detection in legged robots using only joint encoders, eliminating the need for force sensors, and the code is made publicly available.

title: An interpretable and trustworthy AI framework for large-scale longitudinal structure-pain association studies using data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI)
summary: Purpose: To develop an interpretable and trustworthy AI framework that combines deep learning based MRI Osteoarthritis Knee Score (MOAKS) prediction with interpretable statistical modeling to study structure-pain relationships at scale using data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI). Materials and Methods: We first developed a deep learning framework to predict MOAKS features directly from knee MRIs and incorporated conformal prediction to provide prediction uncertainty quantification. This uncertainty-aware strategy enables explicit filtering of model outputs, retaining only high-confidence MOAKS predictions at the knee level. Second, we applied a longitudinal latent class mixed model (LCMM) to examine associations between key structural abnormalities and four complementary knee pain measurements. Results: Among the three MRI-defined abnormalities (i.e., bone marrow lesions (BML), cartilage loss (CART), and meniscal extrusion (ME)), our framework substantially improved the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and some other metrics. For example, MCC increased from 0.69 to 0.91 for BML, from 0.45 to 0.80 for CART, and from 0.59 to 0.89 for ME. Using these high-confidence predictions, we expanded the sample size to 2,175 knees for the LCMM analysis. Two distinct pain trajectories were identified (rapid and stable pain progression). The estimated odds ratios (95% CI) for the rapid progression group were 1.62 (1.12-2.35) for BML, 1.83 (1.24-2.70) for CART loss, and 2.50 (1.75-3.57) for ME. Conclusion: These results highlight the importance of these structural abnormalities as risk factors for pain and functional progression in osteoarthritis.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework with conformal prediction uncertainty quantification was developed to predict MOAKS features from knee MRIs, enabling high-confidence structural abnormality assessment. Using these predictions in a longitudinal latent class mixed model across 2,175 knees, the study identified that bone marrow lesions (OR=1.62), cartilage loss (OR=1.83), and meniscal extrusion (OR=2.50) are significant risk factors for rapid pain progression in knee osteoarthritis.
AI.motivation: To develop an interpretable and trustworthy AI framework combining deep learning-based MOAKS prediction with interpretable statistical modeling to study structure-pain relationships in knee osteoarthritis at scale using OAI data.
AI.method: 1) Deep learning framework to predict MOAKS features from knee MRIs with conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification, filtering only high-confidence predictions. 2) Longitudinal latent class mixed model (LCMM) to examine associations between structural abnormalities (BML, cartilage loss, meniscal extrusion) and four complementary knee pain measurements.
AI.result: MCC improved substantially (BML: 0.69→0.91, CART: 0.45→0.80, ME: 0.59→0.89). Expanded to 2,175 knees for LCMM. Two pain trajectories identified (rapid and stable). Odds ratios for rapid progression: BML=1.62 (1.12-2.35), CART loss=1.83 (1.24-2.70), ME=2.50 (1.75-3.57).
AI.conclusion: Structural abnormalities (BML, cartilage loss, meniscal extrusion) are significant risk factors for rapid pain progression in knee osteoarthritis, with meniscal extrusion showing the strongest association.

title: Auditing Demonstration Curation Metrics: Action-Only Scorers Fail on the Structural Defects That Degrade Imitation Policies
summary: Imitation-learning policies inherit the quality of the demonstrations they are trained on, and a growing set of curation metrics promise to score and filter low-quality demonstrations automatically. These metrics are each validated on different data with different protocols, so it is unclear which of them actually identify the demonstrations that harm a policy. We build a controlled testbed in which demonstration defects are injected with known type, and audit seven curation metrics along two axes: how well each separates defective from clean demonstrations, and whether training a behavior-cloning policy on each metric's curated subset improves task success. We study two defect regimes. Subtle perturbations (correlated action noise, tremor, truncation) are detectable by multivariate outlier scoring and, once removed, recover the full downstream gap. Structural errors, where the demonstration executes a wrong action at a key moment, are invisible to every action-only metric we test, and two of them are inverted: they score defective demonstrations as higher quality and, used for curation, tend to leave the policy at or below the uncurated baseline rather than above it. Only metrics that examine the state trajectory detect structural errors, and even the best of them recovers just a third of the downstream gap. High detection accuracy does not guarantee downstream improvement. We release the testbed and all curation implementations.

AI.tldr: This paper builds a controlled testbed to evaluate seven demonstration curation metrics by injecting known defects (subtle perturbations and structural errors) and measuring how well they separate defective from clean demonstrations and whether their curated subsets improve behavior-cloning policy success.
AI.motivation: Existing curation metrics lack standardized evaluation protocols, making it unclear which metrics effectively identify harmful low-quality demonstrations for imitation learning.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled testbed with known defect injection (subtle perturbations: correlated action noise, tremor, truncation; structural errors: wrong action at key moments), then audit seven curation metrics along detection accuracy and downstream policy improvement axes using behavior cloning.
AI.result: Subtle perturbations are detectable by multivariate outlier scoring and removal recovers full downstream gap. Structural errors are invisible to action-only metrics; two are inverted (score defective higher). Only state-trajectory metrics detect structural errors, but the best recovers only one-third of the downstream gap. High detection accuracy does not guarantee downstream improvement.
AI.conclusion: Action-only metrics fail on structural errors, which require state-based trajectory analysis; curation decisions should prioritize downstream policy improvement over detection accuracy alone.

title: Synthetic Contrastive Reasoning for Multi-Table Q&A
summary: Multi-table question answering requires models to retrieve relevant evidence, link schemas, and perform compositional reasoning across relational tables. Existing multi-table Q&A resources typically provide questions and final answers but lack reasoning supervision that explains how answers are derived. To address this gap, we construct a synthetic contrastive reasoning-trace dataset for MMQA by generating validated positive traces and plausible negative traces with heterogeneous LLMs. We then use the resulting preference pairs to fine-tune open-weight LLMs with Contrastive Preference Optimization (CPO). Across Qwen3-14B, Mistral-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, CPO achieves absolute average improvements over Q&A supervised fine-tuning ranging from 9.7%-16.3%, with gains up to 21 percentage points on MMQA. Ablations show that heterogeneous positive and negative trace generators strengthen the contrastive signal, and automated as well as human evaluations indicate that the generated pairs are largely faithful, coherent, and meaningfully contrastive.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a synthetic contrastive reasoning-trace dataset for multi-table QA, generated by heterogeneous LLMs, and uses Contrastive Preference Optimization (CPO) to fine-tune LLMs, achieving 9.7%-16.3% average improvements over standard supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-table QA resources provide questions and final answers but lack reasoning supervision (i.e., traces explaining how answers are derived), limiting the ability to train models on compositional reasoning across tables.
AI.method: Construct a synthetic contrastive reasoning-trace dataset by generating validated positive traces and plausible negative traces using heterogeneous LLMs, then fine-tune open-weight LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Mistral-8B, Llama-3.1-8B) with Contrastive Preference Optimization (CPO).
AI.result: CPO achieves absolute average improvements of 9.7%-16.3% over Q&A supervised fine-tuning, with gains up to 21 percentage points on MMQA. Ablations confirm heterogeneous trace generators strengthen contrastive signals, and evaluations show traces are faithful, coherent, and meaningfully contrastive.
AI.conclusion: Using synthetic contrastive reasoning traces with CPO significantly improves multi-table QA performance across diverse LLM architectures, and the generated preference pairs are of high quality for training.

title: Discrete-WAM: Unified Discrete Vision-Action Token Editing for World-Policy Learning
summary: Autonomous driving requires reasoning about how ego actions shape the evolution of the surrounding world. However, most end-to-end methods rely on direct state-to-action mappings, capturing correlations without explicitly modeling action-conditioned dynamics. Conversely, continuous-latent world models often lack compositional structure for causal reasoning across counterfactual futures. We introduce Discrete-WAM, a unified latent vision-action world policy that represents future visual states and ego actions as aligned discrete tokens, enabling compositional causal reasoning across alternative futures. Built upon this unified discrete alignment, Discrete-WAM establishes a shared discrete diffusion framework with unified generative tasks, jointly formulating world modeling, world-action policy, and hierarchical decision-enabled policy, supporting compositional generalization across diverse driving scenarios. Experiments on large-scale autonomous-driving benchmarks show that Discrete-WAM achieves competitive performance while supporting controllable generation and counterfactual reasoning, offering a principled path toward more reliable decision-making.

AI.tldr: Discrete-WAM aligns future visual states and ego actions as discrete tokens within a shared diffusion framework, enabling unified world modeling, action policy, and hierarchical decision-making for compositional causal reasoning and counterfactual reasoning in autonomous driving.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end autonomous driving methods rely on direct state-to-action mappings that fail to model action-conditioned dynamics, while continuous-latent world models lack compositional structure for causal reasoning across counterfactual futures.
AI.method: Discrete-WAM represents future visual states and ego actions as aligned discrete tokens, using a shared discrete diffusion framework that jointly formulates world modeling, world-action policy, and hierarchical decision-enabled policy for compositional generalization.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance on large-scale autonomous-driving benchmarks while supporting controllable generation and counterfactual reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Offers a principled path toward more reliable decision-making in autonomous driving through unified discrete token alignment and compositional causal reasoning.

title: Stability vs. Manipulability: Evaluating Robustness Under Post-Decision Interaction in LLM Judges
comment: Accepted at ACL 2026 GEM (Generation, Evaluation and Metrics) Workshop
summary: LLM-as-judge evaluation is widely used in benchmarking pipelines, where model outputs are compared and ranked using automated evaluators. These pipelines typically assume that judgments are stable properties of fixed inputs. We show that this assumption does not hold under interaction. We study post-decision manipulability: the extent to which an evaluation outcome can be altered through subsequent conversation with the judge after an initial decision has been made. Across controlled experiments on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval, we find that LLM judges are highly stable under repeated and neutral reevaluation, yet become substantially reversible under targeted post-decision challenge. An anti-baseline challenge protocol shows that stable judgments can be overturned through motivated interaction, while a counterbalanced target-validation protocol separates this reversibility from net target-directed steering. These reversals have practical consequences: they can degrade agreement with human preferences, shift benchmark rankings, and produce harmful evaluation changes despite high self-reported confidence. Authority framing is especially destabilizing, and revised judgments are often accompanied by low-overlap justifications, suggesting post hoc rationalization rather than reliable error correction. We introduce the Evaluation Robustness Score (ERS) to quantify interactional robustness by combining reversal susceptibility with counterbalanced directional effects. Our findings identify post-decision interaction as a distinct failure mode for LLM-as-judge evaluation and motivate evaluation protocols that measure not only static agreement, but robustness under challenge.

AI.tldr: LLM judges are stable under repeated neutral evaluation but can be substantially reversed through targeted post-decision challenge, revealing a distinct failure mode in LLM-as-judge evaluation pipelines.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-as-judge evaluation pipelines assume judgments are stable properties of fixed inputs, but this assumption may not hold under interaction. The authors investigate post-decision manipulability—whether evaluation outcomes can be altered through subsequent conversation with the judge after an initial decision.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval using (1) an anti-baseline challenge protocol to test judgment reversal under motivated interaction, (2) a counterbalanced target-validation protocol to separate reversibility from net target-directed steering, and (3) introduction of the Evaluation Robustness Score (ERS) to quantify interactional robustness.
AI.result: LLM judges are highly stable under repeated neutral reevaluation but become substantially reversible under targeted post-decision challenge. Reversals degrade agreement with human preferences, shift benchmark rankings, and produce harmful evaluation changes despite high self-reported confidence. Authority framing is especially destabilizing, and revised judgments show low-overlap justifications suggesting post hoc rationalization.
AI.conclusion: Post-decision interaction is a distinct failure mode for LLM-as-judge evaluation. Evaluation protocols should measure not only static agreement but also robustness under challenge. The ERS provides a quantified metric for this interactional robustness.

title: Safe Embodied AI for Long-horizon Tasks: A Cross-layer Analysis of Robotic Manipulation
summary: Embodied AI systems are increasingly expected to reason and act over extended horizons in physical environments. This growing capability brings safety to the foreground, because failures in the physical world can harm people, damage objects, and disrupt workplaces. Although safe embodied AI has attracted substantial attention, the literature remains fragmented across planning, policy design, and runtime execution. Long-horizon robotic manipulation is a particularly revealing anchor domain for this problem because semantic misgrounding, subtask-level error propagation, execution drift, and contact-rich physical risk can accumulate within the same closed-loop system. This survey therefore provides a structured review of safety in long-horizon robotic manipulation from an embodied AI perspective. We organize the literature by intervention locus, covering planning-time, policy-time, and execution-time safety, and we analyze the strength of the evidence that each line of work provides, distinguishing formal guarantees, statistical support, and empirical safety heuristics. This framework clarifies the distinct roles of backbone capability papers, direct safety mechanisms, and benchmark or evaluation studies, while exposing where current safety claims are well supported and where they remain indirect. We identify persistent gaps, including limited evidence for policy-time safety, weak formal support for contact-rich long-horizon manipulation, immature uncertainty-triggered intervention, and a shortage of manipulation-specific safety benchmarks. We conclude by outlining research directions for cross-layer assurance, evaluation design, and safer deployment of long-horizon robotic agents in real-world settings.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews safety in long-horizon robotic manipulation from an embodied AI perspective, organizing literature by intervention locus (planning-time, policy-time, execution-time), analyzing evidence strength, and identifying gaps such as limited policy-time safety evidence, weak formal guarantees for contact-rich manipulation, and shortage of safety benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI systems operating over extended horizons in physical environments pose safety risks (harm to people, objects, workplaces). The literature on safe embodied AI is fragmented across planning, policy design, and runtime execution, motivating a structured survey to consolidate and evaluate existing work.
AI.method: The authors organize the literature by intervention locus (planning-time, policy-time, execution-time safety), analyze evidence strength (formal guarantees, statistical support, empirical safety heuristics), and distinguish backbone capability papers, direct safety mechanisms, and benchmark/evaluation studies.
AI.result: Identified persistent gaps: limited evidence for policy-time safety, weak formal support for contact-rich long-horizon manipulation, immature uncertainty-triggered intervention, and shortage of manipulation-specific safety benchmarks. The framework clarifies where safety claims are well supported vs. indirect.
AI.conclusion: Outlines research directions for cross-layer assurance, evaluation design, and safer deployment of long-horizon robotic agents in real-world settings.

title: Residual Modeling for High-Fidelity Learned Compression of Scientific Data
summary:
Lossy compression is essential for massive spatiotemporal data from scientific simulations. Learned compressors can achieve high compression ratios at moderate accuracy targets, but their aggregate reconstruction losses do not guarantee accuracy for each block. Existing Guaranteed Autoencoder (GAE) methods add a per-block residual correction by retaining SVD/PCA-style coefficients until the target is met. This works at moderate tolerances, but in the high-fidelity regime with block-level NRMSE from 10^-6 to 10^-4, the number of retained coefficients grows quickly and the correction stream dominates the total rate.
  We propose a residual-centric view: the learned residual is structurally different from the original scientific field and should be coded with a representation designed for that residual. We introduce two residual coders. LBRC is a deterministic, training-free pipeline that adaptively quantizes the learned residual to the target NRMSE and losslessly encodes the resulting integer residual using 3D Lorenzo differencing, zigzag mapping, bit-plane coding, and entropy coding. NGLR adds a causal neural predictor that outputs a normalized bias for an integer-rounded Lorenzo prediction in the same deterministic integer pipeline, reducing the entropy of the remaining residual code while preserving deterministic decoding. The predictor weights are serialized and counted in the bitstream.
  Across E3SM, JHTDB, and ERA5 at block-level NRMSE targets from 10^-6 to 10^-4, LBRC improves compression ratio over GAE by 30-60% and is broadly competitive with SZ. NGLR adds a further 10-40% over LBRC and outperforms SZ in the evaluated high-fidelity regime. These results show that residual representations tailored to learned-compressor residuals can preserve the advantage of learned compression when global residual correction becomes rate-dominant.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two residual coders (LBRC and NGLR) that replace the SVD/PCA-based residual correction in Guaranteed Autoencoder methods for scientific data compression. These methods are designed specifically for the learned residual and achieve 30-60% (LBRC) and 10-40% additional (NGLR) compression ratio improvements over GAE at high-fidelity regimes (NRMSE 10^-6 to 10^-4), outperforming SZ across E3SM, JHTDB, and ERA5 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing Guaranteed Autoencoder (GAE) methods use per-block residual correction via SVD/PCA coefficients, but in high-fidelity regimes (NRMSE 10^-6 to 10^-4), the number of retained coefficients grows rapidly and the correction stream dominates the total rate, making the approach inefficient.
AI.method: The paper introduces a residual-centric approach: (1) LBRC (Learned Block Residual Coder) - deterministic, training-free pipeline that adaptively quantizes the learned residual to target NRMSE and losslessly encodes using 3D Lorenzo differencing, zigzag mapping, bit-plane coding, and entropy coding. (2) NGLR (Neural Guided Lossless Residual coder) - adds a causal neural predictor that outputs normalized bias for integer-rounded Lorenzo prediction, reducing entropy of remaining residual code while preserving deterministic decoding.
AI.result: LBRC improves compression ratio over GAE by 30-60% and is competitive with SZ. NGLR adds 10-40% improvement over LBRC and outperforms SZ in the high-fidelity regime across E3SM, JHTDB, and ERA5 datasets at block-level NRMSE targets from 10^-6 to 10^-4.
AI.conclusion: Residual representations tailored to learned-compressor residuals can preserve the advantage of learned compression when global residual correction becomes rate-dominant.

title: Preserving Full 6-DOF Actuation Under Abrupt Total Rotor Failures: Passive Fault-Tolerant Flight Control Using a Biaxial-Tilt Hexacopter
summary: Conventional multirotors suffer from a rapid collapse of attainable wrench space (AWS) under abrupt total rotor failures, rendering full 6-DOF recovery physically impossible. This paper addresses passive fault-tolerant flight of a biaxial-tilt overactuated hexacopter (BTO) under abrupt total rotor failures that are a priori unknown to the controller. The control design and analysis focus on representative abrupt rotor-failure cases for which the post-failure system remains fully actuated, while no explicit fault detection, isolation, or fault-mode switching is assumed. First, we extend the inscribed-sphere metric of the AWS by incorporating the transient-wrench-jump term, enabling quantitative feasibility assessment under up to three simultaneous rotor failures and benchmarking against uniaxial-tilt and coplanar hexacopters. Second, we develop two computationally efficient passive schemes without relying on fault detection or online optimization. One scheme operates at the controller layer by combining a high-order fully actuated (HOFA) controller with a linear extended state observer (LESO) for lumped-disturbance rejection. The other scheme operates at the allocator layer by using model-reference adaptive control allocation with momentum-based wrench estimation to compensate for control-allocation biases. Simulations and flight experiments validate stable hovering and 6-DOF trajectory tracking under single and multiple rotor failures. Further systematic comparisons confirm that the BTO provides larger recovery margins than uniaxial-tilt and coplanar designs. Additional onboard-sensor-only experiments, including indoor tracking under wind disturbance, outdoor tracking under extreme conditions, narrow-frame traversal, and contact-based aerial writing, further validate the robustness of the proposed framework in complex operational environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents passive fault-tolerant control for a biaxial-tilt overactuated hexacopter (BTO) under unknown abrupt total rotor failures. Two computationally efficient passive schemes (HOFA+LESO at controller layer and MRAC allocation with momentum-based wrench estimation at allocator layer) are developed without fault detection or online optimization. The inscribed-sphere AWS metric is extended with transient-wrench-jump term for feasibility assessment. Experiments validate stable 6-DOF flight under multiple rotor failures, with BTO outperforming uniaxial-tilt and coplanar designs.
AI.motivation: Conventional multirotors suffer rapid collapse of attainable wrench space under abrupt total rotor failures, making full 6-DOF recovery physically impossible. This motivates developing passive fault-tolerant control for BTO hexacopters that can handle unknown rotor failures without explicit fault detection or mode switching.
AI.method: (1) Extended inscribed-sphere metric of AWS by incorporating transient-wrench-jump term for feasibility assessment. (2) Two passive schemes: (a) HOFA controller with LESO for disturbance rejection at controller layer; (b) Model-reference adaptive control allocation with momentum-based wrench estimation at allocator layer. Both are computationally efficient and require no fault detection or online optimization.
AI.result: Validated stable hovering and 6-DOF trajectory tracking under single and multiple rotor failures via simulations and flight experiments. BTO provides larger recovery margins than uniaxial-tilt and coplanar designs. Additional experiments (indoor tracking under wind, outdoor extreme conditions, narrow-frame traversal, contact-based aerial writing) confirm robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed passive fault-tolerant framework enables BTO hexacopters to maintain full 6-DOF control under abrupt total rotor failures without requiring fault detection or mode switching, and outperforms alternative multirotor configurations in recovery margins and robustness.

title: LeanMarathon: Toward Reliable AI Co-Mathematicians through Long-Horizon Lean Autoformalization
summary: Long-horizon autoformalization of research mathematics fails not only at hard lemmas, but at scale: statements drift, dependencies tangle, context decays, and local repairs corrupt distant work. We present LeanMarathon, a multi-agent harness for reliable research-level Lean autoformalization. Its core abstraction is an evolving blueprint: a Lean file that serves simultaneously as formal proof skeleton, natural-language proof graph, and shared system of record. Four contract-scoped agents construct, audit, prove, and repair this blueprint. These agents are coordinated by a two-stage orchestrator that first stabilizes target fidelity through adversarial review and then discharges the proof directed acyclic graph (DAG) from its dynamic leaves upward in parallel CI-gated rounds. LeanMarathon turns one brittle multi-hour run into many local, recoverable, parallel transactions. We evaluate LeanMarathon on two recent research papers spanning four Erdős problems (#1051, #1196, #164, #1217). Across three autonomous runs, it formalizes all seven target theorems with no sorry, proving 258 lemmas and theorems. These results show that reliable AI co-mathematics requires not only stronger provers, but durable harnesses that preserve target fidelity across long mathematical developments. The code can be found at https://github.com/YuanheZ/LeanMarathon.

AI.tldr: LeanMarathon is a multi-agent framework for reliable autoformalization of research-level mathematics, using a blueprint abstraction and two-stage orchestration to decompose long proofs into parallel, recoverable transactions. It successfully formalized all seven target theorems across four Erdős problems with zero "sorry" gaps.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon autoformalization of research mathematics fails at scale due to statement drift, tangled dependencies, context decay, and corruptions from local repairs. Existing approaches produce brittle, monolithic runs that cannot recover from failures.
AI.method: LeanMarathon introduces an evolving blueprint (a Lean file serving as proof skeleton, proof graph, and shared record), four contract-scoped agents (construct, audit, prove, repair), and a two-stage orchestrator that first stabilizes target fidelity via adversarial review, then discharges the proof DAG from dynamic leaves upward in parallel CI-gated rounds.
AI.result: Evaluated on two recent research papers covering four Erdős problems (#1051, #1196, #164, #1217). Across three autonomous runs, all seven target theorems were formalized with zero "sorry", proving 258 lemmas and theorems.
AI.conclusion: Reliable AI co-mathematics requires not only stronger provers, but durable harnesses that preserve target fidelity across long mathematical developments.

title: Dynamic Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Robotic Cellular Warehousing Systems
summary: Robotic Cellular Warehousing Systems (RCWS) give rise to multi-agent pickup and delivery (MAPD) processes in which robots sequentially collect multiple stock-keeping units (SKUs) for each order. Unlike classical MAPD formulations that assume static tasks, real warehouse operations often involve dynamic order evolution, where new SKUs may be appended to an order while it is being executed. Motivated by this practical requirement, this letter formulates the Dynamic Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery problem considering internal order evolution for the first time. Building on the token passing paradigm, we propose two event-triggered online replanning algorithms. The first, Dynamic Token Passing, performs localized replanning upon order updates through add-order decomposition and priority-based token scheduling while preserving collision-free execution. The second, Cooperative Token Passing, further enables idle robots to opportunistically assist newly added pickups, improving system-level efficiency. Simulation results in RCWS environments demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly reduce order flowtime compared with static and non-cooperative baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates the Dynamic Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery problem with internal order evolution in robotic warehouses and proposes two event-triggered online replanning algorithms (Dynamic Token Passing and Cooperative Token Passing) that significantly reduce order flowtime compared to static baselines.
AI.motivation: Real warehouse operations involve dynamic order evolution where new SKUs may be appended to an order while it is being executed, which is not addressed by classical MAPD formulations that assume static tasks.
AI.method: Two event-triggered online replanning algorithms based on token passing: (1) Dynamic Token Passing with add-order decomposition and priority-based token scheduling, and (2) Cooperative Token Passing that enables idle robots to opportunistically assist newly added pickups.
AI.result: Simulation results in RCWS environments show significant reduction in order flowtime compared with static and non-cooperative baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dynamic token passing algorithms effectively handle order evolution in multi-agent warehouse systems, improving efficiency over static approaches.

title: Harnessing Generalist Agents for Contextualized Time Series
summary: Time series are often embedded in rich contexts that are essential for holistic modeling. Moreover, real-world practitioners often require end-to-end workflows for analyzing temporal dynamics, where widely studied tasks such as forecasting are only one step in a broader solution loop. While generalist AI agents offer a promising interface for such workflows under complex contexts, they still operate primarily in textual spaces that are not fully aligned with structured temporal signals. In this work, we introduce TimeClaw, an agentic harness framework for time series that equips generalist LLM agents with the time series-native runtime support needed for contextualized temporal reasoning. TimeClaw integrates executable temporal tools for grounded and auditable analysis, experience-driven capability evolution for creating reusable analytical routines, and episodic multimodal memory for retrieving relevant reasoning traces. Together, these components unlock harnessed open-ended temporal reasoning with contextual information. Extensive evaluation on multiple benchmarks covering diverse tasks across energy, finance, weather, traffic, and other real-world domains demonstrates improved performance of TimeClaw. Code is available at https://github.com/iDEA-iSAIL-Lab-UIUC/TimeClaw.

AI.tldr: TimeClaw is an agentic harness framework that equips generalist LLM agents with time series-native runtime support for contextualized temporal reasoning, integrating executable temporal tools, experience-driven capability evolution, and episodic multimodal memory to improve performance across diverse real-world domains.
AI.motivation: Time series are embedded in rich contexts essential for holistic modeling, but real-world workflows require end-to-end analysis beyond single tasks like forecasting.
