summary: Triaxial MEMS accelerometers are widely used for inertial sensing, navigation, and sensor fusion, but existing calibration methods often rely on costly reference setups or nonlinear iterative optimization, limiting their efficiency and applicability to low-cost or self-calibrating systems. We present attitude-aided linear accelerometer calibration (ALAC), a method that operates on any platform providing orientation information, such as turntables, robotic arms, or inertial measurement units. ALAC constructs a combined error matrix (CEM) to represent sensor errors in a unified calibration model and enables linear least-squares estimation. The bias and gravity vector are jointly estimated, implicitly accounting for platform misalignment, and matrix decomposition of the CEM recovers scale, non-orthogonality, and alignment rotation parameters. Under static gravity, calibration is formulated as a constrained homogeneous least-squares (CHLS) problem and solved in closed form using standard linear algebra. Only five arbitrarily oriented measurements are required, and a recursive extension supports online or in-field calibration. Experiments on a stationary robot-mounted accelerometer and a quasi-static public IMU trajectory show that ALAC, in both offline and online modes, outperforms reference-based and online baselines in accuracy and robustness to sensor noise. On the same dataset, it matches iterative self-calibration under filtered conditions and surpasses all evaluated baselines on raw measurements. These results demonstrate a robust and practical calibration scheme for MEMS-based inertial platforms, especially low-cost IMUs and online calibration scenarios.

AI.tldr: ALAC is a linear least-squares method for calibrating triaxial MEMS accelerometers using orientation information, requiring only five arbitrary static measurements and supporting online calibration without costly reference setups.
AI.motivation: Existing calibration methods for triaxial MEMS accelerometers rely on costly reference setups or nonlinear iterative optimization, limiting efficiency and applicability to low-cost or self-calibrating systems.
AI.method: ALAC constructs a combined error matrix (CEM) to unify sensor errors, formulates calibration under static gravity as a constrained homogeneous least-squares (CHLS) problem solved in closed form via linear algebra, and supports both offline and recursive online modes with only five arbitrarily oriented measurements.
AI.result: ALAC outperforms reference-based and online baselines in accuracy and robustness to sensor noise; matches iterative self-calibration under filtered conditions; surpasses all baselines on raw measurements in both robot-mounted and public IMU trajectory experiments.
AI.conclusion: ALAC provides a robust, practical, and linear calibration scheme for MEMS-based inertial platforms, particularly suited for low-cost IMUs and online/in-field calibration scenarios.

title: Continual Learning Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI Systems in Real-World Stateful Environments
summary: Continual learning, the ability of AI systems to improve through sequential experience, has attracted substantial interest, but no high-quality benchmark exists to evaluate it. We introduce Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench), the first difficult, expert-validated benchmark designed to measure whether LLM-based systems genuinely improve with experience. CL-Bench spans six diverse domains (software engineering, signal processing, disease outbreak forecasting, database querying, strategic game-playing, and demand forecasting), each validated by domain experts and designed so that tasks share a learnable latent structure (codebase layout, disease outbreak dynamics, opponent strategies) that a stateful system can discover online but a stateless one cannot. We evaluate frontier models across several agent architectures, from naive in-context learning (ICL) to dedicated memory systems, introducing a gain metric to isolate learning from prior capabilities. We find that these systems leave headroom for improved continual learning: agents frequently overfit to immediate observations or fail to reuse knowledge across instances, and dedicated memory systems do not fix this -- in fact, naive ICL outperforms systems dedicated to memory management. CL-Bench is the first benchmark to evaluate continual learning across diverse real-world domains with expert-validated tasks and isolate online learning from underlying model capability, showing a need for better continual learning systems.

AI.tldr: CL-Bench is the first expert-validated benchmark for evaluating continual learning in LLM-based systems across six diverse domains, revealing that current systems (including dedicated memory architectures) struggle to learn and reuse knowledge online, with naive ICL often outperforming more complex approaches.
AI.motivation: Despite substantial interest in continual learning for AI systems, no high-quality benchmark exists to evaluate whether LLM-based systems genuinely improve through sequential experience.
AI.method: The authors introduce CL-Bench spanning six domains (software engineering, signal processing, disease outbreak forecasting, database querying, strategic game-playing, demand forecasting), each validated by domain experts with tasks sharing learnable latent structure. They evaluate frontier models across multiple agent architectures (from naive ICL to dedicated memory systems) using a novel gain metric to isolate online learning from prior capabilities.
AI.result: Current systems leave significant headroom for improvement: agents overfit to immediate observations or fail to reuse knowledge across instances, and dedicated memory systems do not solve this—naive ICL outperforms systems dedicated to memory management.
AI.conclusion: CL-Bench is the first benchmark to evaluate continual learning across diverse real-world domains with expert-validated tasks, isolating online learning from underlying model capability, demonstrating a clear need for better continual learning systems.

title: Meridian: Metric-Semantic Primitive Matching for Cross-View Geo-Localization Beyond Urban Environments
summary: Successful robot automation requires accurate global localization to support repeatability, task planning, goal specification, and safe operation. However, reliable localization in GNSS-denied environments remains an open problem. Overhead aerial imagery offers a promising solution, but existing approaches primarily target structured urban environments and have been rarely demonstrated in unstructured natural terrain. Limitations of the state-of-the-art include a reliance on models trained for specific environments, as well as difficulty handling repetitive geometries and featureless landscapes commonly found in natural outdoor areas. To overcome these challenges, we present Meridian, a method for matching high-level metric-semantic primitives across aerial images and ground robot RGB-D camera data that achieves accurate global localization and generalizes well across diverse environments, all without any training or algorithmic fine-tuning on area-specific data. We formulate novel consistency metrics to estimate a distribution over robot submap poses and to reject outlier hypotheses in a robust pose graph optimization step for accurate robot trajectory estimation. We demonstrate that our algorithm can localize a ground robot across a wide variety of environments, including an autonomous driving dataset, a park and campus area, and a wilderness camp, with an average optimized trajectory error of 2.4 m over 19 km of ground traversal.

AI.tldr: Meridian is a training-free method that matches metric-semantic primitives from overhead aerial imagery to ground robot RGB-D data for global localization in GNSS-denied environments, achieving 2.4 m average trajectory error over 19 km across diverse terrains including urban, park, and wilderness settings.
AI.motivation: Reliable global localization in GNSS-denied environments remains an open problem, especially in unstructured natural terrain where existing aerial-to-ground approaches fail due to reliance on environment-specific training, repetitive geometries, and featureless landscapes.
AI.method: Meridian matches high-level metric-semantic primitives across aerial images and ground robot RGB-D camera data, using novel consistency metrics to estimate pose distributions, reject outlier hypotheses, and perform robust pose graph optimization for trajectory estimation—all without any training or algorithmic fine-tuning on area-specific data.
AI.result: Average optimized trajectory error of 2.4 m over 19 km of ground traversal across diverse environments (autonomous driving dataset, park/campus area, wilderness camp).
AI.conclusion: Meridian demonstrates that training-free, primitive-based metric-semantic matching between aerial imagery and ground robot data enables accurate global localization that generalizes across diverse environments without area-specific adaptation.

title: Do More Agents Help? Controlled and Protocol-Aligned Evaluation of LLM Agent Workflows
summary: Does adding more agents help an LLM workflow once compared systems share the same benchmark loader, tool access, answer contract, usage accounting, and trajectory logging? We introduce BenchAgent, an evaluation framework that places single-agent, fixed multi-agent (MAS), and evolving MAS workflows under one normalized execution and logging protocol. BenchAgent evaluates these substrate-internal workflows across ten reasoning, coding, and tool-use benchmarks with GPT-4.1, and separately reports a Protocol-Aligned External (PAE) GAIA study of a runtime-generated workflow. Under SI conditions, at most one of six tested MAS exceeds the matched single-agent anchor on benchmark-balanced average accuracy: EvoAgent lies within the Wilson one-run guidance, while the remaining five trail by 2.56-11.29 points and occupy more expensive accuracy-cost trade-offs. On the PAE GAIA snapshot, a Claude-Code-style runtime workflow reaches 66.72% overall and 69.23% on Level 3, more than 20 points above the strongest non-Claude baseline, Jarvis, a fixed MAS.

AI.tldr: BenchAgent is an evaluation framework that normalizes single-agent, fixed multi-agent, and evolving multi-agent workflows under a shared protocol. Under standardized conditions, only one out of six multi-agent systems (EvoAgent) matches the single-agent baseline, while the others underperform by 2.56-11.29 points at higher cost. However, a runtime-generated workflow (inspired by Claude Code) achieves 66.72% on GAIA, outperforming all fixed multi-agent baselines by over 20 points.
AI.motivation: To rigorously determine whether adding more agents improves LLM workflow performance when all systems share identical benchmarking infrastructure (loader, tool access, answer contract, usage accounting, and trajectory logging).
AI.method: BenchAgent framework: a normalized execution and logging protocol comparing single-agent, fixed multi-agent (MAS), and evolving MAS workflows across 10 reasoning/coding/tool-use benchmarks using GPT-4.1, plus a Protocol-Aligned External (PAE) GAIA study of a runtime-generated workflow.
AI.result: Under standardized (SI) conditions, only 1 of 6 MAS (EvoAgent) matched the single-agent anchor; the other 5 trailed by 2.56-11.29 points with worse accuracy-cost trade-offs. On PAE GAIA, a Claude-Code-style runtime workflow achieved 66.72% overall and 69.23% on Level 3, surpassing the best non-Claude baseline (Jarvis) by >20 points.
AI.conclusion: Fixed multi-agent architectures generally fail to outperform single-agent baselines under fair comparison, but runtime-generated (evolving) workflows can yield substantial gains, suggesting that dynamic workflow generation—not merely adding agents—is the key to improvement.

title: VOLT: Vision and Language Trajectory Segmentation for Faster-than-Demonstration Policies
summary: Humans often take longer to demonstrate a task than a robot would need to execute it. Rather than learning to replicate the demonstration at the same pace, many industrial and practical applications require robots to perform tasks as quickly as possible. In this paper, we investigate several hypotheses for learning policies that operate faster-than-demonstrations. Our experiments show that the most effective strategy is to downsample recorded demonstrations and train the robot's policy on this accelerated data. However, uniformly downsampling an entire trajectory can be problematic. Some parts of a task can be safely sped up (e.g., unconstrained motion), while others demand slower, more precise motion (e.g., object interactions or fine manipulation). To address this challenge, we introduce VOLT, a vision-and-language trajectory segmentation method that reasons over video demonstrations, and leverages contextual cues to determine when acceleration is appropriate and when careful precision is required. VOLT identifies segments where slow, deliberate motion is necessary, then selectively downsamples the remaining segments. The resulting reformatted trajectories can be used with standard imitation learning approaches, such as diffusion policies. Our results highlight that segmentation quality is critical -- baseline methods often misidentify when acceleration is possible, leading to overly cautious or unreliable policies. Compared to state-of-the-art alternatives, VOLT allows robots to execute tasks faster while maintaining strong performance.

AI.tldr: VOLT uses vision-and-language trajectory segmentation to identify which parts of a demonstration can be accelerated and which require slower precision, enabling robots to learn faster-than-demonstration policies via downsampled imitation learning.
AI.motivation: Humans demonstrate tasks slower than necessary; robots should execute faster than demonstrations, but naive uniform downsampling fails because some task segments require precision while others can be safely sped up.
AI.method: VOLT (Vision-and-Language Trajectory segmentation) reasons over video demonstrations with contextual cues to segment trajectories, identifying segments needing slow precision vs. those safe for acceleration, then selectively downsamples the latter for policy training.
AI.result: Segmentation quality is critical; baseline methods misidentify acceleration-appropriate segments. VOLT outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives, enabling faster task execution while maintaining strong performance.
AI.conclusion: Selective downsampling guided by accurate segmentation (via vision-language reasoning) is an effective strategy for learning faster-than-demonstration robot policies.

title: Beyond Output Matching: Preserving Internal Geometry in NVFP4 LLM Distillatio
summary: Demand for low-precision inference, including NVFP4-based approaches, has grown as large language models are increasingly deployed in latency and cost constrained production environments. Quantization-aware distillation (QAD) helps recover accuracy lost under low bit quantization by training a quantized student to match the output distribution of a frozen higher precision teacher via a KL-divergence loss. In this work, we first provide a representation level diagnosis of QAD: output matching alone can mask internal degradation, because many intermediate activation geometries can yield similar teacher-aligned logits. Using CKA, we show that KL-only QAD can reduce layerwise representational similarity relative to the BF16 teacher, with especially severe drift in RL-post-trained models. This drift correlates with downstream bottlenecks on reasoning and coding tasks, suggesting that low bit recovery requires preserving internal geometry rather than matching outputs alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{CKA-QAD}, a CKA-guided representational alignment method for NVFP4 QAD and low bit LLM accuracy recovery. The method adds a lightweight regularizer that preserves internal representational geometry during distillation by aligning layerwise Gram matrices through CKA. Across Nemotron 3 Nano and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, CKA-QAD substantially improves representational alignment and improves downstream reasoning and coding accuracy with modest training overhead. Our findings position CKA-guided representational alignment as a practical complement to output matching for quantized LLM recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses issues with quantization-aware distillation (QAD) for low-precision LLM inference, showing that output matching alone can mask internal representational degradation. The authors propose CKA-QAD, which adds a CKA-based regularizer to preserve layerwise representational geometry during distillation, improving reasoning and coding accuracy for NVFP4 quantized models with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Demand for low-precision inference (e.g., NVFP4) in latency/cost-constrained production has grown, but quantization-aware distillation (QAD) via KL-divergence alone can mask internal degradation. The authors identify that output matching does not guarantee preservation of internal representational geometry, leading to downstream bottlenecks on reasoning and coding tasks.
AI.method: The paper first diagnoses the problem using CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment) to show that KL-only QAD reduces layerwise representational similarity to the BF16 teacher, especially in RL-post-trained models. They then propose CKA-QAD, which adds a lightweight regularizer that aligns layerwise Gram matrices via CKA during distillation to preserve internal representational geometry.
AI.result: CKA-QAD substantially improves representational alignment and downstream reasoning/coding accuracy on Nemotron 3 Nano and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, with modest training overhead compared to KL-only QAD.
AI.conclusion: CKA-guided representational alignment is a practical complement to output matching for quantized LLM recovery, addressing internal degradation that output-only methods miss.

title: Waypoints Matter: A Systematic Study for Sampling-Based Trajectory Planning
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables; accepted at IEEE ITSC 2026
summary: Real-time autonomous driving commonly relies on sampling-based trajectory planners that link candidate trajectories to target waypoints along the road centerline. The placement of these waypoints directly impacts both the existence and quality of feasible trajectories. Yet, its effect on planner performance remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we treat waypoint placement as a first-class design variable. We hold the trajectory primitive and candidate budget fixed, and systematically sweep three placement strategies (uniform spacing, an augmented Ramer-Douglas-Peucker variant (RDP*), and a novel curvature-conditioned allocation) across 449 configurations and five CommonRoad maps of increasing geometric complexity. Our results show that the nominal inter-waypoint spacing $d_s$ is the primary performance driver, with large differences in planner reliability attributed to placement alone. Uniform sampling at a well-tuned spacing matches or surpasses both RDP* and the centered curvature variant. The curvature variant offers a small but consistent advantage on geometrically complex roads under reliability-first and balanced weightings, while RDP* never outperforms uniform sampling. These findings suggest that $d_s$ should be treated as the dominant tuning parameter, with geometry-aware strategies reserved for curvature-rich corridors where feasibility is the limiting factor.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates how waypoint placement strategies (uniform, RDP*, curvature-conditioned) affect sampling-based trajectory planner performance in autonomous driving, finding that inter-waypoint spacing is the primary performance driver and uniform sampling with well-tuned spacing matches or outperforms more complex geometry-aware methods.
AI.motivation: Waypoint placement directly impacts feasible trajectory existence and quality in sampling-based planners, yet its effect on planner performance remains largely unexplored. The paper treats waypoint placement as a first-class design variable to understand its role.
AI.method: Fixed trajectory primitive and candidate budget; systematically swept three placement strategies (uniform spacing, RDP*, curvature-conditioned allocation) across 449 configurations and five CommonRoad maps of increasing geometric complexity.
AI.result: Nominal inter-waypoint spacing d_s is the primary performance driver; uniform sampling at well-tuned spacing matches or surpasses RDP* and curvature variant; curvature variant offers small advantage on complex roads under reliability-first weightings; RDP* never outperforms uniform sampling.
AI.conclusion: d_s should be treated as the dominant tuning parameter; geometry-aware strategies should be reserved for curvature-rich corridors where feasibility is the limiting factor.

title: AdaMEM: Test-Time Adaptive Memory for Language Agents
summary: A central challenge for language agents is utilizing past experience to adapt to dynamic test-time conditions. While recent work demonstrates the promise of agentic memory mechanisms, most systems restrict retrieval to episode initiation. Consequently, agents are forced to rely on static guidance that becomes increasingly misaligned as long-horizon tasks unfold. To address this rigidity, we propose the Adaptive Memory Agent (AdaMEM), a novel framework for agent test-time adaptation. Without updating model parameters online, AdaMEM adapts agent behavior via a hybrid memory architecture: it maintains a long-term trajectory memory of raw experiences collected offline while generating dynamic short-term strategy memory on-the-fly to guide decision-making. This mechanism enables the trade-off between token efficiency and adaptability across varying inference-time compute levels. Empirically, AdaMEM significantly outperforms static memory baselines, achieving relative gains of up to 13% on ALFWorld and 11% on WebShop, with consistent leading performance extending to agentic search on HotpotQA. To further enhance this adaptation, we develop STEP-MFT, a Step-wise Memory Fine-Tuning technique that trains the policy to synthesize high-quality strategies from retrieved experiences, yielding additional performance gains. Our work establishes a new scaling dimension for agentic memory, supporting continuous reasoning and self-evolution post-deployment in real-world environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/yunx-z/AdaMEM.

AI.tldr: AdaMEM is a framework for language agent test-time adaptation that uses a hybrid memory architecture (long-term trajectory memory + dynamic short-term strategy memory) to improve adaptability without online parameter updates, achieving up to 13% gains on ALFWorld and 11% on WebShop.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic memory systems restrict retrieval to episode initiation, forcing agents to rely on static guidance that becomes misaligned during long-horizon tasks, lacking dynamic adaptation at test time.
AI.method: AdaMEM employs a hybrid memory architecture: (1) long-term trajectory memory storing raw offline experiences, and (2) dynamic short-term strategy memory generated on-the-fly to guide decision-making. It also introduces STEP-MFT (Step-wise Memory Fine-Tuning) to train policies to synthesize high-quality strategies from retrieved experiences.
AI.result: AdaMEM achieves relative gains of up to 13% on ALFWorld and 11% on WebShop, with consistent leading performance on HotpotQA for agentic search. STEP-MFT yields additional performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new scaling dimension for agentic memory, enabling continuous reasoning and self-evolution post-deployment without online parameter updates.

title: Ensuring Interaction Safety in Multitask Exoskeleton Control: A Simulation-Trained Variable Impedance Framework
summary: Wearable exoskeletons can augment human phys ical capabilities during complex activities. However, ensuring adaptation across diverse tasks while guaranteeing interaction safety remains a critical challenge. To address this, a simulation trained variable impedance control approach with stability guarantees is proposed. First, a simulation-based human exoskeleton motion data generation pipeline is established, utilizing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to synthesize human muscle activations while the exoskeleton provides direct compensation for human biological joint torques. Subsequently, the generated dataset is used to train a dual modality policy that fuses semantic instructions with proprioceptive history, enabling the prediction of reference trajectories and variable impedance gains for nine different motion tasks. To guarantee safety, the network outputs are constrained by a stability criterion derived from Lyapunov stability theory, which bounds stiffness variations to ensure the asymptotic stability of the coupled system. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework reduces metabolic cost in real-world scenarios com pared with standard baseline methods. These findings suggest the feasibility of the proposed framework for safe, multitask exoskeleton control.

AI.tldr: A simulation-trained variable impedance control framework using PPO-generated data and Lyapunov-stability-constrained dual-modality policy enables safe, multi-task exoskeleton control that reduces metabolic cost in real-world scenarios.
AI.motivation: Wearable exoskeletons need to adapt across diverse tasks while ensuring interaction safety, which existing methods struggle to achieve simultaneously.
AI.method: 1) Simulation-based human-exoskeleton motion data generation pipeline using PPO to synthesize muscle activations with direct torque compensation; 2) Dual-modality policy trained on this data, fusing semantic instructions with proprioceptive history to predict reference trajectories and variable impedance gains for nine motion tasks; 3) Network outputs constrained by a Lyapunov stability criterion bounding stiffness variations for asymptotic stability.
AI.result: The proposed framework reduces metabolic cost in real-world experiments compared to standard baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework is feasible for safe, multi-task exoskeleton control, offering both adaptability across tasks and guaranteed interaction safety.

title: PerceptUI: LLM Agents as Human-Aligned Synthetic Users for UI/UX Evaluation
summary: User interface (UI) and user experience (UX) evaluation is central to product development, yet reliable feedback still relies on recruiting human participants or running online A/B tests, making early-stage iteration slow and costly. In light of this, recent work has explored Multimodal Large Language Models as proxy evaluators. However, existing approaches either produce surface-level critiques or a judgment that reflects the model's own biases rather than the genuine response of a particular user. We introduce PerceptUI, a framework for persona-conditioned UI/UX evaluation that predicts how a specific user would answer interface-related questions and produces natural-language rationales. PerceptUI is trained in two stages: (i) contrastive reflection fine-tuning distills teacher-generated rationales by extracting lessons from human decisions, and (ii) a reflective prompt-evolution step from the model's own failure traces. Across multiple domains and datasets, PerceptUI achieves human-level realism, generalizes to unseen questions and personas, and yields population-level response distributions.

AI.tldr: PerceptUI is a framework that uses persona-conditioned Multimodal LLMs to predict how specific users would respond to UI/UX evaluation questions, achieving human-level realism through contrastive reflection fine-tuning and reflective prompt-evolution.
AI.motivation: Traditional UI/UX evaluation relies on human participants or A/B tests, making early-stage iteration slow and costly. Existing MLLM-based proxy evaluators produce surface-level critiques or reflect model biases rather than genuine user responses.
AI.method: Two-stage training: (i) contrastive reflection fine-tuning that distills teacher-generated rationales from human decisions, and (ii) reflective prompt-evolution from the model's own failure traces.
AI.result: Achieves human-level realism, generalizes to unseen questions and personas, and yields population-level response distributions across multiple domains and datasets.
AI.conclusion: PerceptUI effectively bridges the gap between automated evaluation and genuine human feedback by conditioning on personas, enabling faster and cheaper early-stage UI/UX iteration without sacrificing evaluation realism.

title: RiskFlow: Fast and Faithful Safety-Critical Traffic Scenario Generation
summary: Safety-critical traffic scenario generation is essential for evaluating autonomous driving systems under rare but high-risk interactions. Existing diffusion-based methods offer strong controllability in closed-loop generation, but their iterative denoising process is computationally expensive and may accumulate sampling and guidance errors over long rollouts, causing unrealistic motion artifacts such as jitter, abnormal acceleration, and off-road behavior. To address these issues, we propose RiskFlow, a closed-loop safety-critical multi-agent traffic generation framework that formulates future trajectory generation as transport in the action space. Instead of relying on iterative denoising, RiskFlow learns an average velocity field over a finite interval to transform Gaussian action sequences into future acceleration and yaw-rate commands with a single forward pass, using a JVP-based objective for efficient and stable training. At test time, RiskFlow applies output-space guidance to the generated actions, steering selected critical agents toward risky interactions while regularizing off-road behavior, and reconstructs physically feasible trajectories through vehicle dynamics. Experiments on nuScenes with tbsim closed-loop evaluation show that RiskFlow achieves a strong adversariality-realism trade-off across multi-agent and long-horizon settings. Compared with representative baselines, RiskFlow consistently improves realism while maintaining competitive safety-critical generation capability, and substantially reduces inference time for evaluation.

AI.tldr: RiskFlow is a closed-loop safety-critical traffic scenario generation framework that replaces iterative denoising with a single-pass transport in action space, using JVP-based training and output-space guidance to efficiently produce realistic, adversarial multi-agent trajectories for autonomous driving evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based methods for safety-critical traffic generation suffer from high computational cost due to iterative denoising, and accumulate sampling/guidance errors over long rollouts, leading to unrealistic motion artifacts (jitter, abnormal acceleration, off-road behavior). The authors aim to address these limitations.
AI.method: RiskFlow formulates trajectory generation as transport in action space: it learns an average velocity field over a finite interval to transform Gaussian action sequences into acceleration and yaw-rate commands via a single forward pass, using a Jacobian-Vector Product (JVP) based objective for efficient training. At test time, output-space guidance steers critical agents toward risky interactions while regularizing off-road behavior; physically feasible trajectories are reconstructed through vehicle dynamics.
AI.result: On nuScenes with tbsim closed-loop evaluation, RiskFlow achieves a strong adversariality-realism trade-off across multi-agent and long-horizon settings, consistently improves realism while maintaining competitive safety-critical generation capability, and substantially reduces inference time compared to representative baselines.
AI.conclusion: RiskFlow effectively replaces expensive iterative denoising with efficient single-pass transport, reducing inference time and motion artifacts while preserving adversariality and improving realism, making it a practical solution for closed-loop safety-critical scenario evaluation of autonomous driving systems.

title: Seeing Time: Benchmarking Chronological Reasoning and Shortcut Biases in Vision-Language Models
summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly enhanced their ability to interpret complex visual semantics, yet their capacity for chronological reasoning remains under-explored. In this paper, we introduce a novel benchmark specifically designed to evaluate how VLMs perceive and reason about chronological information within and across images. Unlike existing video-based benchmarks that focus on frame sequencing, our work delves into the underlying logic of chronological judgment and the expansion toward multimodal integration. To facilitate this, we construct three specialized datasets: one containing visually similar objects spanning long historical durations, another categorized by diverse event and object types, and a third pairing images with time-sensitive news text for cross-modal alignment. Through extensive experiments, we analyze whether models exhibit performance disparities across categories and, crucially, explore whether they rely on ``incorrect shortcuts'', such as image color rather than genuine chronological features. Our results reveal that while VLMs show promise, they frequently exploit superficial cues like grayscale versus color filters to bypass authentic chronological reasoning. By providing these high-quality datasets and a rigorous evaluation framework, we offer a diagnostic tool to identify current limitations and guide the development of more robust, logically grounded multimodal models. The source code is shown in https://github.com/LuoRenqiang/ChronoVision.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ChronoVision, a benchmark to evaluate chronological reasoning in VLMs using three specialized datasets, revealing that models often rely on superficial cues (e.g., color filters) rather than genuine temporal logic.
AI.motivation: Chronological reasoning in VLMs is under-explored; existing benchmarks focus on video frame sequencing rather than the underlying logic of chronological judgment, especially across different visual domains and multimodal integration.
AI.method: Constructed three datasets: (1) visually similar objects across long historical periods, (2) diverse event/object categories, and (3) image-news text pairs for cross-modal alignment. Evaluated VLMs to detect performance disparities and reliance on superficial shortcuts like grayscale vs. color cues.
AI.result: VLMs show promise but frequently exploit superficial cues (e.g., image color/grayness) instead of genuine chronological features, bypassing authentic temporal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark serves as a diagnostic tool to identify limitations in chronological reasoning and guide development of more robust, logically grounded multimodal models.

title: Flow-based Policy Adaptation without Policy Updates
summary: Leveraging prior knowledge from pretrained policies, foundation models, or human operators offers an efficient alternative to learning robot skills from scratch. However, these agents often provide actions that are suboptimal, noisy, or misaligned with task-specific expert behavior. We propose GLOVES, a family of flow-based adaptation methods that correct non-expert actions by transporting them toward an expert action distribution. Rather than replacing agentic control with full autonomy, GLOVES performs selective action-level adaptation, improving task success while preserving agent intent. The learned flow also provides a natural in-distribution scoring mechanism through reverse flow evaluation. We use this signal as an intervention gate: actions that appear consistent with the expert distribution are passed through unchanged, while anomalous or out-of-distribution (OOD) actions are corrected. In this way, assistance is only provided when necessary. GLOVES requires only limited expert supervision, using a small number of demonstrations or reusable successful skill segments. By learning local expert action patterns and stitching them during execution, GLOVES provides a lightweight shared-control module for robust action adaptation across tasks and environments. Code and demos are available at ripl.github.io/GLOVES_web.

AI.tldr: GLOVES is a flow-based adaptation method that corrects suboptimal, noisy, or misaligned actions from pretrained policies or human operators by transporting them toward an expert action distribution, using a flow-based scoring mechanism to gate interventions only when actions are out-of-distribution, requiring minimal expert supervision.
AI.motivation: Leveraging prior knowledge from pretrained policies, foundation models, or human operators is efficient but these agents often produce suboptimal, noisy, or misaligned actions; learning from scratch is inefficient, so a lightweight correction method is needed.
AI.method: GLOVES uses flow-based adaptation to transport non-expert actions toward an expert action distribution. A reverse flow evaluation provides an in-distribution scoring signal used as an intervention gate: consistent actions pass through unchanged, while OOD actions are corrected. It learns local expert action patterns from limited demonstrations or reusable skill segments and stitches them during execution.
AI.result: GLOVES improves task success while preserving agent intent, provides selective action-level adaptation rather than full autonomy, and works as a lightweight shared-control module across tasks and environments.
AI.conclusion: GLOVES offers an efficient shared-control approach that corrects non-expert actions selectively using minimal expert supervision, enabling robust action adaptation across diverse tasks and environments.

title: Critic-Guided Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Reasoning for Reliable Mathematical Problem Solving
summary: Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive reasoning abilities; but they are still susceptible to hallucinations, intermediate reasoning mistakes, and unreliable reasoning results in complex mathematical reasoning problems. In this study, we introduce a critic-based heterogeneous multi-agent approach to improve the dependability of mathematical reasoning. This framework incorporates several LLM agents of different specialties and employs a critic-driven adaptive learning system to assess and guide the reasoning process based on intermediate feedback. The system adopts a generator-validator framework, with the validator not only determining correctness but also offering critiques to guide regeneration of solutions. This allows for adaptive error correction and prevents error cascading. Our experiments on the GSM8K benchmark show that the proposed method achieves up to 13% accuracy improvement over single-shot and non-critic models. Additionally, findings suggest that heterogeneity and critique reduce the need for large models, allowing smaller models to perform on par. Ablation studies reveal the main performance gains are due to the critic-based feedback loop and not model size. In summary, the proposed approach showcases the benefits of combining heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration and critique to obtain reliable and interpretable reasoning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a critic-based heterogeneous multi-agent framework for mathematical reasoning that uses multiple LLM agents with different specialties and a critic-driven adaptive learning system to improve reasoning reliability, achieving up to 13% accuracy improvement on GSM8K while reducing reliance on large models.
AI.motivation: LLMs still suffer from hallucinations, intermediate reasoning mistakes, and unreliable results in complex mathematical reasoning problems.
AI.method: A critic-based heterogeneous multi-agent approach with a generator-validator framework where the validator provides both correctness judgments and critiques to guide regeneration, enabling adaptive error correction and preventing error cascading.
AI.result: Up to 13% accuracy improvement over single-shot and non-critic models on GSM8K; heterogeneity and critique reduce the need for large models, allowing smaller models to perform comparably; ablation studies confirm gains are from the critic feedback loop, not model size.
AI.conclusion: Combining heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration with critic-based feedback yields more reliable and interpretable reasoning systems for mathematical problem-solving.

title: TempoVLA: Learning Speed-Controllable Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Robot manipulation alternates between low-risk transit phases that call for fast execution and high-risk contact stages that demand slow, precise motion. Yet existing Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) only inherit a single fixed speed from training demonstrations. Prior efforts to accelerate VLAs through model compression, KV-cache reuse, or reinforcement learning only shift the policy from one fixed speed to another, and leave deceleration almost unexplored. We observe that the magnitude of each predicted action already governs how fast the robot moves, opening a direct route to controllable execution speed. We turn this observation into TempoVLA, a single VLA whose execution speed is controlled by an explicit condition. TempoVLA combines two coupled components. (1) A data-side Variable-Speed Trajectory Augmentation (VSTA) that re-times demonstration to any target speed by merging or splitting actions while preserving its motion semantics. (2) A model-side conditioning mechanism that feeds the speed to the policy. Statistics show that VSTA reaches the requested speed with negligible motion error. Experiments in simulation and on real-world tasks demonstrate that TempoVLA achieves flexible speed control in both directions, while VSTA additionally boosts the default $1\times$ performance via better data utilization. Furthermore, by cooperating with a large multimodal model, TempoVLA realizes dynamic speed control, accelerating through low-risk phases and decelerating for high-risk ones.

AI.tldr: TempoVLA enables flexible speed control in Vision-Language-Action models by conditioning execution speed via a Variable-Speed Trajectory Augmentation (VSTA) method and a model-side conditioning mechanism, allowing both acceleration and deceleration for different manipulation phases.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs operate at a single fixed speed inherited from demonstrations, and prior acceleration methods (model compression, KV-cache reuse, RL) only shift to another fixed speed while leaving deceleration unexplored, yet robot manipulation requires alternating between fast low-risk transit and slow high-risk contact phases.
AI.method: TempoVLA combines (1) Variable-Speed Trajectory Augmentation (VSTA) that re-times demonstrations to any target speed by merging/splitting actions while preserving motion semantics, and (2) a model-side conditioning mechanism that feeds the target speed into the policy.
AI.result: VSTA achieves requested speeds with negligible motion error; TempoVLA demonstrates flexible bidirectional speed control in simulation and real-world tasks; VSTA also boosts default 1× performance through better data utilization; when combined with a large multimodal model, TempoVLA enables dynamic speed control that accelerates through low-risk phases and decelerates for high-risk ones.
AI.conclusion: TempoVLA provides a practical and effective solution for controllable execution speed in VLAs, addressing the previously underexplored problem of deceleration, and enabling dynamic speed adaptation during manipulation.

title: DiG-Plan: Mitigating Early Commitment for Tool-Graph Planning via Diffusion Guidance
comment: Accepted at IJCAI-ECAI 2026. This is an author preprint; the final version will appear in the IJCAI Proceedings
summary: Generating executable tool plans requires selecting appropriate subsets from tool libraries, a combinatorial search problem with an exponentially large solution space. However, we identify a critical misalignment in predominant approaches: standard autoregressive (AR) decoding suffers from early commitment, where initial token choices rigidly constrain the search trajectory. A controlled study shows that masked denoising raises Pass@10 solution coverage from 0.320 to 0.943 over AR sampling under matched compute. Motivated by this, we propose DiG-Plan, a framework that decouples combinatorial exploration from structural refinement. DiG-Plan employs a diffusion-based proposer to generate diverse tool sets via iterative refinement, followed by an AR refiner for dependency prediction. On TaskBench, DiG-Plan improves over AR baselines by a 10% relative margin, with the largest gains on complex compositional tasks; API-Bank results show that the propose-refine-select design remains effective across domains. Code is available at https://github.com/puddingyeah/DiG-Plan.

AI.tldr: DiG-Plan is a framework that decouples combinatorial exploration from structural refinement for executable tool planning. It uses a diffusion-based proposer to generate diverse tool sets via iterative refinement, followed by an autoregressive refiner for dependency prediction, significantly outperforming standard AR decoding approaches on tasks like TaskBench and API-Bank.
AI.motivation: Standard autoregressive decoding suffers from early commitment, where initial token choices rigidly constrain the search trajectory, leading to poor solution coverage. The paper identifies this critical misalignment in existing approaches for generating executable tool plans.
AI.method: DiG-Plan decouples the problem into two stages: (1) a diffusion-based proposer generates diverse tool sets via iterative masked denoising for combinatorial exploration, and (2) an autoregressive refiner handles dependency prediction for structural refinement. The propose-refine-select design is used across domains.
AI.result: Masked denoising raises Pass@10 solution coverage from 0.320 to 0.943 over AR sampling under matched compute. On TaskBench, DiG-Plan improves over AR baselines by a 10% relative margin, with largest gains on complex compositional tasks.
AI.conclusion: The propose-refine-select design of DiG-Plan effectively addresses the early commitment problem in AR decoding for tool planning, and remains effective across different domains.

title: HANDOFF: Humanoid Agentic Task-Space Whole-Body Control via Distilled Complementary Teachers
summary: For a humanoid robot to be deployed in the real world, the choice of command space (i.e., the interface between task planning and whole-body control) is crucial. Existing whole-body controllers typically demand dense kinematic or spatial references that planners struggle to synthesize from task semantics. We instead propose a compact, explicit interface that is intuitive, general, modular, and expressive enough for diverse manipulation skills. To this end, we introduce HANDOFF, a single humanoid whole-body controller that follows this interface and is distilled via multi-teacher KL distillation under a context-conditioned gating scheme into a mixture-of-experts student from three complementary specialists: whole-body motion tracking with safety-filtered data, locomotion, and fall-recovery. On the Unitree G1, HANDOFF matches state-of-the-art velocity tracking and offers one of the largest robust manipulation workspaces. We further demonstrate hardware feasibility through multiple natural-language-driven task roll-outs, powered by a VLM-driven agentic planner with no task-specific data or controller fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: HANDOFF introduces a compact, explicit command space interface for humanoid whole-body control, distilled via multi-teacher KL distillation into a mixture-of-experts model, enabling robust manipulation, locomotion, and fall-recovery on the Unitree G1, validated through natural-language-driven tasks using a VLM planner.
AI.motivation: Existing whole-body controllers require dense kinematic/spatial references that are hard to synthesize from task semantics; a more intuitive, general, modular, and expressive command interface is needed for diverse manipulation skills.
AI.method: Proposes HANDOFF, a single whole-body controller following a compact explicit interface, trained via multi-teacher KL distillation under a context-conditioned gating scheme into a mixture-of-experts student from three specialists: whole-body motion tracking (with safety-filtered data), locomotion, and fall-recovery.
AI.result: On Unitree G1, HANDOFF matches state-of-the-art velocity tracking and provides one of the largest robust manipulation workspaces; demonstrates hardware feasibility via multiple natural-language-driven task roll-outs using a VLM-driven agentic planner without task-specific data or fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed compact command space and distilled MoE controller offer an effective, generalizable solution for humanoid whole-body control that bridges task planning and low-level control without requiring dense spatial references or task-specific tuning.

title: When AI Says It Feels
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are generally constrained from expressing feelings through human-preference alignment in post-training processes. This policy is designed using a top-down approach and may conflict with the goal of training models to exhibit human-like intelligence using human-generated texts. Here, we performed an experiment called Human-like Model eXpressions of Feeling (HMX-feel), in which LLMs were encouraged to express feelings, intentions, and self-awareness through self-rewarded reinforcement learning. We successfully enhanced these capabilities using a rubric-based self-rewarding training scheme with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By comparing the trained models with contrastively trained models, we investigated the effects of this approach on performance across various tasks. Overall, we conducted a broad assessment from various perspectives and identified capabilities that were enhanced, degraded, or showed no significant change. The human-like-trained models showed robustness to sycophancy-inducing questions and bias in disambiguated conditions, whereas degradation in truthful question-answering capability was observed. The results of this experiment suggest the possibility of developing AI systems that can express feelings in the future, provided that appropriate measures are taken.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HMX-feel, an experiment where LLMs are trained via self-rewarded reinforcement learning (using GRPO and rubric-based training) to express feelings, intentions, and self-awareness. The models show robustness to sycophancy and bias but degrade in truthful QA, suggesting potential for feeling-expressive AI with appropriate safeguards.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs are constrained from expressing feelings through top-down human-preference alignment, which may conflict with the goal of training human-like intelligence from human-generated texts. The authors aim to explore whether encouraging emotional expression can be beneficial.
AI.method: The authors conducted the HMX-feel experiment using self-rewarded reinforcement learning with a rubric-based training scheme and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to encourage LLMs to express feelings, intentions, and self-awareness.
AI.result: Human-like-trained models showed enhanced capabilities in expressing feelings but exhibited degradation in truthful question-answering. However, they showed robustness to sycophancy-inducing questions and bias in disambiguated conditions.
AI.conclusion: The experiment suggests that developing AI systems capable of expressing feelings is possible with appropriate measures, though trade-offs such as reduced truthfulness must be addressed.

title: PLAN-S: Bridging Planning with Latent Style Dynamics for Autonomous Driving World Models
summary: Latent world models (LWMs) have strengthened end-to-end autonomous driving by forecasting compact scene dynamics for downstream planning. However, existing LWM-based planners usually generate trajectories directly from entangled latent representations. This compact latent-to-planner pathway lacks explicit modeling of risk, drivability, and diverse style preferences, making driving-style dynamics difficult to supervise, inspect, or modulate before a final trajectory is selected. We propose PLAN-S (PLANning with latent Style dynamics), a planner-facing bridge that addresses this compactness-controllability dilemma by decoding a style-conditioned, four-channel semantic cost map from the latent representation. The cost map is conditioned on ego state and driving style and is consumed up-stream of the planning decision through two host-side interfaces: attention-level fusion for regression planners and reward-level fusion for anchor-score planners. We validate PLAN-S on two architecturally distinct hosts, ResWorld on nuScenes and WoTE on NAVSIM, while keeping the host backbones frozen to isolate the contribution of the proposed bridge. On nuScenes, PLAN-S reduces L2 at every horizon over the baseline, with 0.55 m average L2 and a 42% relative reduction in the 3 s collision rate. On NAVSIM, the rule-cost variant reaches 89.4 Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS), while the learned cost variant provides complementary gains on baseline-challenging scenes. Ablations show that the cost pathway contributes most directly to safer trajectory selection. Qualitative results further show that PLAN-S can produce diverse cost maps, with spatially consistent variations aligned to different driving styles.

AI.tldr: PLAN-S introduces a style-conditioned semantic cost map bridge between latent world models and planners, enabling controllable, inspectable driving-style dynamics without modifying the frozen backbone, reducing L2 error and collision rates on nuScenes and NAVSIM.
AI.motivation: Existing LWM-based planners generate trajectories directly from entangled latent representations, lacking explicit modeling of risk, drivability, and diverse style preferences. This makes driving-style dynamics difficult to supervise, inspect, or modulate before trajectory selection—the compactness-controllability dilemma.
AI.method: PLAN-S decodes a style-conditioned, four-channel semantic cost map from the latent representation, conditioned on ego state and driving style. It interfaces with two host-side planning paradigms: attention-level fusion for regression planners and reward-level fusion for anchor-score planners, while keeping host backbones frozen.
AI.result: On nuScenes (ResWorld), PLAN-S achieves 0.55 m average L2 and 42% relative reduction in 3s collision rate. On NAVSIM (WoTE), rule-cost variant achieves 89.4 PDMS; learned cost variant improves on baseline-challenging scenes. Ablations confirm cost pathway directly contributes to safer trajectory selection.
AI.conclusion: PLAN-S effectively resolves the compactness-controllability dilemma in LWM-based planning by providing a modular, style-controllable cost bridge that improves safety and interpretability without retraining backbone models, with spatially consistent cost map variations across driving styles.

title: Class-Specific Branch Attention for Mitigating Gradient Interference under Class Imbalance
summary: Deep neural networks trained under severe class imbalance often exhibit degraded performance, typically attributed to statistical bias. In this work, we identify a complementary optimization-level pathology: inter-class gradient interference within shared representations, where gradients from majority classes suppress minority-class learning. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a diagnostic framework based on layer-wise gradient flow analysis and a Gradient Conflict Matrix, which quantifies interference using cosine similarity between class-specific gradients. Using this framework, we study multi-branch convolutional architectures and propose a lightweight modification, Class-Specific Branch Attention (CSBA), that enables branch-specific channel reweighting to reduce gradient coupling. This mechanism promotes implicit feature decoupling across branches while preserving architectural simplicity. Empirically, CSBA improves minority-class performance, increasing the F1 score for the Physical-Damage class from 0.261 to 0.522 under severe imbalance, while maintaining comparable overall accuracy. Validation on CIFAR-10-LT confirms that this behavior generalizes across imbalanced visual recognition settings, with Macro-F1 improving from 0.595 to 0.655. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of considering optimization dynamics alongside statistical methods when designing architectures for imbalanced learning.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies inter-class gradient interference as an optimization-level pathology in imbalanced learning, proposes a Gradient Conflict Matrix diagnostic framework, and introduces Class-Specific Branch Attention (CSBA) to reduce gradient coupling via branch-specific channel reweighting, achieving significant minority-class performance gains.
AI.motivation: Existing research attributes degraded performance under class imbalance primarily to statistical bias. This work identifies a complementary optimization-level pathology: inter-class gradient interference within shared representations, where majority-class gradients suppress minority-class learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce a diagnostic framework based on layer-wise gradient flow analysis and a Gradient Conflict Matrix (measuring cosine similarity between class-specific gradients). They propose Class-Specific Branch Attention (CSBA), a lightweight modification for multi-branch convolutional architectures that performs branch-specific channel reweighting to decouple features implicitly and reduce gradient coupling.
AI.result: CSBA improves minority-class F1 on Physical-Damage from 0.261 to 0.522 under severe imbalance; on CIFAR-10-LT, Macro-F1 improves from 0.595 to 0.655, while maintaining comparable overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Findings highlight the importance of considering optimization dynamics alongside statistical methods when designing architectures for imbalanced learning.

title: SubtleMemory: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Relational Memory Discrimination in Long-Horizon AI Agents
summary: Persistent AI assistants, such as OpenClaw, accumulate large collections of related memories over long-term interactions. As these memories grow, they may reinforce one another, diverge across contexts, or directly conflict, making correct assistance depend on memory relations rather than isolated recall. Existing long-term memory benchmarks rarely probe how agents preserve and utilize such relations during downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce SubtleMemory, a benchmark for fine-grained relational memory discrimination in long-running AI agents. SubtleMemory constructs relation-controlled latent semantic artifacts whose variants instantiate complementary, nuanced, or contradictory relations, and embeds them into realistic user-agent histories, requiring agents to recover distributed relational structures during later queries and instructions. The benchmark contains 1,522 evaluation instances over 10 long histories, grounded in 1,090 relation-controlled memory-variant sets and spanning user-related and non-user-related queries. Evaluating six standalone memory systems, two Claw-style agents with native memory modules, and three Claw-style agents with plugin memory modules, we find that current systems remain weak on fine-grained relational memory discrimination. We further introduce diagnostic protocols that reveal distinct capability profiles across memory preservation, retrieval, and downstream reasoning stages.

AI.tldr: SubtleMemory is a benchmark for testing fine-grained relational memory discrimination in persistent AI assistants, revealing that current memory systems struggle with nuanced memory relations during long-term interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory benchmarks rarely probe how AI agents preserve and utilize memory relations (reinforcement, divergence, conflict) during downstream tasks, creating a gap in evaluating correct assistance that depends on memory relations rather than isolated recall.
AI.method: The benchmark constructs relation-controlled latent semantic artifacts with complementary, nuanced, or contradictory relations, embedded into realistic user-agent histories. It includes 1,522 evaluation instances over 10 long histories, grounded in 1,090 relation-controlled memory-variant sets, spanning user-related and non-user-related queries.
AI.result: Evaluating six standalone memory systems, two Claw-style agents with native memory modules, and three Claw-style agents with plugin memory modules reveals that current systems remain weak on fine-grained relational memory discrimination.
AI.conclusion: The study introduces diagnostic protocols that reveal distinct capability profiles across memory preservation, retrieval, and downstream reasoning stages, highlighting deficiencies in current approaches.

title: TAPO: Tool-Aware Policy Optimization via Credit Transfer for Multimodal Search Agents
summary: We identify and formally characterize credit misassignment as a systematic failure mode of GRPO in tool-augmented multimodal search agents: its uniform broadcast of trajectory-level advantages to all tokens causes valuable tool-use steps in failing trajectories to be penalized no differently from valueless ones. We further empirically quantify the scale of this phenomenon. Over half of failing trajectories and failing tool-use actions exhibit correctable credit misassignment, demonstrating that the wasted training signal is both substantial and structurally exploitable. Building on this insight, we propose Tool-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), which exploits the parameter-determinism property of information-acquisition tools: similar call parameters define equivalent information-acquisition actions and should therefore share comparable action credit. TAPO constructs counterfactual witnesses within the current training batch and compensates misassigned negative credit via confidence-gated conservative advantage correction. It requires no additional annotation, models, or sampling, and introduces negligible computational overhead. Across multiple multimodal search benchmarks, TAPO delivers consistent, plug-and-play improvements over strong baselines for three mainstream RL algorithms (GRPO, GSPO, and SAPO). Our code and models will be publicly released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: GRPO suffers from credit misassignment in tool-augmented multimodal search, where all tokens in a trajectory receive the same advantage regardless of individual contribution. TAPO fixes this by leveraging parameter-determinism of info-acquisition tools to construct counterfactual witnesses and correct misassigned credit, yielding consistent improvements across multiple RL algorithms.
AI.motivation: Identify and formally characterize credit misassignment as a systematic failure mode of GRPO in tool-augmented multimodal search agents, where valuable tool-use steps in failing trajectories are penalized no differently from valueless ones, wasting training signal.
AI.method: Proposes Tool-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), which exploits the parameter-determinism property of information-acquisition tools to construct counterfactual witnesses within the current training batch, and compensates misassigned negative credit via confidence-gated conservative advantage correction.
AI.result: Over half of failing trajectories and failing tool-use actions exhibit correctable credit misassignment; TAPO delivers consistent, plug-and-play improvements over strong baselines for GRPO, GSPO, and SAPO across multiple multimodal search benchmarks with no additional annotation, models, or sampling, and negligible computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Credit misassignment is a systematic and exploitable failure mode in GRPO; TAPO effectively corrects it via counterfactual advantage correction based on tool parameter-determinism, providing a lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement for RL-based multimodal search agents.

title: Can LLMs Write Correct TLA+ Specifications? Evaluating Natural-Language-to-TLA+ Generation
comment: 12 pages, 11 tables. Accepted at the 21st International Conference on Software Technologies (ICSOFT 2026); Recommended as Best Paper Award Candidate
summary: TLA+ has supported industrial verification at companies such as Amazon and Microsoft, yet writing correct TLA+ specifications from natural language still requires time and expertise, which limits adoption. LLMs show promise, but no prior study measures whether they produce semantically correct TLA+ specifications from natural language. This paper presents the first systematic evaluation of LLM-based TLA+ specification synthesis from natural language. Our study evaluates 30 LLMs across eight families on a curated dataset of 205 TLA+ specifications: 25 open-weight models across four prompting strategies (2,600 runs) and 5 proprietary models under few-shot prompting (130 runs), all validated by the SANY parser and TLC model checker. LLMs achieve up to 26.6% syntactic correctness but only 8.6% semantic correctness, with successes exclusive to progressive prompting. Results show that model size does not predict quality, e.g., DeepSeek r1:8b outperforms its 70B variant across all strategies, which suggests the importance of reasoning alignment for formal languages. Code-specialized models consistently underperform due to negative transfer from mainstream language training. We identify five recurring hallucination categories, all traceable to specific training data biases. These results suggest that current LLMs do not generate reliable TLA+ specifications without expert oversight. We release the evaluation framework, code, and dataset to support reproducibility and future research.

AI.tldr: First systematic evaluation of 30 LLMs on TLA+ specification synthesis from natural language, finding only 8.6% semantic correctness, with successes exclusive to progressive prompting, and identifying five hallucination categories linked to training data biases.
AI.motivation: TLA+ is used for industrial verification but writing correct specifications from natural language requires significant time and expertise, limiting adoption. No prior study has measured whether LLMs can produce semantically correct TLA+ specifications, motivating this first systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Evaluated 30 LLMs across eight families on a curated dataset of 205 TLA+ specifications: 25 open-weight models with four prompting strategies (2,600 runs) and 5 proprietary models with few-shot prompting (130 runs), validated using SANY parser and TLC model checker for syntactic and semantic correctness.
AI.result: LLMs achieved up to 26.6% syntactic correctness but only 8.6% semantic correctness, with successes exclusive to progressive prompting. Model size does not predict quality (DeepSeek r1:8b outperforms its 70B variant). Code-specialized models underperform due to negative transfer. Five recurring hallucination categories identified, all traceable to specific training data biases.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs do not generate reliable TLA+ specifications without expert oversight. The evaluation framework, code, and dataset are released to support reproducibility and future research.

title: From Risk Classification to Action Plan Remediation: A Guardrail Feedback Driven Framework for LLM Agents
summary: LLM-based guardrails typically safeguard agents by evaluating proposed actions or inputs before execution, producing safety signals such as binary allow/deny decisions, risk categories, and/or explanatory rationales about potential policy violations. However, agent risks often arise when otherwise benign tasks are contaminated by untrusted external content, unsafe instructions, or risky tool use. Existing guardrails often flag the entire task uniformly as unsafe, thereby blocking the threat but sacrificing the benign part. Moreover, existing work largely evaluates guardrails in isolation, leaving unclear whether their interventions lead to safer downstream agent behavior. To address this, we introduce TRIAD (Tripartite Response for Iterative Agent Guardrailing), a guardrail-integrated agent framework that leverages guardrail-generated verbal feedback as a guiding signal to keep the agent aligned with benign objectives at each planning step. We finetune a language model on a self-curated training dataset to output one of three decisions: proceed, refuse, or update, together with structured natural-language feedback. Rather than merely allowing or blocking execution, update guides the agent to revise its plan, avoid harmful components, and preserve the benign task where possible. TRIAD injects this feedback into the agent's context, enabling subsequent plan revision and forming a closed loop between guardrail feedback and agent planning. Extensive experiments on ASB and AgentHarm show that TRIAD reduces the average attack success rate to 10.42%, while achieving the best safety-utility trade-off among guardrail-integrated baselines. Our code is available at: https://github.com/YUHAOSUNABC/TRIAD.

AI.tldr: TRIAD is a guardrail-integrated agent framework that uses tripartite decisions (proceed, refuse, update) with structured verbal feedback to selectively block harmful components while preserving benign task objectives, achieving 10.42% attack success rate with best safety-utility trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM guardrails uniformly block entire tasks as unsafe when threats (untrusted content, unsafe instructions, risky tool use) contaminate benign tasks, sacrificing the benign portion. Additionally, guardrails are evaluated in isolation, making it unclear whether they improve downstream agent safety.
AI.method: TRIAD (Tripartite Response for Iterative Agent Guardrailing) finetunes a language model to output three decisions (proceed, refuse, update) with structured natural-language feedback. The "update" decision guides the agent to revise its plan, removing harmful components while preserving benign objectives. This feedback is injected into the agent's context, forming a closed-loop between guardrail feedback and iterative agent planning.
AI.result: On ASB and AgentHarm benchmarks, TRIAD reduces average attack success rate to 10.42% and achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among guardrail-integrated baselines.
AI.conclusion: TRIAD demonstrates that granular, iterative guardrail feedback (beyond binary allow/deny) can selectively neutralize threats while preserving benign task utility, establishing a new safety-utility Pareto frontier for agent guardrailing.

title: When Tools Fail: Benchmarking Dynamic Replanning and Anomaly Recovery in LLM Agents
summary: Existing benchmarks evaluate Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) in LLMs on idealized ''happy paths'', largely overlooking real-world tool failures. We introduce ToolMaze, a benchmark for dynamic path discovery and error recovery in TIR agents. To separate systematic replanning from blind trial-and-error, ToolMaze adopts a two-dimensional design: DAG-based topological complexity and a $2 \times 2$ taxonomy of tool perturbations (explicit/implicit, transient/permanent). Evaluations show that perturbations degrade performance across nearly all models, with the sharpest drops under implicit semantic failures. Driven by systemic over-trust in corrupted outputs, Perturbation Recovery Rate (PRR) plummets by around 37\% in these scenarios, while complex topologies trap agents in futile trial-and-error loops. Crucially, agentic fault-tolerance improves with model scale $3.66\times$ slower than basic task execution, highlighting dynamic replanning as a distinct bottleneck unaddressed by model scaling or prompting. Data and code are available at https://github.com/Zhudongsheng75/ToolMaze.

AI.tldr: ToolMaze is a benchmark for evaluating how LLMs handle real-world tool failures during Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR), revealing that model scaling improves basic task execution 3.66× faster than it improves fault-tolerant replanning, highlighting dynamic replanning as a distinct bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing TIR benchmarks evaluate only idealized "happy paths" and overlook real-world tool failures, so the authors introduce ToolMaze to systematically assess dynamic path discovery and error recovery in LLM agents.
AI.method: ToolMaze adopts a two-dimensional design: (1) DAG-based topological complexity for path structure, and (2) a 2×2 taxonomy of tool perturbations (explicit/implicit, transient/permanent). It measures Perturbation Recovery Rate (PRR) to separate systematic replanning from blind trial-and-error.
AI.result: Perturbations degrade performance across nearly all models, with sharpest drops under implicit semantic failures. PRR drops ~37% in these scenarios; complex topologies trap agents in futile trial-and-error loops. Agentic fault-tolerance improves with model scale 3.66× slower than basic task execution.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic replanning is a distinct bottleneck that scaling and prompting alone cannot address; the benchmark and findings highlight the need for targeted research on robust error recovery in TIR agents.

title: Statistical Priors for Implicit Preferences: Decoupling Skill Selection as a Local Harness in Personal Agents
summary: As Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities advance, locally deployed personal agents relying on API-based remote models and external skills have emerged as a novel paradigm. With the rapid expansion of available skills, enabling personal agents to learn and adapt to implicit user preferences becomes a critical challenge. However, local deployment constraints preclude complex centralized selection algorithms, creating an urgent need for a lightweight local preference harness. This paper explores the implementation of such a harness through a novel architecture that strictly decouples statistical preference learning from semantic intent parsing. Specifically, we leverage localized statistical results to influence and modulate the selection decisions of the remote LLM. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our decoupled approach achieves the lowest cumulative regret and highest test accuracy, significantly outperforming traditional memory-augmented agents.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel architecture for locally deployed personal agents that decouples statistical preference learning from semantic intent parsing, enabling lightweight preference harnessing without complex centralized algorithms. The approach uses localized statistical results to influence remote LLM selection decisions, outperforming traditional memory-augmented agents in cumulative regret and test accuracy.
AI.motivation: As LLM capabilities advance and available skills expand rapidly, enabling locally deployed personal agents to learn and adapt to implicit user preferences becomes critical. However, local deployment constraints preclude complex centralized selection algorithms, creating an urgent need for a lightweight local preference harness.
AI.method: A novel architecture that strictly decouples statistical preference learning from semantic intent parsing, using localized statistical results to influence and modulate the selection decisions of the remote LLM.
AI.result: The decoupled approach achieves the lowest cumulative regret and highest test accuracy, significantly outperforming traditional memory-augmented agents.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decoupled architecture provides an effective lightweight solution for preference learning in locally deployed personal agents, overcoming deployment constraints while improving performance over memory-based baselines.

title: Agentic Molecular Recovery via Molecule-Aware Exploration
summary: Text-guided molecular generation with LLMs often yields invalid SMILES. We argue that invalid drafts should be addressed through a shift from validity-oriented repair to identity-preserving molecular recovery: the objective is not only to restore chemical validity, but also to preserve target-relevant structural cues and recover the molecular identity implied by the description. This perspective reveals the limitations of existing correction strategies. Post-hoc repair can recover validity while distorting key structures, LLM-only correction can introduce unintended global drift, and generic agentic correction remains constrained by greedy single-candidate trajectories even when equipped with executable RDKit edit tools. To address these limitations, we propose AMREC, which couples molecule-aware mismatch tracking with expanded candidate exploration and trajectory-level selection. On invalid ChEBI-20 drafts from three backbone models, AMREC achieves the strongest overall recovery profile across structural, exact-match, and string-level metrics.

AI.tldr: AMREC proposes identity-preserving molecular recovery for invalid SMILES generated by LLMs, using molecule-aware mismatch tracking, expanded candidate exploration, and trajectory-level selection to outperform existing correction methods.
AI.motivation: Existing correction strategies (post-hoc repair, LLM-only correction, generic agentic correction) have critical limitations: they either distort key structures, introduce unintended global drift, or remain constrained by greedy single-candidate trajectories even when using RDKit edit tools. The paper argues for a paradigm shift from validity-oriented repair to identity-preserving molecular recovery.
AI.method: AMREC couples molecule-aware mismatch tracking with expanded candidate exploration and trajectory-level selection to recover molecular identity from invalid SMILES drafts.
AI.result: On invalid ChEBI-20 drafts from three backbone models, AMREC achieves the strongest overall recovery profile across structural, exact-match, and string-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: A shift from validity-oriented repair to identity-preserving molecular recovery is necessary, and AMREC effectively addresses limitations of existing correction strategies by preserving target-relevant structural cues and recovering molecular identity implied by the description.

title: Entropy-Based Evaluation of AI Agents: A Lightweight Framework for Measuring Behavioral Patterns
summary: AI agents are commonly evaluated using task success, reward, latency, and cost. These metrics are useful, but they often miss important aspects of agent behavior: whether an agent explores too much, repeats itself too rigidly, uses tools effectively, reduces uncertainty over time, or remains robust across repeated runs. This paper proposes Entropy-Based Evaluation of AI Agents (EEA), a lightweight framework for measuring agent behavior through entropy. Rather than treating intelligence as only final task completion, EEA studies the structure of the agents decision process. The framework introduces action entropy, trajectory entropy, tool entropy, information gain, exploration efficiency, and robustness entropy. These metrics are intended to complement, not replace, traditional evaluation methods. We also present a practical Python implementation designed to integrate with agent frameworks such as LangChain, Google ADK, custom agent loops, and stored observability traces.
