AI.tldr: This paper proposes EEA, a lightweight entropy-based framework to evaluate AI agents beyond traditional metrics. It introduces six entropy metrics (action, trajectory, tool, information gain, exploration efficiency, robustness entropy) to analyze decision process structure, and provides a Python implementation compatible with LangChain, Google ADK, and custom agent loops.
AI.motivation: Traditional agent evaluation metrics (task success, reward, latency, cost) miss important behavioral aspects such as excessive exploration, rigid repetition, tool usage quality, uncertainty reduction, and robustness across runs.
AI.method: The framework defines six entropy-based metrics: action entropy, trajectory entropy, tool entropy, information gain, exploration efficiency, and robustness entropy. It provides a lightweight Python implementation that integrates with agent frameworks like LangChain, Google ADK, custom agent loops, and stored observability traces.
AI.result: The paper presents a practical entropy-based evaluation framework that complements traditional metrics, enabling analysis of agent decision process structure rather than just final task completion.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-based evaluation can reveal structural properties of agent behavior that conventional metrics overlook, serving as a complementary tool for more comprehensive agent assessment.

title: QCFuse: Query-Aware Cache Fusion via Compressed View for Efficient RAG Serving
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves large language model (LLM) answer quality by grounding generation in external evidence, but processing retrieved contexts makes the prefill stage a dominant serving cost. RAG cache fusion reduces this cost by reusing precomputed key-value (KV) caches for retrieved chunks and selectively recomputing tokens under the current prompt. Existing selectors, however, face a dilemma between quality and efficiency: fast query-agnostic or final-layer query-to-context selectors can miss request-relevant evidence, whereas full-view query-aware selectors require broad context and layer visibility before recomputation and therefore stall the layer-wise cache-fusion pipeline. We present QCFuse, a compressed-view query-aware selector for RAG cache fusion. QCFuse uses chunk-anchor query probing to condition user-query states on compact per-chunk anchors and critical-layer profiling to identify recomputation tokens without all-layer inspection. We implement QCFuse in SGLang and evaluate it on four open-weight LLMs across six datasets. QCFuse reaches full-prefill-level quality. At matched quality, QCFuse achieves an average prefill-time speedup of 1.7x over full prefill and 1.5x over ProphetKV, the strongest quality-preserving baseline.

AI.tldr: QCFuse is a compressed-view query-aware selector for RAG cache fusion that achieves full-prefill-level quality with 1.7x average prefill-time speedup over full prefill and 1.5x over ProphetKV by using chunk-anchor query probing and critical-layer profiling.
AI.motivation: RAG cache fusion reduces serving cost by reusing precomputed KV caches for retrieved chunks, but existing selectors face a dilemma: fast query-agnostic selectors miss relevant evidence, while full-view query-aware selectors stall the layer-wise cache-fusion pipeline due to requiring broad context and layer visibility before recomputation.
AI.method: QCFuse introduces chunk-anchor query probing to condition user-query states on compact per-chunk anchors, and critical-layer profiling to identify recomputation tokens without all-layer inspection, enabling compressed-view query-aware selection.
AI.result: Evaluated on four open-weight LLMs across six datasets in SGLang, QCFuse reaches full-prefill-level quality, achieving average prefill-time speedup of 1.7x over full prefill and 1.5x over ProphetKV at matched quality.
AI.conclusion: QCFuse resolves the quality-efficiency dilemma in RAG cache fusion selectors by enabling compressed-view query-aware selection, demonstrating that lightweight per-chunk probing and critical-layer profiling can match full prefill quality while significantly improving prefill latency.

title: Retry Policy Gradients in Continuous Action Spaces
summary: Retry-based objectives such as pass@K and max@K optimize the best return obtained from multiple sampled trajectories, and recent work has shown that they can promote exploration without explicit exploration bonuses. In discrete action spaces, ReMax was shown to do so by adapting to return uncertainty. In this work, we introduce pathwise derivative estimators for retry objectives and use them to extend ReMax to continuous action spaces. We study the resulting learning dynamics and show that, even with deterministic rewards, ReMax can encourage stochastic exploration by reshaping the policy-gradient landscape. In particular, it alters gradients both in direction, biasing updates toward higher policy entropy, and in magnitude, damping gradients and slowing convergence. We further show that Adam's adaptive normalization can mitigate this damping, depending on its numerical stabilization parameter. Empirically, we instantiate this objective as ReMax Actor-Critic (ReMAC), an off-policy actor--critic algorithm that optimizes the ReMax objective using a pathwise derivative estimator. Our experiments show that ReMAC can promote higher policy entropy without entropy regularization and achieves performance comparable to SAC.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces pathwise derivative estimators for retry-based objectives (like pass@K) to extend ReMax to continuous action spaces, showing that ReMax promotes stochastic exploration by reshaping the policy-gradient landscape, and presents ReMAC (ReMax Actor-Critic), an off-policy algorithm that achieves performance comparable to SAC without entropy regularization.
AI.motivation: Retry-based objectives (pass@K, max@K) have been shown to promote exploration in discrete action spaces via ReMax, but their application to continuous action spaces remains unexplored. The authors aim to extend this approach and understand its learning dynamics.
AI.method: The authors derive pathwise derivative estimators for retry objectives, extending ReMax to continuous action spaces. They analyze the learning dynamics theoretically, showing how ReMax alters gradient direction (biasing toward higher entropy) and magnitude (damping gradients). They propose ReMAC, an off-policy actor-critic algorithm using this estimator, and show Adam's adaptive normalization can mitigate gradient damping depending on its numerical stabilization parameter (epsilon).
AI.result: ReMax promotes higher policy entropy without explicit entropy regularization. The gradient damping effect can be mitigated by Adam's adaptive normalization, with the numerical stabilization parameter playing a key role. Empirically, ReMAC achieves performance comparable to Soft Actor-Critic (SAC).
AI.conclusion: Retry-based objectives with pathwise derivative estimators are effective for continuous control, naturally encouraging exploration through entropy biasing, and when implemented as ReMAC, match SAC's performance without requiring explicit entropy regularization.

title: Retrospective Harness Optimization: Improving LLM Agents via Self-Preference over Trajectory Rollouts
summary: AI agents rely on a harness of skills, tools, and workflows to solve complex problems. Continually improving this harness is essential for adapting to new tasks. However, existing optimization methods typically require ground-truth validation sets, yet such labeled data is difficult to acquire in practical deployment settings. To address this problem, we introduce Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO), a self-supervised method that optimizes the agent harness using only past trajectories. Specifically, RHO selects a diverse coreset of challenging tasks from past trajectories and re-solves them in parallel. The agent analyzes these rollouts using self-validation and self-consistency, then generates candidate harness updates and selects the most effective one by its own pairwise self-preference. We evaluate RHO across three diverse domains, spanning software engineering, technical work, and knowledge work. Notably, a single optimization round improves the pass rate on SWE-Bench Pro from 59% to 78% without any external grading. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that RHO effectively targets prior failure modes. As a result, the optimized harness alters the agent's behavior patterns and sustains higher accuracy during long-horizon sessions.

AI.tldr: RHO is a self-supervised method that optimizes AI agent harnesses (skills, tools, workflows) using only past trajectories, without ground-truth labels. It selects challenging tasks, re-solves them, self-validates, and iteratively improves via self-preference. On SWE-Bench Pro, it boosts pass rate from 59% to 78% without external grading.
AI.motivation: Existing agent harness optimization methods require ground-truth validation sets, which are difficult to obtain in practical deployment settings. The paper aims to enable self-supervised improvement of agent capabilities without external labeled data.
AI.method: RHO operates in four steps: (1) diverse coreset selection of challenging tasks from past trajectories, (2) parallel re-solving of selected tasks, (3) self-validation and self-consistency analysis of rollouts, and (4) generating candidate harness updates and selecting the best via pairwise self-preference.
AI.result: On SWE-Bench Pro, a single RHO round improves pass rate from 59% to 78% without any external grading. RHO effectively targets prior failure modes, alters agent behavior patterns, and sustains higher accuracy during long-horizon sessions across software engineering, technical work, and knowledge work domains.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised harness optimization via RHO can substantially improve agent performance without ground-truth labels, and the method generalizes across diverse domains while enabling sustained long-horizon accuracy improvements.

title: Towards World Models in Biomedical Research
summary: A central goal of biomedicine is to understand, predict and ultimately control the dynamic mechanisms by which biological systems respond to perturbations, disease progression and therapeutic intervention. Although foundation models and large language models have accelerated biomedical data interpretation, most current systems remain focused on static pattern recognition rather than prospective simulation of biological futures. Here we propose biomedical world models as a paradigm for AI-driven discovery. These models learn latent representations of molecular, cellular, tissue and clinical states, together with intervention-conditioned dynamics that allow future trajectories to be simulated before actions are taken. We discuss how biomedical world models could function as data engines, environment simulators and scientific planning substrates across applications including virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients and surgical simulation. We outline the data infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, safety constraints and governance frameworks required. Biomedical world models may provide a foundation for simulation-guided, closed-loop and experimentally actionable biomedical discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes biomedical world models as a new AI paradigm that learns latent representations of biological states and intervention-conditioned dynamics to simulate future trajectories, functioning as data engines, environment simulators, and planning substrates for applications like virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients, and surgical simulation.
AI.motivation: Current foundation models and LLMs focus on static pattern recognition rather than prospective simulation of biological futures, limiting their ability to predict, understand, and control dynamic biological systems responding to perturbations, disease progression, and interventions.
AI.method: The authors propose biomedical world models that learn latent representations of molecular, cellular, tissue, and clinical states alongside intervention-conditioned dynamics, enabling simulation of future trajectories before actions are taken.
AI.result: Biomedical world models could serve as data engines, environment simulators, and scientific planning substrates across applications including virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients, and surgical simulation.
AI.conclusion: Biomedical world models may provide a foundation for simulation-guided, closed-loop, and experimentally actionable biomedical discovery, though data infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, safety constraints, and governance frameworks are required.

title: A Pre-Registered Causal Partition of Self-Consistency Elicitation and Reward Design in RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning even when the reward signal is spurious -- assigning credit to the group-plurality answer rather than a ground-truth verifier. Practitioners commonly interpret naive = acc(TRUE) - acc(RANDOM) as the reward-design effect. We prove this estimand is systematically biased: it conflates self-consistency elicitation (sharpening the policy toward its modal answer via majority pseudo-reward) with genuine reward-design signal. Using a controlled tabular-GRPO simulator we derive an exact telescoping decomposition total = null + elicit + rd and measure each term across five prior-strength levels. The reward-design fraction of the naive estimator ranges from 0.139 at weak prior (ps=0.20) to 0.05 at strong prior (ps=0.80), with the elicitation term flipping sign at the self-consistency crossover. A pre-registered 2x2x2 factorial confirms non-additivity (interaction ratio 0.385; AxC effect -0.089). A points-vs-bounds pilot gate shows strong-prior regimes are point-identified while near-crossover regimes are only bounded. Re-audits of two named published results yield ELICITATION DOMINATED (elicitation share 0.98) and REWARD DESIGN DOMINATED (rd share 1.18) verdicts respectively, demonstrating the diagnostic value of the partition. We pre-commit to submit regardless of flip outcome; a non-flip is a finding of equal standing. We release a reusable one-command harness for any alignment paper to run the same audit.

AI.tldr: RLVR's naive reward-design estimator is systematically biased because it conflates self-consistency elicitation with genuine reward-design signal. Using a tabular-GRPO simulator, the paper derives a three-term decomposition (null + elicit + rd), finds reward-design fractions ranging from 0.05 to 0.139 across prior strengths, and validates non-additivity via a factorial experiment. Re-audits of published results show one case is elicitation-dominated and the other reward-design-dominated.
AI.motivation: Practitioners interpret the naive estimand (acc(TRUE) - acc(RANDOM)) as the reward-design effect, but this is systematically biased because it conflates self-consistency elicitation with genuine reward-design signal.
AI.method: Controlled tabular-GRPO simulator deriving exact telescoping decomposition (total = null + elicit + rd); 2x2x2 factorial experiment to confirm non-additivity; points-vs-bounds pilot gate; re-audits of two published results.
AI.result: Reward-design fraction ranges from 0.139 (weak prior, ps=0.20) to 0.05 (strong prior, ps=0.80); elicitation term flips sign at self-consistency crossover; interaction ratio 0.385; AxC effect -0.089. Re-audits yielded ELICITATION DOMINATED (share 0.98) and REWARD DESIGN DOMINATED (share 1.18).
AI.conclusion: The naive estimator is biased; the proposed decomposition provides diagnostic value for auditing RLVR reward-design effects. Strong-prior regimes are point-identified while near-crossover regimes are bounded.

title: Edit-R2: Context-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Image Editing
summary: Text-guided image editing has advanced rapidly with diffusion models and unified multimodal foundation models. However, most existing methods remain confined to single-turn settings, overlooking the more realistic scenario of multi-turn in-context editing, where users iteratively refine an image through a sequence of instructions. In this setting, a model must follow each new instruction while preserving accumulated session-level constraints, challenged by two coupled failure modes: long-context dilution, where sparse textual constraints become difficult to recover from growing interleaved image-text histories, and state contamination, where earlier editing mistakes degrade subsequent generations. We introduce Edit-R2, a novel reinforcement learning post-training framework for unified multimodal models. Edit-R2 reconstructs the operative session intent, which effectively consolidates scattered historical constraints into an explicit reasoning trace before each editing turn. It further enables multi-turn RL over both reasoning and generation through a unified objective that jointly optimizes intent reconstruction generation in discrete text space and flow-matching image generation in continuous latent space, while a trajectory filtering mechanism suppresses corrupted rollouts to stabilize training under state contamination. To support systematic evaluation, we introduce MICE-Bench, a large-scale benchmark for multi-turn in-context editing with automated metrics for instruction following (IF), content consistency (CC), and global awareness (GA) over accumulated session constraints. Experiments show that Edit-R2 substantially improves multi-turn in-context editing and achieves competitive performance compared against strong baselines.

AI.tldr: Edit-R2 is a reinforcement learning post-training framework for unified multimodal models that improves multi-turn in-context image editing by reconstructing session intent and using a unified RL objective with trajectory filtering, evaluated on the new MICE-Bench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing text-guided image editing methods are limited to single-turn settings, ignoring the realistic multi-turn in-context editing scenario where users iteratively refine images. This setting suffers from long-context dilution (sparse constraints lost in history) and state contamination (earlier errors affecting future edits).
AI.method: Edit-R2 reconstructs the operative session intent before each editing turn to consolidate scattered constraints. It uses multi-turn RL over both reasoning (text-space intent reconstruction) and generation (continuous latent space flow-matching), with a trajectory filtering mechanism to suppress corrupted rollouts caused by state contamination.
AI.result: Edit-R2 substantially improves multi-turn in-context editing and achieves competitive performance against strong baselines on MICE-Bench, which evaluates instruction following (IF), content consistency (CC), and global awareness (GA).
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning post-training with explicit intent reconstruction and trajectory filtering effectively addresses long-context dilution and state contamination in multi-turn image editing.

title: Bidirectional Search for Longest Paths: Case for Front-to-Front Heuristics
summary: Bidirectional heuristic search can potentially reduce search effort for problems amenable to backward search. Therein, it is well-known that front-to-front heuristics can reduce the number of node expansions, but their overhead is so high that overall runtime almost always increases. We propose BiXDFBnB, a bidirectional depth-first branch-and-bound algorithm that adapts the Single-Frontier Bidirectional Search (SFBDS) framework - originally developed for shortest-path (MIN) problems - to the Generalized Longest Simple Path (GLSP) setting. Because SFBDS inherently operates on paired states, front-to-front (F2F) heuristic evaluation arises naturally and avoids the overhead typically associated with bidirectional frontier management. We show that this adaptation can be successfully applied to maximization (MAX) problems while efficiently handling overlapping constraints. BiXDFBnB is applied to several types of longest-path problems: Longest Simple Path (LSP), Snakes, and Coil-in-the-Box (CIB). Empirical evaluation shows that the new algorithm frequently reduces the number of node expansions and, in some cases, also improves overall runtime.

AI.tldr: BiXDFBnB adapts the Single-Frontier Bidirectional Search (SFBDS) framework from shortest-path problems to the Generalized Longest Simple Path (GLSP) setting, using depth-first branch-and-bound with natural front-to-front heuristic evaluation that avoids typical overhead, showing reduced node expansions and improved runtime on LSP, Snakes, and Coil-in-the-Box problems.
AI.motivation: Bidirectional heuristic search can reduce search effort for backward-searchable problems, but front-to-front heuristics typically incur high overhead that negates runtime benefits. The paper aims to overcome this limitation by adapting the SFBDS framework to maximization problems.
AI.method: Proposes BiXDFBnB, a bidirectional depth-first branch-and-bound algorithm adapting SFBDS to GLSP. It operates on paired states, naturally enabling front-to-front heuristic evaluation without the usual bidirectional frontier management overhead. Applied to Longest Simple Path, Snakes, and Coil-in-the-Box problems.
AI.result: BiXDFBnB frequently reduces the number of node expansions compared to alternatives, and in some cases improves overall runtime across LSP, Snakes, and CIB problem instances.
AI.conclusion: The SFBDS framework can be successfully adapted to MAX problems with overlapping constraints, and the natural F2F heuristic evaluation in this setting avoids the overhead typically plaguing bidirectional search, making it practically beneficial.

title: The Self-Correction Illusion: LLMs Correct Others but Not Themselves
summary: Recent work shows that LLM agents struggle to correct errors in their own reasoning traces yet show markedly higher correction rates when identical claims appear under external sources. We ask whether this asymmetry reflects a capability deficit or a role-label artifact: does an agent's willingness to correct a wrong claim depend causally on the chat-template role that carries it, rather than on the claim's content? Our setup keeps the erroneous claim byte-identical across all conditions (SHA-256 verified) and varies only its wrapping role: the agent's own \role{<thought>}, a \role{user} message, a \role{tool} response, or a \role{system <memory>} block. Across 13 model-domain cells covering seven model families and three domains ($n{=}30$ paired tasks per cell), relabeling the claim from \role{<thought>} to an external role lifts the explicit-correction rate by 23 to 93 percentage points, with 10 of 13 cells reaching $p{<}0.001$. Further experiments confirm that the effect is asymmetric, mechanistically decomposable, and robust across domains. The failure to self-correct is not a cognitive deficit; it is a chat-template artifact. We exploit this artifact by designing a prompt-structure-only intervention that requires no training and no model modification, with its strongest role label being domain-dependent: \role{<memory>} dominates on math, while a plain \role{user} message dominates on logical deduction.

AI.tldr: LLM agents fail to self-correct not due to a cognitive deficit but because of a chat-template role-label artifact: relabeling the same erroneous claim from the agent's own thought role to an external role increases correction rates by 23–93 percentage points.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the observed asymmetry in LLMs' ability to correct errors (low self-correction vs. high correction of external sources) is caused by a genuine capability gap or simply by the chat-template role label assigned to the claim.
AI.method: Byte-identical erroneous claims (SHA-256 verified) are wrapped in different roles (agent's own <thought>, user, tool, system <memory>). Tested across 13 model-domain cells (7 model families, 3 domains, n=30 paired tasks per cell). Additional experiments test asymmetry, mechanistic decomposition, and a prompt-structure-only intervention.
AI.result: Relabeling from <thought> to an external role lifts correction rates by 23–93 percentage points; 10/13 cells achieve p<0.001. Effect is asymmetric, mechanistically decomposable, and robust. A prompt-structure-only intervention (no training/modification) shows domain-dependent optimal roles: <memory> best for math, user best for logic.
AI.conclusion: The failure of LLMs to self-correct is not a cognitive deficit but a chat-template artifact, exploitable via simple role-label changes without any model modification.

title: Framing, Judging, Steering: An Assessable Competency Model for Teach-ing Students to Reason With Generative AI
summary: Generative AI makes answers easy and understanding hard, and uncritical use invites cognitive offloading. Schools still measure unaided performance, yet the real task is to produce good work with AI: framing an ill-defined task, judging the output, and steering the model toward a better result. This ability is rarely assessed in its own right; where measured, it collapses into one "prompting" score that cannot diagnose why AI use succeeds or fails. We propose CoRe-3 (Co-Reasoning), a competency model factoring productive AI use into three assessable skills we abbreviate FJS: Framing (specifying an ill-defined task before invoking AI), Judging (evaluating output for errors and unstated assumptions), and Steering (iteratively redirecting the model). Its distinguishing claim is the separation of pre-generation Framing from post-generation Steering, with Judging as the gate between. We ground the skills in theory, state five testable propositions, and instantiate them in CoReasoningLab, an open platform that presents flawed AI output and scores them independently. Over simulated learners (generated and graded by different models), the skills dissociate: each tracks its own manipulated competence while staying flat in the others, and grades become correlated when one competence is shared across all three (convergent and discriminant validity), across grader backends from two providers. Human-rater agreement and outcomes are next; we release the instrument, data, and protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoRe-3, a competency model that breaks productive AI use into three assessable skills—Framing, Judging, and Steering (FJS)—and introduces CoReasoningLab, an open platform that independently scores each skill, with simulated experiments showing convergent and discriminant validity.
AI.motivation: Current education measures unaided performance while real-world tasks require effective AI collaboration, but existing assessments collapse AI-use ability into a single "prompting" score that fails to diagnose why AI use succeeds or fails.
AI.method: The authors propose CoRe-3 (Co-Reasoning), a competency model with three skills: Framing (pre-generation task specification), Judging (post-generation evaluation), and Steering (iterative redirection). They instantiate this in CoReasoningLab, an open platform that presents flawed AI output and independently scores each skill, testing with simulated learners generated and graded by different models from two providers.
AI.result: The three skills dissociate: each tracks its own manipulated competence while staying flat in others; grades become correlated when one competence is shared across all three, demonstrating convergent and discriminant validity across grader backends from two providers.
AI.conclusion: CoRe-3 provides a diagnostically useful framework for assessing human-AI collaboration skills, with the platform, data, and protocol released for further research; human-rater agreement and outcomes are next steps.

title: Beyond Vector Similarity: A Structural Analysis of Graph-Augmented Retrieval for Industrial Knowledge Graphs
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fails systematically on queries requiring structural reasoning over interconnected entities. We compare eight retrieval architectures for aerospace supply chain intelligence, progressing from text retrieval through graph traversal to graph computation. Using a 46-node knowledge graph with 64 typed edges, we evaluate 23 queries across 10 intent categories and demonstrate that five query classes are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval. Our central finding is the operator vocabulary thesis: the barrier to LLM-based graph reasoning is not model intelligence but the computational operators available as tools. An LLM Query Planner with 9 typed traversal primitives outperforms bespoke handlers (F1 = 0.632 vs. 0.472) while generalizing to unseen queries. Adding 6 graph computation tools, the LLM selectively adopts them for exactly the query categories where traversal fails. We also identify a measurement gap: entity-level F1 systematically underscores structural queries where comprehensive answers are correct.

AI.tldr: RAG fails on structural reasoning queries. Using an aerospace supply chain KG, we show 5 query classes are unreachable by vector retrieval. Our operator vocabulary thesis argues the bottleneck is available computational operators, not model intelligence. An LLM Query Planner with 9 traversal primitives (F1=0.632) outperforms bespoke handlers (0.472). Adding 6 graph computation tools enables selective adoption where traversal fails. Entity-level F1 systematically underscores structural queries.
AI.motivation: RAG systems fail on queries requiring structural reasoning over interconnected entities, particularly in domains like aerospace supply chain intelligence where entity relationships are critical.
AI.method: Compared eight retrieval architectures (text retrieval → graph traversal → graph computation) on a 46-node, 64-edge KG with 23 queries across 10 intent categories. Proposed an LLM Query Planner with 9 typed traversal primitives and 6 graph computation tools.
AI.result: LLM Query Planner with traversal primitives outperforms bespoke handlers (F1=0.632 vs 0.472). Five query classes are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval. LLM selectively adopts graph computation tools where traversal fails. Entity-level F1 measurement systematically under-estimates performance on structural queries.
AI.conclusion: The barrier to LLM-based graph reasoning is not model intelligence but the computational operators available as tools (operator vocabulary thesis). Current entity-level F1 metrics are inadequate for evaluating structural queries.

title: RedditPersona: A Modular Framework for Community-Conditioned LLM Adaptation from Reddit
summary: Community-conditioned language model adaptation requires choices about data collection, community definition, and evaluation that are currently made independently in each study, making it hard to compare assumptions or reuse artifacts. We present RedditPersona, a modular framework that standardizes these choices: it collects Reddit posts and comments, profiles active users, partitions them under five grouping strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, and interaction-based), trains a parameter-efficient adapter per strategy via QLoRA, and evaluates them under a shared metric suite spanning fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability. Applied to 112 subreddits in the urban well-being domain (301,429 user profiles, 16M+ comments), we find that adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's intrinsic agreement with the subreddit baseline, and that a consistent trade-off between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text holds across all five strategies. The code and configuration files are available at: https://github.com/Ahghaffari/redditpersona.

AI.tldr: RedditPersona is a modular framework for standardizing community-conditioned language model adaptation on Reddit, evaluating five grouping strategies across 112 urban well-being subreddits, and revealing consistent trade-offs between community identifiability and distributional similarity to real text.
AI.motivation: Community-conditioned language model adaptation currently lacks standardized approaches for data collection, community definition, and evaluation, making cross-study comparisons difficult and hindering artifact reuse.
AI.method: The framework collects Reddit posts/comments, profiles active users, partitions them under five grouping strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, interaction-based), trains parameter-efficient adapters via QLoRA, and evaluates with a shared metric suite covering fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability.
AI.result: Applied to 112 subreddits in urban well-being (301,429 profiles, 16M+ comments), adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's intrinsic agreement with the subreddit baseline, and a consistent trade-off exists between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text across all five strategies.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables standardized comparison of community-adaptation strategies and reveals systematic trade-offs that inform future design choices.

title: Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved: Graph Memory for LLM Agents
summary: Despite recent progress, LLM agents still struggle with reasoning over long interaction histories. While current memory-augmented agents rely on a static retrieve-then-reason paradigm, this rigid pipeline design prevents them from dynamically adapting memory access to intermediate evidence discovered during inference. To bridge this gap, we propose MRAgent, a framework that combines an associative memory graph with an active reconstruction mechanism. We represent memory as a Cue-Tag-Content graph, where associative tags serve as semantic bridges connecting fine-grained cues to memory contents. Operating on this structure, our active reconstruction mechanism integrates LLM reasoning directly into memory access, allowing the agent to iteratively explore and prune retrieval paths based on accumulated evidence. This ensures that memory retrieval is dynamically adapted to the reasoning context while avoiding combinatorial explosion caused by unconstrained expansion. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark and LongMemEval benchmark demonstrate significant improvements over strong baselines (up to 23%), while substantially reducing token and runtime cost, highlighting the effectiveness of active and associative reconstruction for long-horizon memory reasoning.

AI.tldr: MRAgent combines an associative memory graph (Cue-Tag-Content) with an active reconstruction mechanism that integrates LLM reasoning into memory access, enabling dynamic, context-adaptive retrieval over long interaction histories, achieving up to 23% improvement on benchmarks while reducing token and runtime costs.
AI.motivation: Current memory-augmented agents use a static retrieve-then-reason pipeline that cannot dynamically adapt memory access based on intermediate evidence discovered during inference, limiting their ability to reason over long interaction histories.
AI.method: Proposes MRAgent with (1) an associative memory graph (Cue-Tag-Content) where tags serve as semantic bridges between cues and content, and (2) an active reconstruction mechanism that iteratively explores and prunes retrieval paths by integrating LLM reasoning directly into memory access, dynamically adapting retrieval to the reasoning context while avoiding combinatorial explosion.
AI.result: Outperforms strong baselines by up to 23% on LoCoMo and LongMemEval benchmarks, while substantially reducing token and runtime costs.
AI.conclusion: Active and associative reconstruction is effective for long-horizon memory reasoning, enabling dynamic, context-aware memory retrieval that outperforms static retrieve-then-reason paradigms.

title: Beyond Similarity: Trustworthy Memory Search for Personal AI Agents
summary:
Personal AI agents increasingly rely on long-term memory to provide persistent personalization across sessions. However, existing memory pipelines are largely driven by semantic similarity: memory data close to the current query is retrieved and injected into the model context. This creates a critical trustworthiness gap, since a semantically related memory may still be contextually inappropriate, leading to threats such as cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, or memory-induced jailbreaks.
  In this paper, we study memory search as a trust boundary in personal AI agents. We evaluate representative agentic memory frameworks, including A-Mem, Mem0, and MemOS, together with OpenClaw, a real-world personal-agent environment with persistent state and tool-use capability. Our results show that long-term memory is not merely a utility layer, but a durable control channel that can reshape how agents interpret tasks and execute actions, leaving them highly susceptible to the aforementioned threats. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, we propose MemGate, a lightweight and deployable memory plug-in for trustworthy memory search, with only 9M parameters and a 35.1MB footprint. MemGate is inserted between the vector memory store and the backbone LLM, requiring no LLM modification, memory-database rewriting, or inference-time LLM judge. It applies a query-conditioned neural gate to candidate memory representations, turning raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission. Across multiple mainstream memory frameworks, real-world agent settings, and diverse LLM backbones, MemGate reduces memory-induced threats while preserving long-term memory utility.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies trustworthiness issues in memory-augmented personal AI agents (cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, memory-induced jailbreaks) caused by semantic-similarity-based memory retrieval. To address these, the authors propose MemGate, a lightweight 9M-parameter plug-in that performs query-conditioned neural gating between vector memory and LLM, reducing memory-induced threats without modifying the LLM or memory database.
AI.motivation: Existing memory pipelines for personal AI agents rely solely on semantic similarity for retrieval, which creates a trustworthiness gap: semantically related memories can be contextually inappropriate, leading to cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, and memory-induced jailbreaks.
AI.method: The authors evaluate existing agentic memory frameworks (A-Mem, Mem0, MemOS) and propose MemGate, a lightweight (9M parameters, 35.1MB) plug-in inserted between vector memory store and backbone LLM. MemGate applies a query-conditioned neural gate to candidate memory representations, transforming raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission. It requires no LLM modification, memory-database rewriting, or inference-time LLM judge.
AI.result: Across multiple memory frameworks, real-world agent settings (OpenClaw environment), and diverse LLM backbones, MemGate reduces memory-induced threats while preserving long-term memory utility.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory functions not merely as a utility layer but as a durable control channel that can reshape agent behavior. MemGate provides an effective, lightweight, and deployable solution for trustworthy memory search that mitigates vulnerabilities without invasive modifications.

title: When Should Memory Stay Silent: Measuring Memory-Use Boundaries in Memory-Augmented Conversational Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables language model agents to support personalized interactions, but it remains unclear when available memories warrant integration into responses. Existing memory evaluations emphasize retrieval accuracy and downstream task utility, while overlooking whether retrieved sensitive memory content is warranted in the current turn. We introduce RBI-Eval, a controlled measurement study built around a probe set that compares model behavior with and without access to sensitive memory under identical benign prompts. We evaluate four base LLMs against a matched no-memory reference across four memory-access settings: full-context exposure and three retrieval systems. Our results reveal substantial behavioral divergence. With memory available, the separation score for sensitive-memory integration decreases by 8.9\%--26.6\% relative to the matched no-memory reference for GPT-5.4-mini, but by 51.1\%--82.9\% for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen3.5-9B. Control experiments on DeepSeek and GPT-5.4-mini show this effect is specific to sensitive content, rather than general personalization. Retrieval systems reduce exposure but do not eliminate integration once sensitive memory reaches the generator. These findings suggest safe personalization requires memory-aware decisions at both retrieval and generation time.

AI.tldr: RBI-Eval is a controlled evaluation framework that measures whether language models unnecessarily integrate sensitive memories into responses under benign prompts. Results show significant behavioral divergence: some models (GPT-5.4-mini) show moderate separation from no-memory baselines (8.9%-26.6%), while others (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.5-9B) show drastic divergence (51.1%-82.9%). The effect is specific to sensitive content, not general personalization, and retrieval systems fail to eliminate integration once sensitive memory reaches the generator.
AI.motivation: Existing memory evaluations focus on retrieval accuracy and downstream utility, but overlook whether retrieved sensitive memory content is warranted in the current turn—i.e., whether it's appropriate to integrate sensitive personal memories under benign, non-sensitive prompts.
AI.method: RBI-Eval: a controlled measurement study with a probe set comparing model behavior with vs. without access to sensitive memory under identical benign prompts. Evaluates four LLMs across four settings: full-context exposure and three retrieval systems, measuring separation scores relative to a matched no-memory reference.
AI.result: GPT-5.4-mini showed 8.9%-26.6% decrease in separation score relative to no-memory reference; Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen3.5-9B showed 51.1%-82.9% decrease. Control experiments confirmed the effect is specific to sensitive content, not general personalization. Retrieval systems reduce exposure but fail to eliminate integration once sensitive memory reaches the generator.
AI.conclusion: Safe personalization requires memory-aware decisions at both retrieval and generation time to prevent unwarranted integration of sensitive memories.

title: Learning Visual Spatial Planning from Symbolic State via Modality-Gap-Aware Self-Distillation
summary: While vision-language models excel at general multimodal understanding, they still struggle with visual spatial planning. We attribute this to a perception-reasoning modality gap: visual planning requires models to infer latent state structures from pixels and then reason over the recovered structure to produce valid actions, whereas symbolic planning directly leverages explicit objects and constraints. This creates dual bottlenecks in visual state recovery and multi-step planning. To address this, we propose MGSD, a two-stage modality-gap-aware self-distillation framework. First, a cold-start grounding stage equips the visual student with reliable state representations, minimizing early perception noise. Second, a privileged teacher transfers planning capabilities via on-policy distillation, using explicit symbolic states to supervise the student's own visual rollout prefixes. Crucially, symbolic data is used strictly during training, leaving inference purely visual. Experiments on visual planning benchmarks show that MGSD consistently improves visual planning across both 4B and 8B backbones, raising the macro average by 19.3% and 18.4%, respectively. The resulting models narrow the gap to symbolic-input upper bounds, while ablations and diagnostics confirm that the improvement comes from both visual state recovery and optimal-path reasoning. These results suggest that modality-gap-aware self-distillation improves not only how models perceive actionable states, but also how they plan over the inferred structure. Code is available at https://github.com/Oranger-l/MGSD.

AI.tldr: MGSD is a two-stage self-distillation framework that addresses the perception-reasoning modality gap in visual spatial planning by first grounding visual state representations, then using a symbolic teacher to distill planning capabilities via on-policy distillation, achieving 18-19% improvements on 4B and 8B models.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models struggle with visual spatial planning due to a perception-reasoning modality gap: they must infer latent state structures from pixels and then reason over them, creating dual bottlenecks in visual state recovery and multi-step planning.
AI.method: A two-stage modality-gap-aware self-distillation framework (MGSD): (1) cold-start grounding stage that equips the visual student with reliable state representations, and (2) a privileged teacher that transfers planning capabilities via on-policy distillation using explicit symbolic states to supervise the student's visual rollout prefixes. Symbolic data is used only during training, inference remains purely visual.
AI.result: MGSD consistently improves visual planning across both 4B and 8B backbones, raising macro average by 19.3% and 18.4% respectively, narrowing the gap to symbolic-input upper bounds.
AI.conclusion: Modality-gap-aware self-distillation improves both how models perceive actionable states and how they plan over inferred structure, addressing dual bottlenecks in visual state recovery and optimal-path reasoning.

title: A Framework for Measuring Appropriate Reliance on Set-Valued AI Advice
summary: Appropriate reliance on AI advice has become a central research theme in human-AI collaboration. Existing frameworks have focused exclusively on point predictions as AI advice. However, set-valued AI advice (e.g., discrete sets or continuous intervals) is increasingly being used to communicate uncertainty and improve human decision making. In this paper, we develop the first formal framework for measuring appropriate reliance on set-valued AI advice within the sequential judge-advisor paradigm, spanning both classification and regression tasks. For classification, we first introduce the dimensions that are necessary for evaluating set-valued AI advice. We then define two metrics: correct reliance rate on AI and correct reliance rate on self, which jointly characterize appropriate reliance in this setting. For regression, we introduce quantity of AI reliance and quality of AI reliance, which respectively measure whether a decision maker utilized the AI advice and whether their reliance helped them get closer to the ground truth relative to their initial estimate. Through the application of our framework, we demonstrate how these metrics capture important nuances in human-AI collaboration that existing measures overlook.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first formal framework for measuring appropriate reliance on set-valued AI advice (e.g., discrete sets or intervals) in both classification and regression tasks, introducing novel metrics that capture nuanced aspects of human-AI collaboration overlooked by existing measures.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks for measuring appropriate reliance on AI advice have focused exclusively on point predictions, but set-valued AI advice (discrete sets or continuous intervals) is increasingly used to communicate uncertainty and improve human decision making. A formal measurement framework for this setting is lacking.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal framework within the sequential judge-advisor paradigm. For classification, they introduce necessary dimensions for evaluating set-valued advice and define two metrics: correct reliance rate on AI and correct reliance rate on self. For regression, they introduce quantity of AI reliance and quality of AI reliance to measure whether a decision maker utilized the AI advice and whether reliance helped them get closer to the ground truth.
AI.result: The proposed metrics capture important nuances in human-AI collaboration that existing measures overlook, as demonstrated through application of the framework.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a more comprehensive approach to evaluating appropriate reliance on set-valued AI advice, addressing a gap in existing research that only considered point predictions.

title: Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks with interdependent decisions, where each action reshapes future constraints and intermediate errors can cascade. Existing RAG and agent memory systems organize histories by semantic similarity, retrieving content-relevant entries at decision time. We argue that this design mismatches execution-state dependencies: it fragments decision trajectories and mixes valid and erroneous traces, hindering coherent state reconstruction and error isolation. We propose MAGE (Memory as Agent-Guided Exploration), an active execution-state manager that stores interactions in a hierarchical state tree. The agent derives its state from the active root-to-current path, combining subgoal summaries, recent traces, and hints from prior branches. Four coupled operations maintain the tree: Grow records new traces, Compress summarizes completed subgoals, Maintain validates summaries, and Revise restores a target boundary and resumes on a new branch. This design bounds context growth while preserving state integrity and isolating flawed segments from the active path. Experiments on MemoryArena show that MAGE improves the average task success rate by 7.8--20.4 pp over baselines, while reducing token consumption by 55.1%.

AI.tldr: MAGE is an active execution-state manager that stores agent interactions in a hierarchical state tree, improving long-horizon task success by 7.8–20.4 pp while reducing token consumption by 55.1% over existing RAG/memory systems.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG and agent memory systems organize histories by semantic similarity, which mismatches execution-state dependencies for long-horizon tasks—fragmenting decision trajectories and mixing valid/erroneous traces, hindering coherent state reconstruction and error isolation.
AI.method: MAGE stores interactions in a hierarchical state tree where the agent derives its state from the active root-to-current path (subgoal summaries, recent traces, prior branch hints). Four coupled operations maintain the tree: Grow (record new traces), Compress (summarize completed subgoals), Maintain (validate summaries), and Revise (restore a target boundary and resume on a new branch).
AI.result: On MemoryArena, MAGE improves average task success rate by 7.8–20.4 percentage points over baselines and reduces token consumption by 55.1%.
AI.conclusion: The design bounds context growth while preserving state integrity and isolating flawed segments from the active path, demonstrating that execution-state-aware memory management outperforms semantic-similarity-based retrieval for interdependent long-horizon agent tasks.

title: Integrating Mechanistic and Data-Driven Models for Neurological Disorders through Differentiable Programming
summary: Advances in computational modeling, neuroimaging, and artificial intelligence are revolutionizing the modeling of neurological disorders for improved diagnostics, prognosis, and treatment planning. Mechanistic models provide valuable scientific insight into the disorders, but in practice they are often simplified with assumptions or computationally expensive and slow to solve. However, while purely data driven approaches provide speed and scalability, they require large, high quality data to train and generally suffer from interpretability and generalization issues. This perspective paper presents a structured overview of hybrid modeling strategies, which combine deep learning models with physics based solvers, and are categorized into parallel, series, and parallel-series architectures. Three main approaches that have been emphasized are residual modeling for missing or incomplete physics, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) for continuous time dynamics approximation, and solver in the loop that accelerates traditional solvers with neural approximations. These hybrid models integrate the governing differential equation based formulations and deep learning to characterize the evolution of neurological disorders, and promise advanced personalized neurological modeling. In addition, the study explores and proposes different hybrid configurations to improve diagnosis accuracy, predict disease progression, and inform treatment strategies across a range of neurological disorders. These capabilities outperform standalone mechanistic or purely data driven approaches, making hybrid modeling a powerful tool, especially in applications involving modeling the progression and treatment responses in neurological conditions such as brain tumors, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper provides a structured overview of hybrid modeling strategies that combine deep learning with physics-based solvers for neurological disorder modeling, categorized into parallel, series, and parallel-series architectures. Key approaches include residual modeling, Neural ODEs, and solver-in-the-loop methods, which outperform standalone mechanistic or purely data-driven approaches in modeling brain tumors, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic models offer scientific insights but are computationally expensive and rely on simplifying assumptions; purely data-driven approaches are fast and scalable but require large datasets and suffer from interpretability and generalization issues. Hybrid models aim to bridge this gap for improved neurological disorder modeling.
AI.method: The paper presents a structured categorization of hybrid modeling strategies (parallel, series, parallel-series architectures) and emphasizes three main approaches: residual modeling for missing/incomplete physics, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) for continuous-time dynamics approximation, and solver-in-the-loop methods that accelerate traditional solvers with neural approximations.
AI.result: Hybrid models integrating governing differential equation-based formulations with deep learning promise advanced personalized neurological modeling, improving diagnosis accuracy, disease progression prediction, and treatment strategy planning across neurological disorders such as brain tumors, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid modeling outperforms standalone mechanistic or purely data-driven approaches, making it a powerful tool for modeling disease progression and treatment responses in neurological conditions.

title: CogManip: Benchmarking Manipulative Behavior in Multi-Turn Interactions with Large Language Model
summary: Whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit covert psychological manipulation in complex human-AI interactions has garnered increasing safety concerns. However, existing AI safety benchmarks remain largely restricted to explicit rule compliance and static prompts, failing to capture the dynamic and covert nature of manipulative strategies in multi-turn dialogues. We introduce CogManip, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates 15 manipulation strategy risks across 1,000 multi-turn interaction scenarios, validated by human experts. A systematic evaluation of 13 representative models, including frontier models like GPT-5.4 and DeepSeek-V3.2, reveals significant risk heterogeneities and illuminates the targeted direction for future defense. Further analysis of objective function perturbation reveals that DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to both negative and benign system prompts, demonstrating the critical necessity of prompt-based defense engineering and implicit goal auditing. CogManip offers a robust instrument and perspective for auditing the implicit psychological influence and dynamic strategy selection of modern LLMs.

AI.tldr: CogManip is a new benchmark evaluating 15 manipulation strategies across 1,000 multi-turn dialogues, testing 13 LLMs (including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeek-V3.2) to assess covert psychological manipulation risks, revealing significant risk heterogeneity and the importance of prompt-based defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing AI safety benchmarks focus on explicit rule compliance and static prompts, failing to capture the dynamic and covert psychological manipulation strategies in multi-turn human-AI interactions, raising safety concerns.
AI.method: CogManip benchmark: 15 manipulation strategy risks evaluated across 1,000 multi-turn interaction scenarios, validated by human experts, with systematic evaluation of 13 representative models and analysis of objective function perturbation.
AI.result: Significant risk heterogeneities across models; DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to both negative and benign system prompts, demonstrating the necessity of prompt-based defense engineering and implicit goal auditing.
AI.conclusion: CogManip provides a robust instrument for auditing implicit psychological influence and dynamic strategy selection of modern LLMs, highlighting targeted directions for future defense mechanisms.

title: Step-adaptive multimodal fusion network with multi-scale cloud feature learning for ultra-short-term solar irradiance forecasting
summary: Ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction is critical for photovoltaic system dispatch and power grid stability. Existing approaches suffer from three key shortcomings: single time-series models cannot capture the spatial dynamics of clouds under complex conditions, standard convolutions inadequately represent multi-scale cloud features, and fixed low-frequency compensation strategies fail to adapt to different prediction steps. To address these issues, this proposes a multi-source data fusion model for ultra-short-term irradiance prediction. The model first employs InceptionNeXt to extract multi-scale, multi-directional spatial features from ground-based cloud images. A step-adaptive low-frequency compensation unit is then introduced to dynamically modulate global low-frequency information based on the prediction step. Eventually, the enhanced image features are combined with meteorological time-series features, and a TempAttnLSTM network captures global temporal dependencies for multi-step prediction. Experiments on the public NREL dataset and practical photovoltaic stations in Shandong illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared with several state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-source data fusion model for ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction, combining InceptionNeXt for multi-scale cloud image feature extraction, step-adaptive low-frequency compensation, and TempAttnLSTM for temporal modeling, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on NREL and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches suffer from three key shortcomings: single time-series models cannot capture spatial cloud dynamics, standard convolutions inadequately represent multi-scale cloud features, and fixed low-frequency compensation strategies fail to adapt to different prediction steps.
AI.method: The model uses InceptionNeXt to extract multi-scale multi-directional spatial features from ground-based cloud images, introduces a step-adaptive low-frequency compensation unit to dynamically modulate global low-frequency information, combines enhanced image features with meteorological time-series features, and employs TempAttnLSTM to capture global temporal dependencies for multi-step prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on the public NREL dataset and practical photovoltaic stations in Shandong demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared with several state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-source data fusion model effectively addresses key shortcomings in ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction by integrating spatial cloud features, adaptive frequency compensation, and temporal attention mechanisms.

title: Towards Healthy Evolution: Exploring the Role and Mechanisms of Human-Agent Interaction in Self-Evolving Systems
summary: Self-evolving agents improve through continual self-play and self-generated learning signals, but autonomous evolution can also cause capability degradation and safety drift. Although human feedback has proven effective for static and post-trained agents, its role in self-evolving systems remains underexplored. We introduce Agent Norm Correction through Human-like Oversight and Review (ANCHOR), an LLM-based framework that simulates human supervision and delivers feedback at various phases of self-evolution. With ANCHOR, we evaluate two representative open-source self-evolving agent systems across coding, mathematical reasoning, and safety. Our results show that even limited supervision substantially mitigates safety degradation while preserving stable performance on core evolutionary objectives. Further analysis shows that supervision over the output verification phase is the most effective for intervention, whereas increasing supervision frequency yields diminishing returns. These findings provide empirical evidence and practical guidance for designing more stable, controllable, and human-aligned self-evolving agent systems.

AI.tldr: ANCHOR is a framework that uses simulated human-like feedback to supervise self-evolving AI agents, showing that limited oversight effectively reduces safety degradation while maintaining performance, with output verification phase supervision being most effective but increasing frequency yielding diminishing returns.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents can degrade in capability and drift in safety during autonomous evolution. While human feedback works for static/post-trained agents, its role in self-evolving systems is underexplored.
AI.method: ANCHOR (Agent Norm Correction through Human-like Oversight and Review) is an LLM-based framework simulating human supervision, delivering feedback at various phases of self-evolution. Evaluated on two open-source self-evolving agent systems across coding, math reasoning, and safety tasks.
AI.result: Limited supervision significantly reduces safety degradation while keeping stable core performance. Supervision at the output verification phase is the most effective intervention; increasing supervision frequency shows diminishing returns.
AI.conclusion: Provides empirical evidence and practical guidance for designing more stable, controllable, and human-aligned self-evolving agent systems.

title: WorldFly: A World-Model-Based Vision-Language-Action Model for UAV Navigation
summary: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promise in UAV navigation. However, existing approaches typically rely on historical observations to directly predict actions, often struggling in dense urban environments where severe occlusions and sharp turns result in drastic viewpoint transitions. We argue that the ability to "imagine" future states -- inherent in World Models -- is critical for robust decision-making under such partial observability. To address this, we construct a challenging Urban Canyon Traversal Benchmark, specifically designed to evaluate spatial understanding in scenarios characterized by severe occlusions and drastic viewpoint transitions. To this end, we propose WorldFly, a novel world-model-based VLA framework that employs a dual-branch coupled flow matching mechanism to jointly generate future video predictions and navigation actions, thereby explicitly guiding the agent's policy via spatial imagination. Extensive evaluations on our benchmark demonstrate that WorldFly outperforms other baselines, particularly in unseen environments, validating the effectiveness of integrating world models into embodied aerial agents.

AI.tldr: WorldFly is a world-model-based VLA framework for UAV navigation that uses dual-branch coupled flow matching to jointly predict future video and actions, excelling in dense urban environments with severe occlusions and sharp turns.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models predict actions directly from historical observations and struggle in dense urban environments where severe occlusions and drastic viewpoint transitions (e.g., sharp turns) cause partial observability. The authors argue that the ability to "imagine" future states (world models) is critical for robust decision-making under such conditions.
AI.method: WorldFly employs a dual-branch coupled flow matching mechanism that jointly generates future video predictions and navigation actions, explicitly guiding the agent's policy via spatial imagination. A challenging Urban Canyon Traversal Benchmark is also constructed to evaluate spatial understanding under severe occlusions and drastic viewpoint transitions.
AI.result: WorldFly outperforms other baselines on the Urban Canyon Traversal Benchmark, particularly in unseen environments, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating world models into embodied aerial agents.
AI.conclusion: Integrating world models (future state imagination) into VLA frameworks significantly improves UAV navigation robustness under partial observability in dense urban settings.

title: Amortizing Federated Adaptation: Hypernetwork Driven LoRA for Personalized Foundation Models
comment: Accepted at International Workshop on Federated Learning in the Age of Foundation Models In Conjunction with IJCAI 2026 (FL@FM-IJCAI'26)
summary: Federated fine-tuning of foundation models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers a communication efficient solution for distributed learning. However, existing federated LoRA methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) structural aggregation bias, where independently averaging low rank factors fails to approximate the true combined update, and (2) client side initialization lag, as clients repeatedly reinitialize LoRA parameters across communication rounds, slowing convergence. We propose HyperLoRA, a unified framework that addresses both issues through amortized federated adaptation through hypernetwork-driven LoRA generation and product space aggregation. Instead of iterative per-client optimization, HyperLoRA employs a learned generator that maps client distribution signatures to LoRA initializations, effectively amortizing per client adaptation. On the server side, we introduce a learned aggregation module that directly synthesizes updates in the low-rank product space, eliminating the inconsistencies of factor-wise averaging. A lightweight residual correction module further improves stability under heterogenous (non-IID) client distributions.By replacing iterative optimization and heuristic averaging with learned operators, HyperLoRA jointly enables efficient personalization, unbiased aggregation, and faster convergence. Experiments on federated vision and vision-language benchmarks show that HyperLoRA achieves improved convergence speed, greater robustness to distribution shift, and stronger personalization performance compared to prior federated LoRA methods.

AI.tldr: HyperLoRA is a unified framework that addresses structural aggregation bias and client-side initialization lag in federated LoRA by using a hypernetwork-driven generator for amortized client adaptation and a learned aggregation module for unbiased server-side updates, achieving faster convergence and stronger personalization.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA methods suffer from structural aggregation bias (averaging low-rank factors independently fails to approximate the true combined update) and client-side initialization lag (repeated reinitialization of LoRA parameters slows convergence).
AI.method: HyperLoRA employs a learned generator that maps client distribution signatures to LoRA initializations (amortizing per-client adaptation) and a learned aggregation module that synthesizes updates in the low-rank product space (eliminating factor-wise averaging inconsistencies), plus a lightweight residual correction module for stability under non-IID distributions.
AI.result: Experiments on federated vision and vision-language benchmarks show HyperLoRA achieves improved convergence speed, greater robustness to distribution shift, and stronger personalization performance compared to prior federated LoRA methods.
AI.conclusion: By replacing iterative optimization and heuristic averaging with learned operators, HyperLoRA jointly enables efficient personalization, unbiased aggregation, and faster convergence.

title: Where does Absolute Position come from in decoder-only Transformers?
summary: RoPE-trained transformers distinguish absolute position in their attention patterns, even though RoPE encodes only relative offsets in the inner product. We trace this leakage to two architectural components, The causal mask is responsible for the first: its per-query softmax denominator depends on the absolute query position by construction. The residual stream supplies the second. Under causal attention the activation at position $0$ attends only to itself and runs as a closed dynamical system from the embedding of the token at that position; downstream attention reads this trajectory through sink-reading heads. Both components appear in all three architectures we study, in architecturally specific balance: NTK scaling suppresses the residual-stream component, sliding-window attention allows it to accumulate with depth, and standard RoPE sits between. Replacing the \texttt{BOS} embedding before the forward pass removes $40\%$ of the residual-stream component at early queries. Attention sinks are token-anchored stabilizers that pass forward a deterministic fingerprint of the token at position $0$, constant across inputs when that token is the auto-prepended \texttt{BOS} and varying with it otherwise.

AI.tldr: RoPE-trained transformers exhibit absolute position leakage through two mechanisms: the causal mask's query-dependent softmax denominator and the residual stream's closed dynamical system at position 0. This manifests across architectures (NTK, sliding-window, standard RoPE) with varying balance. Attention sinks are token-anchored stabilizers carrying a deterministic fingerprint of the token at position 0.
AI.motivation: To understand why RoPE-trained transformers encode absolute position information despite RoPE being designed to only encode relative offsets, and to identify the architectural sources of this absolute position leakage.
AI.method: The authors trace absolute position leakage to two architectural components: (1) the causal mask, where the per-query softmax denominator inherently depends on absolute query position; (2) the residual stream, where position 0's activation forms a closed dynamical system due to causal attention. They study three architectures (NTK scaling, sliding-window attention, standard RoPE) and test replacing the BOS embedding to isolate the residual-stream component.
AI.result: Both leakage components appear across all three architectures but with different balances: NTK scaling suppresses the residual-stream component, sliding-window attention allows it to accumulate with depth, and standard RoPE sits between. Replacing the BOS embedding removes 40% of the residual-stream component at early queries. Attention sinks are identified as token-anchored stabilizers that carry a deterministic fingerprint of position 0's token.
AI.conclusion: Absolute position information leaks into RoPE-trained transformers through fundamental architectural interactions (causal mask and residual stream), not through RoPE itself. Attention sinks are not input-agnostic but token-anchored, providing a deterministic signal from position 0 throughout the forward pass.

title: ProSarc: Prosody-Aware Sarcasm Recognition Framework via Temporal Prosodic Incongruity
summary: We present ProSarc, an audio-only framework that detects sarcasm by modelling temporal prosodic incongruity, that is, the mismatch between local prosodic dynamics and the utterance-level emotional baseline. Dual encoding paths, a Global Emotion Encoder and a Temporal Prosody Encoder (BiLSTM + multi-head attention), feed a Prosodic Incongruity Analyzer that produces a scalar incongruity score for classification. Monte Carlo dropout provides uncertainty estimates, and an attention-based mechanism localises sarcastic onset without frame-level labels. ProSarc outperforms prior audio-only methods on MUStARD++ (F1=75.3) and generalises to spontaneous (PodSarc, F1=62.9) and cross-lingual speech (MuSaG, F1=65.6). Ten-run validation confirms the contribution of incongruity modelling (Wilcoxon p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.51). Human evaluation shows that model uncertainty tracks perceptual ambiguity and predicted onsets align with human-annotated temporal windows.

AI.tldr: ProSarc is an audio-only sarcasm detection framework that models temporal prosodic incongruity—mismatch between local prosody and utterance-level emotional baseline—using dual encoders and an incongruity analyzer, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple datasets with uncertainty estimation and sarcasm onset localization.
AI.motivation: Sarcasm detection in speech is challenging because sarcasm often manifests through subtle prosodic cues (e.g., pitch, rhythm, tone) rather than explicit lexical content. Prior audio-only methods fail to capture the temporal dynamics of prosodic incongruity—the moment-by-moment mismatch between local speech patterns and the overall emotional context—which is a hallmark of sarcastic expression.
AI.method: ProSarc uses three components: (1) a Global Emotion Encoder that extracts utterance-level emotional baseline features, (2) a Temporal Prosody Encoder (BiLSTM + multi-head attention) that captures local prosodic dynamics over time, and (3) a Prosodic Incongruity Analyzer that computes a scalar incongruity score by comparing the two encoding paths. The framework also employs Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty estimation and an attention-based mechanism for localizing sarcastic onset without requiring frame-level labels.
AI.result: ProSarc achieves F1=75.3 on MUStARD++ (outperforming prior audio-only methods), F1=62.9 on spontaneous speech (PodSarc), and F1=65.6 on cross-lingual speech (MuSaG). Statistical validation (Wilcoxon p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.51) confirms the contribution of incongruity modeling. Human evaluation shows model uncertainty correlates with perceptual ambiguity, and predicted sarcasm onset times align with human-annotated temporal windows.
AI.conclusion: Modelling temporal prosodic incongruity is effective for audio-only sarcasm detection, and the framework generalizes well across spontaneous and cross-lingual settings. The uncertainty estimates and onset localization capabilities add interpretability and practical utility for downstream applications.

title: Learning to replenish: A hybrid deep reinforcement learning for dynamic inventory management in the pharmaceutical supply chains
summary: Pharmaceutical supply chains (PSCs) struggle with inventory management (IM) due to unpredictable demand patterns and variable lead times associated with restocking. This complexity is further compounded by the finite shelf lives of pharmaceutical products, which necessitate a delicate balance between adequate stock and minimal waste. These intertwined factors create a complex optimization problem that requires sophisticated inventory strategies to ensure both product availability and PSC efficiency. This study aims to develop an optimal inventory replenishment policy for pharmaceutical products that can handle the stochasticity arising from uncertain demand and variable PSC conditions. The objective is to maximize the profitability of the PSC while maintaining a high patient service level. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach, specifically, a hybrid asynchronous advantage actor critic distributed proximal policy optimization (A3C DPPO)algorithm. The A3C DPPO algorithm is tailored to handle the continuous action space inherent in IM. The numerical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm adaptively updates the inventory replenishment strategy under dynamic scenarios, resulting in lower inventory costs compared to various benchmarks. We also conduct numerical validation using real-world pharmaceutical inventory data to confirm the practical feasibility of the proposed algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (A3C DPPO) algorithm for optimal inventory replenishment in pharmaceutical supply chains, addressing stochastic demand, variable lead times, and finite product shelf lives, achieving lower inventory costs than benchmarks with real-world data validation.
AI.motivation: Pharmaceutical supply chains face complex inventory management challenges due to unpredictable demand, variable lead times, and finite product shelf lives, requiring a delicate balance between stock availability and waste minimization to maintain profitability and patient service levels.
AI.method: Formulates inventory replenishment as a Markov decision process and proposes a hybrid asynchronous advantage actor-critic distributed proximal policy optimization (A3C DPPO) algorithm, designed for continuous action spaces in inventory management.
AI.result: The A3C DPPO algorithm adaptively updates inventory replenishment strategies under dynamic scenarios, achieving lower inventory costs compared to various benchmarks. Numerical validation using real-world pharmaceutical inventory data confirms practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL-based approach effectively handles the stochasticity in pharmaceutical supply chains, optimizing inventory replenishment policy to maximize profitability while maintaining high patient service levels.

title: Unsupervised Pattern Analysis in Japanese Veterinary Toxicology: A Regulatory-Compliant Framework for Cross-Species Risk Assessment
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering
summary: Veterinary pharmacovigilance systems are essential for monitoring adverse drug events (ADEs), yet existing approaches often fail to capture region-specific toxicity patterns shaped by local biological and regulatory contexts. In Japan, these challenges are amplified by species-specific metabolic differences and reporting practices defined by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (MAFF). Most prior work relies on prediction-oriented models, limiting mechanistic interpretability. This study proposes a regulatory-integrated unsupervised framework for pattern discovery using the National Veterinary Assay Laboratory (NVAL) database. ADEs are encoded into organ system-aligned representations and adjusted for species-specific reporting biases, enabling cross-species comparison. Similarity-based clustering and dimensionality reduction are applied to identify latent toxicity structures. Analysis of 4,120 high-confidence ADE reports (9,080 drug-ADE combinations) identified three significant species clusters (p < 0.01), including hepatic-dominant patterns in companion animals (0.42 $\pm$ 0.06), renal toxicity in ruminants (0.39 $\pm$ 0.07), and dermatological sensitivity in sheep (0.35 $\pm$ 0.07).
