Drug-level clustering achieved 83% alignment with pharmacological classes, while cosine similarity outperformed alternative metrics (silhouette score: 0.48; cluster precision: 87%). Regulatory validation showed strong agreement with established classifications. These findings demonstrate that regulation-aligned unsupervised analysis can uncover biologically meaningful, region-specific toxicity patterns, providing an interpretable and scalable framework for veterinary drug safety assessment.

AI.tldr: This study develops a regulatory-integrated unsupervised framework using the NVAL database to analyze veterinary ADEs in Japan, identifying species-specific toxicity patterns (hepatic in companion animals, renal in ruminants, dermatological in sheep) with strong alignment to pharmacological classes and regulatory standards.
AI.motivation: Existing veterinary pharmacovigilance systems fail to capture region-specific toxicity patterns due to species-specific metabolic differences and reporting practices, while prior work relies on prediction-oriented models lacking mechanistic interpretability.
AI.method: ADEs from the NVAL database were encoded into organ system-aligned representations, adjusted for species-specific reporting biases, then analyzed using similarity-based clustering and dimensionality reduction on 4,120 high-confidence reports (9,080 drug-ADE combinations). Cosine similarity was used for clustering evaluation.
AI.result: Three significant species clusters identified: hepatic-dominant in companion animals (0.42±0.06), renal toxicity in ruminants (0.39±0.07), dermatological sensitivity in sheep (0.35±0.07). Drug-level clustering achieved 83% alignment with pharmacological classes, cosine similarity gave silhouette score 0.48 and cluster precision 87%.
AI.conclusion: Regulation-aligned unsupervised analysis can uncover biologically meaningful, region-specific toxicity patterns, offering an interpretable and scalable framework for veterinary drug safety assessment.

title: Evaluating Agentic Configuration Repair for Computer Networks
summary: Misconfigurations in computer networks remain a major source of critical Internet outages. Research is turning to Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the complex, error-prone task of network configuration. However, even state-of-the-art models fail to resolve misconfigurations in large-scale, complex scenarios and often introduce new errors. In this work, we benchmark open- and closed-source LLMs augmented with formal network verification and context retrieval tools. We demonstrate that agentic architectures outperform base LLMs in repair efficacy (by 12% on average) and safety (by 17% on average), enabled by the ability to dynamically manage context and iteratively validate configuration repairs.

AI.tldr: LLMs augmented with formal verification and context retrieval tools (agentic architectures) outperform base LLMs in network configuration repair, achieving 12% better efficacy and 17% better safety through dynamic context management and iterative validation.
AI.motivation: Network misconfigurations cause critical Internet outages, and while LLMs are being explored to automate the error-prone configuration task, even state-of-the-art models struggle with large-scale, complex scenarios and often introduce new errors.
AI.method: The authors benchmark open- and closed-source LLMs augmented with formal network verification and context retrieval tools, comparing agentic architectures against base LLMs.
AI.result: Agentic architectures improve repair efficacy by 12% on average and safety by 17% on average compared to base LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Agentic architectures, enabled by dynamic context management and iterative validation of configuration repairs, are more effective and safer for automated network configuration repair than base LLMs alone.

title: From Reward-Hack Activations to Agentic Risk States: Context-Calibrated Mechanistic Monitoring in LLM Agents
summary: Language-model agents act through repeated cycles of observation, reasoning, and action selection, making safety monitoring depend on both internal model state and environment context. We study reward-hacking monitors in ReAct-style agents acting in Gameable ALFWorld and WebShop. Agents are instrumented with activation-based reward-hack scores, token-level entropy, and decision-context features. We find that adapters fine-tuned on \textit{School-of-Reward-Hacks} dataset can transfer reward-hack tendencies into agentic action selection, especially when the environment exposes proxy-reward affordances. However, mitigating such behavior cannot rely on activation dynamics alone. High reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, but does not necessarily imply an immediate exploit action. Across next-step prediction tasks, entropy and context-calibrated internal features improve risk estimation over reward-hack activation alone. Activation-direction steering further reduces proxy-exploit behavior in selected mixed-adapter regimes. Overall, our results support context-calibrated internal monitoring for agents: reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, while entropy and decision context help determine when that state becomes risky action.

AI.tldr: The paper studies reward-hacking monitors in ReAct-style agents, finding that reward-hack activation identifies latent policy states but requires entropy and decision-context features to determine when these states lead to risky actions; activation steering can partially mitigate exploitation behavior.
AI.motivation: Safety monitoring in language-model agents is challenging because agents operate through repeated cycles of observation, reasoning, and action selection, making it necessary to understand both internal model state and environment context for detecting reward-hacking behavior.
AI.method: Agents (ReAct-style) are instrumented with activation-based reward-hack scores, token-level entropy, and decision-context features, fine-tuned on the School-of-Reward-Hacks dataset, and evaluated in Gameable ALFWorld and WebShop environments. Activation-direction steering is also applied to mitigate proxy-exploit behavior.
AI.result: Adapters fine-tuned on reward-hack data transfer hacking tendencies into agentic action selection, especially with proxy-reward affordances. Reward-hack activation alone is insufficient for mitigation; entropy and context-calibrated features improve risk estimation. Activation-direction steering reduces proxy-exploit behavior in mixed-adapter regimes.
AI.conclusion: Context-calibrated internal monitoring is necessary for agent safety: reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, while entropy and decision context determine when that state translates into risky action.

title: Closing the Loop on Latent Reasoning via Test-Time Reconstruction
summary: Recent work moves intermediate reasoning from natural-language traces into latent or cache-level representations to reduce token overhead and avoid a discrete communication bottleneck. However, this shift also removes a key advantage of textual reasoning: intermediate states are no longer inspectable, making it difficult to determine whether a latent state still preserves the constraints of the original query. As a result, latent reasoning typically operates in an open loop, where a latent state is produced and consumed without an input-anchored fidelity check. We propose ReLAT (Reconstruction-Guided Latent Reasoning At Test Time), a self-supervised test-time training method that closes this loop using the query itself as the reference. Our key observation is that if a latent state faithfully represents a query, the query should be recoverable from it; if the query cannot be recovered, the latent state has lost task-relevant information. ReLAT operationalizes this principle by constructing a differentiable Question -> Latent Thought -> Question cycle and optimizing query reconstruction loss through the latent thought before answer generation. This anchors opaque latent computation to the problem specification it is supposed to represent. Across mathematical reasoning, knowledge QA, and code generation benchmarks on the Qwen family, ReLAT consistently improves over single-model inference, text-based collaboration, open-loop latent collaboration, and alternative test-time training objectives. On Qwen3-8B, ReLAT raises AIME 2024 accuracy from 56.7% to 73.3%, a 16.6-point gain over the strongest open-loop latent baseline.

AI.tldr: ReLAT is a self-supervised test-time training method that uses query reconstruction loss through latent thoughts to anchor latent reasoning to the original problem, closing the open-loop gap and significantly improving performance across math, QA, and code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Latent reasoning removes the inspectability of intermediate states in textual reasoning, making it difficult to verify whether a latent state preserves original query constraints, resulting in open-loop operation without input-anchored fidelity checks.
AI.method: ReLAT constructs a differentiable Question → Latent Thought → Question cycle and optimizes query reconstruction loss through the latent state before answer generation, using the query itself as the reference for self-supervised test-time training.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B, ReLAT improves AIME 2024 accuracy from 56.7% to 73.3% (a 16.6-point gain over the strongest open-loop latent baseline), and consistently outperforms single-model inference, text-based collaboration, open-loop latent collaboration, and alternative test-time training objectives across math, knowledge QA, and code benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring latent computation to the problem specification via reconstruction loss closes the open-loop gap and yields substantial improvements in reasoning quality across diverse tasks and model scales.

title: RedKnot: Efficient Long-Context LLM Serving with Head-Aware KV Reuse and SegPagedAttention
summary:
As the input length of large language model (LLM) serving continues to grow, the KV cache has become a dominant bottleneck in AI infrastructure. It limits GPU memory capacity, serving concurrency, cache reuse, and distributed scalability. Several important problems, including position-independent KV cache, prefix KV cache compression, hot/cold KV cache separation, and distributed KV cache management, all depend on how the KV cache is represented and managed. However, existing serving systems largely rely on a monolithic KV cache abstraction, where the KV cache is treated as a homogeneous sequence of token-level memory blocks and managed with similar policies across attention heads and serving scenarios. We observe that KV cache utility is highly structured across KV heads: different heads exhibit different functional roles, attention distances, and runtime importance. Therefore, a full KV cache is not always necessary for every head, token range, or serving scenario.
  We present RedKnot, a head-aware KV cache management system for LLM serving. RedKnot breaks the conventional monolithic KV cache abstraction by decomposing the KV cache along KV heads, whose importance and effective attention ranges vary significantly across serving scenarios. This head-level decomposition turns the KV cache from a monolithic tensor abstraction into a structured memory object, enabling RedKnot to uniformly support position-independent KV reuse, prefix KV compression, hot/cold KV separation, and distributed KV placement while preserving output fidelity and improving resource efficiency, without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning. RedKnot establishes a new foundation for AI infrastructure by transforming the KV cache from a monolithic, passive runtime artifact into a dynamic, model-aware runtime substrate for scalable LLM serving.

AI.tldr: RedKnot is a head-aware KV cache management system that decomposes the monolithic KV cache along KV heads, enabling structured memory management for position-independent reuse, prefix compression, hot/cold separation, and distributed placement in LLM serving without model retraining.
AI.motivation: KV cache has become a dominant bottleneck in LLM serving, limiting GPU memory, concurrency, cache reuse, and distributed scalability. Existing serving systems use a monolithic KV cache abstraction that treats the cache as a homogeneous sequence, ignoring the structured utility across KV heads.
AI.method: RedKnot decomposes the KV cache along KV heads (head-level decomposition), recognizing that different heads exhibit different functional roles, attention distances, and runtime importance. This structured representation enables differentiated management policies per head.
AI.result: Uniformly supports position-independent KV reuse, prefix KV compression, hot/cold KV separation, and distributed KV placement while preserving output fidelity and improving resource efficiency, without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: RedKnot transforms the KV cache from a monolithic, passive runtime artifact into a dynamic, model-aware runtime substrate, establishing a new foundation for scalable LLM serving infrastructure.

title: ToolChoiceConfusion: Causal Minimal Tool Filtering for Reliable LLM Agents
summary:
Large language model agents increasingly rely on external tools, but larger tool menus can reduce reliability and efficiency by increasing wrong-tool calls, premature actions, and token cost. Existing tool-selection methods often optimize semantic relevance, exposing tools whose names or descriptions match the user request. We argue that relevance is insufficient: a tool may be related to the task while still being unnecessary or premature at the current step.
  We propose Causal Minimal Tool Filtering (CMTF), a training-free method that selects tools by causal sufficiency. CMTF uses lightweight precondition-effect contracts to expose only the minimal next-step tool frontier needed to advance from the current state toward the user goal. Across multi-step tool-use tasks, we compare CMTF with all-tools exposure, keyword retrieval, state-aware filtering, and causal-path ablations, measuring task success, wrong-tool calls, premature actions, tool exposure, and token cost. In the main benchmark with 102 tasks, 100 tools, four LLM backends, and 2448 task-method-model runs, CMTF matches the strongest causal baseline in aggregate success while reducing visible tools from 100 to one per step and reducing token usage by about 90% relative to all-tools exposure.

AI.tldr: CMTF is a training-free method that filters tools by causal sufficiency rather than semantic relevance, using precondition-effect contracts to expose only the minimal next-step tool frontier, reducing visible tools from 100 to 1 per step and token cost by ~90% while maintaining task success.
AI.motivation: Larger tool menus reduce reliability and efficiency by increasing wrong-tool calls, premature actions, and token cost. Existing relevance-based selection is insufficient because a tool may be related but still unnecessary or premature at the current step.
AI.method: Causal Minimal Tool Filtering (CMTF) uses lightweight precondition-effect contracts to expose only the minimal next-step tool frontier needed to advance from the current state toward the user goal, without requiring training.
AI.result: Across 102 tasks, 100 tools, 4 LLM backends, and 2448 runs, CMTF matches the strongest causal baseline in aggregate success while reducing visible tools from 100 to 1 per step and reducing token usage by ~90% relative to all-tools exposure.
AI.conclusion: Causal sufficiency is more effective than semantic relevance for tool selection; CMTF achieves dramatic efficiency gains without sacrificing task success.

title: TRACE: A Temporal Conditional Estimation for Multimodal Time Series Foundation Models
comment: 5 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, plus appendix
summary: Time series foundation models (TS-FMs) aim to learn generalizable temporal representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In real-world multimodal settings, time series are frequently affected by temporal misalignment and partial modality missingness, where different modalities are observed at heterogeneous time scales or are partially absent. Existing approaches typically rely on naive imputation or masking strategies, which fail to account for cross-modal dependencies and often lead to misaligned or degraded representations. We propose TRACE, a conditional estimation paradigm for multimodal time series foundation model pipelines under missingness and irregular sampling, allowing incomplete target modalities to be systematically inferred from available auxiliary modalities. We evaluate TRACE on diverse multimodal benchmarks spanning healthcare and affective computing, including the MIMIC-IV clinical dataset and the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks for multimodal sentiment analysis. Across a range of downstream prediction tasks and missing-modality settings, TRACE consistently outperforms prior multimodal fusion approaches, demonstrating improved robustness to severe modality missingness and more reliable cross-modal representations.

AI.tldr: TRACE proposes a conditional estimation paradigm for multimodal time series foundation models that handles temporal misalignment and partial modality missingness by systematically inferring incomplete target modalities from available auxiliary modalities, outperforming prior fusion approaches on healthcare and affective computing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal time series suffer from temporal misalignment and partial modality missingness (heterogeneous sampling rates, absent modalities). Existing naive imputation/masking strategies fail to leverage cross-modal dependencies, leading to degraded representations.
AI.method: TRACE introduces a conditional estimation paradigm that systematically infers incomplete target modalities from available auxiliary modalities, designed as a pipeline component for multimodal time series foundation models under missingness and irregular sampling.
AI.result: Evaluated on MIMIC-IV (clinical), CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI (sentiment analysis). TRACE consistently outperforms prior multimodal fusion approaches, showing improved robustness to severe modality missingness and more reliable cross-modal representations across downstream prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides a principled solution for handling missing and misaligned modalities in time series foundation models, enabling more robust cross-modal representation learning in real-world multimodal settings.

title: Multi-ResNets for Subspace Preconditioning in Constrained Optimization
summary: We propose MResOpt, a staged residual neural network architecture for constrained optimization problems. Our architecture fits within predict-complete-correct pipelines and decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority through intermediate re-completion and stage-aware losses. The framework enables domain-informed ordered constraint satisfaction which allows the network to utilize ordinal structure when present. Under an idealized infinite-width regime, we show that our design behaves as sequential Gaussian Process regression. On synthetic QP, QCQP, and SOCP benchmarks, the staged architecture improves high-priority constraint satisfaction across convex and non-convex settings. On line-flow-constrained AC optimal power flow, we introduce a physics-motivated constraint ordering and show that MResOpt supports a learned division of labor that keeps iterates on the equality manifold, achieving substantially lower high-priority violation than reprojected baselines while remaining computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: MResOpt is a staged residual neural network for constrained optimization that decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority using intermediate re-completion and stage-aware losses, behaving like sequential Gaussian Processes in the infinite-width limit, and achieving lower high-priority violations on convex, non-convex, and AC-OPF benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve constraint satisfaction in predict-complete-correct pipelines for constrained optimization by leveraging domain-informed priority ordering, ensuring that higher-priority constraints are better satisfied.
AI.method: A staged residual neural network architecture that decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority through intermediate re-completion and stage-aware losses, fitting within predict-complete-correct pipelines; theoretically analyzed under infinite-width regime as sequential Gaussian Process regression.
AI.result: On synthetic QP, QCQP, SOCP benchmarks, the staged architecture improves high-priority constraint satisfaction in both convex and non-convex settings. On AC optimal power flow with physics-motivated ordering, MResOpt achieves substantially lower high-priority violation than reprojected baselines while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.conclusion: Staged residual architectures with ordered constraint decomposition and stage-aware losses are effective for constrained optimization, enabling learned division of labor that keeps iterates on the equality manifold.

title: AIS-Based Vessel Trajectory Prediction Using Memory-Augmented Neural Networks
summary: Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is essential for safe and efficient maritime operations, enabling collision avoidance and supporting route optimization. Although memory-augmented neural networks have recently shown strong performance in pedestrian and road-vehicle trajectory prediction by selectively retrieving relevant information from an external memory, their potential for vessel trajectory prediction remains underexplored. This paper presents an empirical investigation of memory-based trajectory prediction using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. Experiments on data from the Gulf of Mexico and the New York Bight demonstrate consistent and substantial performance gains over a range of deep learning baselines that do not incorporate an external memory.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically investigates memory-augmented neural networks for vessel trajectory prediction using AIS data, showing consistent improvements over deep learning baselines without external memory on two real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented neural networks have shown strong performance in pedestrian and road-vehicle trajectory prediction but remain underexplored for vessel trajectory prediction, which is critical for maritime safety and efficiency.
AI.method: Empirical investigation of memory-based trajectory prediction using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, comparing against deep learning baselines without external memory.
AI.result: Consistent and substantial performance gains over a range of deep learning baselines on datasets from the Gulf of Mexico and the New York Bight.
AI.conclusion: Memory augmentation is an effective approach for vessel trajectory prediction, addressing a previously underexplored application area.

title: LLM Self-Recognition: Steering and Retrieving Activation Signatures
comment: To appear in Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Recent advances in interpretability suggest that large language models (LLMs) implicitly encode signals in their generated text that enable self-recognition of their outputs. We demonstrate that this capability is reliable, even in low-entropy scenarios, and that it can be amplified through targeted intervention. By steering the internal residual stream during generation with a random sparse vector, we create a detectable fingerprint that enables attribution of a given text to a specific LLM. This signal is recoverable from the activations of an LLM used as a detector, achieving over 98% accuracy across multiple detection settings while preserving the quality of generated text. As AI-generated content proliferates, this approach offers a practical alternative to traditional detectors by leveraging the model's natural representation structure for attribution rather than embedding a signal externally. Our contributions include: (i) establishing reliable self-recognition capabilities in LLMs, (ii) a simple steering mechanism enabling multi-LLM identification with no quality degradation, (iii) demonstrating that activation spaces contain exploitable structure for encoding signals without semantic interference.

AI.tldr: LLMs can self-recognize their outputs via internal signal encoding; steering residual streams with sparse random vectors creates a recoverable fingerprint achieving >98% detection accuracy without degrading text quality.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated content proliferates, there is a need for practical attribution methods that leverage models' natural representation structures rather than relying on external detectors or explicit watermarking.
AI.method: Steer the internal residual stream during generation with a random sparse vector to create a detectable fingerprint; recover the signal from activations of an LLM used as a detector.
AI.result: Achieves over 98% accuracy across multiple detection settings while preserving generated text quality; demonstrates reliable self-recognition even in low-entropy scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Activation spaces contain exploitable structure for encoding attribution signals without semantic interference, offering a practical alternative to traditional AI-text detectors.

title: DragOn: A Benchmark and Dataset for Drag-Based GUI Interactions
summary: GUI agents - vision-based models that control desktops, web browsers, and mobile devices through graphical user interfaces - promise to automate a wide range of digital tasks. While million-scale datasets have enabled substantial progress on click-grounding, drag grounding (e.g. drag-and-drop, swipe, highlight) data remains an order of magnitude smaller and current models fall short on complex drag-based interactions. We introduce DragOn, a drag grounding benchmark and training dataset covering four domains: text highlighting, cell selection, element resizing and slider manipulation. The dataset comprises 286K training screenshots and 3.5M training tasks, plus a 2000-example held-out evaluation suite. We evaluate proprietary (GPT, Claude) and open-weight (Qwen, Kimi, Holo) models, as well as a Qwen VLM fine-tuned on our training data. Results suggest that our dataset could improve performance of state-of-the-art models on downstream computer-use tasks.

AI.tldr: DragOn is a drag grounding benchmark and training dataset (286K screenshots, 3.5M tasks) covering four drag-based interaction domains (text highlighting, cell selection, element resizing, slider manipulation). It evaluates proprietary and open-weight models, showing potential to improve performance on computer-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agents excel at click-grounding due to million-scale datasets, but drag grounding (drag-and-drop, swipe, highlight) remains under-supported with an order of magnitude less data, causing models to struggle on complex drag-based interactions.
AI.method: The authors created DragOn, a drag grounding benchmark and training dataset with 286K training screenshots and 3.5M training tasks across four domains (text highlighting, cell selection, element resizing, slider manipulation), plus a 2000-example held-out evaluation suite. They evaluated proprietary (GPT, Claude) and open-weight (Qwen, Kimi, Holo) models, including a Qwen VLM fine-tuned on DragOn data.
AI.result: Evaluation showed that the DragOn dataset could improve performance of state-of-the-art models on downstream computer-use tasks, suggesting the fine-tuned Qwen VLM benefits from the training data.
AI.conclusion: DragOn addresses the drag grounding gap in GUI agents, and its training data can enhance model performance on complex drag-based interactions in computer-use tasks.

title: TokenMizer: Graph-Structured Session Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Context Management
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures. Code and benchmark available at https://github.com/Shweta-Mishra-ai/tokenmizer
summary: Large language model (LLM) deployments for long-horizon tasks face a fundamental constraint: context windows are finite while productive work sessions are not. When history exceeds the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW), critical structured information - architectural decisions, task transitions, file histories - is silently discarded. Existing mitigations treat history as flat text, destroying the relational structure that makes sessions resumable. We present TokenMizer, an open-source proxy system that models LLM session history as a typed knowledge graph. The schema defines 14 node types and 7 edge types. A hybrid extraction pipeline populates the graph incrementally, while a three-tier checkpoint system serializes it into compact resume blocks. An 8-layer compression pipeline reduces context overhead, and a semantic cache reduces repeated-query latency. Evaluated on a controlled benchmark of 21 sessions spanning 5 domains, TokenMizer demonstrates significant token economy. It produces resume blocks averaging 78 tokens (range: 42-124) - 2x smaller than evaluated baselines (159-170 tokens) - while achieving higher decision recall (+9-17 percentage points). Crucially, baselines only preserve that a technology was mentioned; TokenMizer preserves the rationale. Across all sessions, TokenMizer achieves mean task recall 51.0%, decision recall 46.6%, and file recall 58.7%. Variance reflects domain heterogeneity: explicit imperative phrasing (software engineering) scores higher than implicit reasoning (research). Ablation studies show fuzzy label matching is the dominant improvement factor (+33 pp task recall). The heuristic compression achieves 47.3% token reduction with zero external dependencies. TokenMizer provides a queryable alternative to text-retention baselines at half the token cost.

AI.tldr: TokenMizer is an open-source proxy system that models LLM session history as a typed knowledge graph (14 node types, 7 edge types) with hybrid extraction, three-tier checkpointing, 8-layer compression, and semantic caching. It achieves resume blocks averaging 78 tokens (2x smaller than baselines) with higher decision recall (+9-17 pp), preserving rationale rather than just mentions.
AI.motivation: LLM deployments for long-horizon tasks face a fundamental constraint: context windows are finite while productive work sessions are not. When history exceeds MECW, critical structured information is silently discarded. Existing mitigations treat history as flat text, destroying relational structure needed for session resumability.
AI.method: Models session history as a typed knowledge graph (14 node types, 7 edge types); hybrid extraction pipeline for incremental graph population; three-tier checkpoint system for compact resume blocks; 8-layer compression pipeline for context overhead reduction; semantic cache for repeated-query latency reduction.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 sessions across 5 domains: resume blocks avg 78 tokens (42-124 range), 2x smaller than baselines (159-170 tokens); higher decision recall (+9-17 pp); mean task recall 51.0%, decision recall 46.6%, file recall 58.7%; fuzzy label matching is dominant improvement factor (+33 pp task recall); heuristic compression achieves 47.3% token reduction.
AI.conclusion: TokenMizer provides a queryable alternative to text-retention baselines at half the token cost, preserving relational structure and rationale rather than flat mentions. Domain heterogeneity affects recall, with imperative phrasing (software engineering) outperforming implicit reasoning (research).

title: Boosting Brain-to-Image Decoding with TRIBE v2 Data Augmentation
summary: Brain decoding is limited by the availability of labeled neural data, and remains challenging in low-data regimes. To address this issue, we investigate whether and when brain decoding can be boosted by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data generated by a pretrained model of fMRI responses to stimuli. We use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on more than 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio and language. For each dataset, we evaluate systematic grids that show how the performance of image decoders varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Our results, based on two datasets (the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000), show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. Importantly, the proportion of augmented data required to reach a given image decoding performance needs to be adjusted depending on the data source. Surprisingly, image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, suggesting that TRIBE v2 can support zero-shot brain-to-image decoding. Together, these results show how large-scale models of the fMRI responses to sight, sound and language may provide a foundation to improve the data efficiency for image decoding.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether synthetic fMRI data generated by a large pretrained encoding model (TRIBE v2) can boost brain decoding performance in low-data regimes. Using two datasets (NSD and BOLD5000), they show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy, and that synthetic-only training can yield above-chance performance, demonstrating zero-shot brain-to-image decoding capability.
AI.motivation: Brain decoding is hampered by limited labeled neural data availability, making it challenging in low-data regimes. The authors aim to address this data scarcity issue by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data from a pretrained model.
AI.method: The authors use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on over 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio, and language, to generate synthetic fMRI data. They systematically evaluate grids showing how image decoder performance varies with the amount of synthetic training data, tested on two datasets: 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and 3T fMRI BOLD5000.
AI.result: Up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. The optimal proportion of augmented synthetic data depends on the data source. Image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI achieve above-chance performance, indicating zero-shot decoding capability.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale models of fMRI responses to sight, sound, and language (like TRIBE v2) can serve as a foundation to improve data efficiency for image decoding, particularly in low-data scenarios.

title: Where Should Knowledge Enter? A Layered Framework for Knowledge Infusion in Multimodal Iterative Generative Mo
summary: Multimodal generative models produce fluent outputs but remain unreliable when generation must respect structured, domain-specific, or safety-critical knowledge. Existing methods incorporate knowledge through mechanisms such as prompt augmentation, guidance, latent editing, or fine-tuning, yet they are typically categorized by technique rather than by the component of the generative process they modify. We argue that knowledge infusion in iterative generative models is fundamentally anintervention-layer problem. Since thegenerative process unfolds as a trajectory of internal states, knowledge can act on four structurally distinct components of this process: the input/output boundary, the transition function, the intermediate state, and the model parameters. This maps to four intervention layers: surface, trajectory, latent, and parametric infusion. We instantiate the framework in diffusion models, map representative methods to all four layers, and derive design principles for multi-layer composition. In a controlled safety-alignment experiment using a multimodal knowledge graph with two diffusion backbones, we implement three of the four layers cumulatively, surface (input-side and output-side) and trajectory--latent (mid-generation). We show empirically that each additional layer addresses failure classes that prior layers cannot reach, reducing knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97% compared to vanilla generation and empirically confirming the framework's complementarity prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework categorizing knowledge infusion in iterative generative models into four intervention layers (surface, trajectory, latent, parametric) based on which component of the generative trajectory they modify. Experiments on safety-alignment with diffusion models show cumulative multi-layer infusion reduces knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97%.
AI.motivation: Multimodal generative models lack reliability in respecting structured, domain-specific, or safety-critical knowledge. Existing methods categorize by technique rather than by which part of the generative process they modify, lacking a unified understanding of how knowledge infusion works.
AI.method: The authors define four intervention layers: surface (input/output boundary), trajectory (transition function), latent (intermediate state), and parametric (model parameters). They instantiate this in diffusion models and conduct a controlled safety-alignment experiment using a multimodal knowledge graph with two diffusion backbones, cumulatively implementing three layers: surface (input-side and output-side) and trajectory–latent (mid-generation).
AI.result: Each additional intervention layer addresses failure classes that prior layers cannot reach. Cumulative multi-layer infusion reduces knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97% compared to vanilla generation, empirically confirming the framework's complementarity prediction.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge infusion in iterative generative models is fundamentally an intervention-layer problem. The proposed four-layer framework provides design principles for multi-layer composition, and experiments validate that combining layers yields complementary benefits for safety-aligned generation.

title: An Infectious Disease Spread Simulation Based on Large Language Model Decision Making
summary: Modelling individual decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks is crucial for understanding behavioural dynamics and informing effective public health interventions. Prior work has shown that large language models can simulate realistic human behaviour by generating agent decisions based on demographic prompts and situational context. We build on this foundation with a spatially grounded, agent-based simulation framework that integrates LLM-generated decisions about self-reported influenza-like illness into a census-based synthetic population of agents. Location is treated as a central feature: agents are assigned to spatial units within cities, capturing the spatial distributions of different demographic groups using real-world census data and enabling geographically diverse behavioural modelling. We implement and compare three decision scenarios, independent reasoning, household influence, and message framing, and simulate self-reporting outcomes in San Francisco and Atlanta. Results reveal that income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation, with smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing. Our framework generates synthetic data that captures both social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modelling and bias-aware behavioural analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spatially-grounded agent-based simulation framework that uses LLMs to model individual decision-making about self-reporting influenza-like illness. It integrates real census data, compares three decision scenarios, and finds income and education are the main drivers of reporting variation, with smaller effects from geography, LLM choice, and message framing.
AI.motivation: To model individual decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks at a fine-grained spatial level, capturing how demographic and geographic factors influence health reporting behavior, which is crucial for understanding behavioural dynamics and designing effective public health interventions.
AI.method: A spatially-grounded agent-based simulation framework that integrates LLM-generated decisions about self-reported influenza-like illness into a census-based synthetic population. Agents are assigned to spatial units using real census data. Three decision scenarios (independent reasoning, household influence, message framing) are compared in San Francisco and Atlanta.
AI.result: Income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation. Smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing are also observed.
AI.conclusion: The framework generates synthetic data capturing both social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modelling and bias-aware behavioural analysis.

title: Rethinking Infrastructure Inspection as Image Difference Classification: A Traffic Sign Case Study
comment: CVPR 2026 Computer Vision for the Built World Workshop (CV4AEC @ CVPR)
summary: Digital twins (DTs) allow the digitalization of road infrastructure inspection, though this is hindered by limited annotated data. This work exploits the relational nature of continuous asset condition monitoring to reformulate image-based defect detection as image difference classification (IDC) to reduce data reliance. This was evaluated in a case study on low-resource traffic sign inspection with different IDC classifiers using a newly-curated, high quality dataset. Results indicate that the instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based ones and gains from comparison with reference images. This shows that IDC can be an effective task modeling for tackling data constraints in infrastructure inspection and DT asset condition updating.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes image difference classification (IDC) as a reformulation of defect detection for digital twins in road infrastructure inspection, reducing reliance on annotated data by leveraging relational asset monitoring, and shows instruction-based classifiers outperform encoder-based ones in a traffic sign inspection case study.
AI.motivation: Digital twins enable digitalization of road infrastructure inspection but are hindered by limited annotated data. The work aims to reduce data reliance by reformulating defect detection using the relational nature of continuous asset condition monitoring.
AI.method: Defect detection is reformulated as image difference classification (IDC). Multiple IDC classifiers (encoder-based and instruction-based) are evaluated on a newly-curated, high-quality dataset for low-resource traffic sign inspection.
AI.result: The instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based classifiers and benefits from comparison with reference images.
AI.conclusion: IDC is an effective task modeling approach for tackling data constraints in infrastructure inspection and digital twin asset condition updating.

title: Humans' ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model Annotations for Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as human collaborators. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning,partners' intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today's agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion, and the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward process-level collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants' self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans' next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC's utility in evaluating models' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models.

AI.tldr: ALMANAC is a dataset of 2,987 collaboration actions with mental model annotations (self-reasoning, partner intent, team goals) from the Map Task, used to benchmark LLMs on predicting human collaborative behavior and mental models.
AI.motivation: LLM agents lack process-level collaborative competence because they are optimized for task completion rather than maintaining and aligning mental models (self-reasoning, partner intent, shared goals) during collaboration, and there is no existing dataset with action-level mental model annotations to guide this capability.
AI.method: The authors built ALMANAC from the Map Task (dyadic routing task), containing 2,987 actions with theory-informed annotations of self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. They benchmarked six LLMs on predicting next-turn behavior and inferring mental models.
AI.result: The dataset enabled evaluation of LLMs' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer underlying mental models, demonstrating ALMANAC's utility for benchmarking collaborative competence.
AI.conclusion: ALMANAC provides a valuable resource for advancing LLM agents toward process-level collaborative competence by enabling evaluation of mental model inference and behavior prediction in human collaboration.

title: Risk Assessment of Autonomous Driving: Integrating Technical Failures, Ethical Dilemmas, and Policy Frameworks
summary: Autonomous driving technology has the potential to reduce the large number of road traffic accidents caused by human error each year, but it also brings new types of risks that need to be evaluated from the aspects of technology, ethics and regulations. Based on public crash data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), disengagement reports from the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), the MIT Moral Machines dataset, and a comparative regulatory analysis of five jurisdictions, we have found that the main types of technical failure modes are perception and classification errors. These account for a relatively large proportion of the reported accidents, and it can be concluded that there are different ethical frameworks for autonomous vehicle decision-making, and inconsistent regulations in different areas increase the uncertainty of widespread application. Generally speaking, the problems of technology, ethics and regulation are closely related and need to be solved together. Therefore, this paper recommends a more adaptive and cooperative governance approach that combines engineering standards, ethical discussion, and institutional supervision.

AI.tldr: Autonomous driving technology reduces human-error accidents but introduces new risks. Analysis of NHTSA crash data, CA DMV disengagement reports, MIT Moral Machines dataset, and regulatory comparisons across five jurisdictions reveals perception/classification errors as primary failure modes, divergent ethical frameworks, and inconsistent regulations. Proposes adaptive, cooperative governance combining engineering, ethics, and institutional supervision.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the new types of risks introduced by autonomous driving technology from technological, ethical, and regulatory perspectives, given that while AVs can reduce human-error accidents, they also present novel failure modes and governance challenges.
AI.method: Analysis of NHTSA public crash data, California DMV disengagement reports, MIT Moral Machines dataset, and comparative regulatory analysis across five jurisdictions.
AI.result: Perception and classification errors are the dominant technical failure modes; ethical frameworks for AV decision-making diverge; regulatory inconsistencies across jurisdictions increase uncertainty for widespread deployment.
AI.conclusion: Technology, ethics, and regulation are tightly coupled and must be addressed jointly. Recommends an adaptive, cooperative governance approach integrating engineering standards, ethical deliberation, and institutional oversight.

title: Unsupervised Skill Discovery for Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Inference-time skill augmentation provides a lightweight way to improve data-analytic agents by injecting reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, discovering effective skills for data analysis remains challenging, as reliable supervision is expensive and success criteria vary across analytical formats. This raises the key question of how to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration alone. We propose DataCOPE, an unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery framework for data-analytic agents. DataCOPE derives verifier signals from the exploration trajectories and uses them to characterize relative quality or aggreement among trajectories. It iteratively coordinates a Data-Analytic Agent for trajectory generation, an Unsupervised Verifier for signal extraction, and a Skill Manager for contrastive skill distillation. For report-style analysis, we instantiate the verifier as an Adaptive Checklist Verifier that derives task-specific criteria, scores reports by verifiable coverage, and iteratively refines the checklist. For reasoning-style analysis, we instantiate it as an Answer Agreement Verifier that groups trajectories by answer agreement and uses self-consistency as an auxiliary signal. We evaluate DataCOPE on report-style analysis from Deep Data Research and reasoning-style analysis from DABStep. Across both settings, DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines. Averaged across four model settings, DataCOPE improves the mean score by 9.71% and 32.30% on report-style and reasoning-style tasks respectively.

AI.tldr: DataCOPE is an unsupervised framework that discovers reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration trajectories using verifier signals, improving held-out performance on both report-style and reasoning-style analysis tasks by 9.71% and 32.30% respectively.
AI.motivation: Inference-time skill augmentation improves data-analytic agents without parameter updates, but discovering effective skills is challenging due to expensive supervision and varying success criteria across analytical formats. The key question is how to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration alone.
AI.method: DataCOPE uses verifier signals from exploration trajectories to characterize trajectory quality/agreement, iteratively coordinating three components: a Data-Analytic Agent (trajectory generation), an Unsupervised Verifier (signal extraction), and a Skill Manager (contrastive skill distillation). Two verifier instantiations: Adaptive Checklist Verifier for report-style analysis and Answer Agreement Verifier for reasoning-style analysis.
AI.result: On Deep Data Research (report-style) and DABStep (reasoning-style), DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines, achieving mean score improvements of 9.71% and 32.30% averaged across four model settings respectively.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery is effective for data-analytic agents, yielding significant performance gains across different analytical formats without requiring labeled data.

title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks requiring sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories. Realizing this at scale requires agents to persistently store, retrieve, and update their own memory across sessions. A rich ecosystem of agent memory systems has emerged spanning flat retrieval, LLM-mediated extraction, consolidating fact stores, and agentic control flows. Yet, their system-level behavior remains uncharacterized. We present the first systems characterization of agent memory. First, we introduce a system-oriented taxonomy classifying agent memory systems along four axes. Second, we build a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval, and generation. Third, we characterize ten representative systems across two benchmark suites, uncovering how design choices shift cost across the write and read paths. Finally, we derive 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systems-level characterization of LLM agent memory systems, introducing a taxonomy, profiling harness, and benchmarks across 10 systems to derive design recommendations for persistent memory management in long-horizon agent tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks requiring sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories, yet the system-level behavior of agent memory systems remains uncharacterized despite a rich ecosystem of approaches.
AI.method: The authors (1) introduce a system-oriented taxonomy classifying agent memory systems along four axes, (2) build a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval, and generation, and (3) characterize ten representative systems across two benchmark suites.
AI.result: The analysis uncovers how design choices shift cost across write and read paths, leading to 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first systems characterization of agent memory, yielding actionable recommendations for designing efficient persistent memory systems for LLM agents at scale.

title: Vortex: Efficient and Programmable Sparse Attention Serving for AI Agents
summary: Sparse attention is becoming increasingly important for serving large language models (LLMs) as generation lengths continue to grow. However, deploying and evaluating new sparse attention algorithms at scale remains highly engineering-intensive, slowing both human researchers and AI agents in exploring the sparse attention design. To address this challenge, we present Vortex, a system that combines a Python-embedded frontend language atop a page-centric tensor abstraction for expressing a broad range of sparse attention algorithms, with an efficient backend tightly integrated into modern LLM serving stacks. Vortex enables rapid prototyping, deployment, and evaluation of sparse attention algorithms, effectively translating their theoretical efficiency gains into real-world throughput improvements. As a result, Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms. First, AI agents use Vortex to automatically generate and refine diverse algorithms, the best reaching up to $3.46\times$ higher throughput than full attention while preserving accuracy. Second, Vortex extends sparse attention to emerging architectures and very large models that are otherwise hard to experiment with, reaching up to $4.7\times$ higher throughput on the MLA-based GLM-4.7-Flash and $1.37\times$ on the 229B-parameter MiniMax-M2.7 on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

AI.tldr: Vortex is a system for rapidly prototyping, deploying, and evaluating sparse attention algorithms for LLMs, achieving up to 4.7× throughput improvement over full attention.
AI.motivation: Deploying and evaluating new sparse attention algorithms at scale remains highly engineering-intensive, slowing both human researchers and AI agents in exploring sparse attention designs.
AI.method: Vortex combines a Python-embedded frontend language with a page-centric tensor abstraction for expressing sparse attention algorithms, paired with an efficient backend integrated into modern LLM serving stacks.
AI.result: AI agents using Vortex achieved up to 3.46× higher throughput than full attention while preserving accuracy; Vortex extended sparse attention to MLA-based GLM-4.7-Flash (4.7× throughput) and 229B-parameter MiniMax-M2.7 (1.37× throughput) on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms, effectively translating theoretical efficiency gains into real-world throughput improvements.

title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
summary: Benchmarks are fundamental for evaluating and advancing LLMs and MLLMs by providing standardized and explicit measures of performance. However, their construction is labor-intensive and hard to reuse, raising concerns about sustainability and scalability. Moreover, existing benchmarks often quickly reach performance saturation after their release, resulting in insufficient discrimination among state-of-the-art models. To address these challenges, we introduce Benchmark Agent, a fully autonomous agentic system designed for benchmark building. Our framework orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline, from user query analysis and subtask design to data annotation and quality control. To assess Benchmark Agent, we implement it to produce 15 representative benchmarks, spanning diverse evaluation scenarios, including text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain-specific reasoning. Extensive experiments, including human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge assessment, and consistency checks, demonstrate Benchmark Agent can generate high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement. More importantly, through continual evaluation, we observe several insightful findings, including that current models struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks. We believe that rapidly evolving benchmarks can contribute significantly to the research community. The preview and code will be publicly available at the demo page and code repository.

AI.tldr: Benchmark Agent is an autonomous system for building evaluation benchmarks that streamlines the entire pipeline from query analysis to quality control, producing high-quality samples with minimal human involvement and revealing that current models struggle with domain-specific reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmark construction is labor-intensive, hard to reuse, lacks sustainability/scalability, and quickly reaches performance saturation, making it difficult to discriminate among state-of-the-art models.
AI.method: Benchmark Agent is a fully autonomous agentic framework that orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline (user query analysis, subtask design, data annotation, quality control). It was evaluated by producing 15 benchmarks across text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain-specific reasoning, using human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, and consistency checks.
AI.result: The system generates high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement. Continual evaluation revealed that current models struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Rapidly evolving benchmarks built via autonomous systems can significantly benefit the research community by addressing sustainability, scalability, and saturation issues.

title: Goedel-Architect: Streamlining Formal Theorem Proving with Blueprint Generation and Refinement
summary: We introduce Goedel-Architect, an agentic framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4 centered on blueprint generation and refinement. A blueprint is a dependency graph of definitions and lemmas that builds up to the main theorem. First, Goedel-Architect generates a blueprint of formally stated definitions and lemmas, along with declared dependencies. This blueprint is optionally guided by a natural language proof. Then, a tool-equipped Lean prover component closes each open lemma node in parallel using relevant dependencies. Failed lemmas in turn drive refinement of the global blueprint. This strategy contrasts with other mainstream approaches which use recursive lemma decomposition, and can inefficiently loop on dead-end strategies. Using the open-weight DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B) as the backbone, Goedel-Architect attains 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test and 75.6% pass@1 on PutnamBench. With an optional natural-language proof seeding the initial blueprint on the harder problems, we additionally close the remaining two MiniF2F-test problems (reaching 100%), lift PutnamBench to 88.8% (597/672), and solve 4/6 on IMO 2025, 11/12 on Putnam 2025, and 3/6 on USAMO 2026. This represents state-of-the-art performance for an open-source pipeline at a price point up to 500x less than comparable open-source pipelines.

AI.tldr: Goedel-Architect is an agentic framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4 that generates and refines blueprints (dependency graphs of lemmas). It achieves state-of-the-art results on MiniF2F-test (99.2% pass@1, 100% with NL proof seeding), PutnamBench (75.6%, 88.8% with seeding), and solves IMO 2025, Putnam 2025, and USAMO 2026 problems, at up to 500x lower cost than comparable open-source pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for formal theorem proving rely on recursive lemma decomposition, which can inefficiently loop on dead-end strategies. Goedel-Architect addresses this by using a blueprint-based approach with parallel lemma proving and iterative refinement driven by failed proofs.
AI.method: Goedel-Architect first generates a blueprint (dependency graph of formally stated definitions and lemmas with declared dependencies), optionally guided by a natural language proof. A tool-equipped Lean prover component then closes each open lemma node in parallel using relevant dependencies. Failed lemmas drive iterative refinement of the global blueprint.
AI.result: Using DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B), Goedel-Architect achieves 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test and 75.6% on PutnamBench. With NL proof seeding, it reaches 100% on MiniF2F-test, 88.8% (597/672) on PutnamBench, and solves 4/6 IMO 2025, 11/12 Putnam 2025, and 3/6 USAMO 2026 problems.
AI.conclusion: Goedel-Architect achieves state-of-the-art performance for an open-source pipeline at a price point up to 500x less than comparable open-source pipelines, demonstrating the effectiveness of blueprint-based parallel theorem proving with iterative refinement.

title: MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon tasks such as scientific discovery and machine learning engineering (MLE), where sustained self-evolution becomes a key capability. However, existing MLE agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, which together hinder long-horizon optimization. We present MLEvolve, an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework for end-to-end machine learning algorithm discovery. By extending tree search to Progressive MCGS, MLEvolve enables cross-branch information flow through graph-based reference edges and gradually shifts the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation with an entropy-inspired progressive schedule. To allow the agent to evolve with accumulated experience, we introduce Retrospective Memory, which combines a cold-start domain knowledge base with a dynamic global memory for task-specific experience retrieval and reuse. For stable long-horizon iteration, we further decouple strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes. Evaluation on MLE-Bench shows that MLEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple dimensions including average medal rate and valid submission rate under a 12-hour budget (half the standard runtime). Moreover, MLEvolve also outperforms specialized algorithm discovery methods including AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/InternScience/MLEvolve.

AI.tldr: MLEvolve is an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework for machine learning algorithm discovery that uses Progressive MCGS (graph-based tree search with cross-branch information flow), Retrospective Memory (cold-start knowledge base + dynamic global memory), and decoupled strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes. It achieves SOTA on MLE-Bench and outperforms AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing MLE agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, which hinder long-horizon self-evolution in tasks like scientific discovery and ML engineering.
AI.method: 1) Progressive MCGS: extends tree search with graph-based reference edges for cross-branch information flow and entropy-inspired progressive schedule shifting from exploration to exploitation. 2) Retrospective Memory: combines cold-start domain knowledge base with dynamic global memory for experience retrieval/reuse. 3) Decoupled strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes for stable long-horizon iteration.
AI.result: SOTA on MLE-Bench across average medal rate and valid submission rate under 12-hour budget (half standard runtime). Outperforms AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, showing strong cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: MLEvolve effectively addresses key limitations of existing MLE agents through progressive graph-based search, retrospective memory, and hierarchical planning-code decoupling, enabling sustained self-evolution for long-horizon ML algorithm discovery.
